comment: Defects found in this repository's own skills and installer.

bugs.title: The shipped core library lost plan_stat_mode and plan_stat_uid, so an installed skill could not read a file mode
bugs.reproduce: bash planning/scripts/build-plan-libs.sh; grep -c "^plan_stat_mode()" planning/scripts/plan-core-lib.sh
bugs.observed: 0 definitions. Two tests said so: test-portable-helpers.sh reported plan_stat_mode: command not found for three assertions, and test-duplication-ratchet.sh reported it is referenced by MAINTAINER.md section 3 but no longer exists.
bugs.expected: Both helpers present in the compiled library; plan_atomic_write calls plan_stat_mode to preserve a file mode.
bugs.mechanism: The re-marking script kept PACKAGE: DEV on any path matching *probe* -- intended for a planted test fixture named plan_probe_dev_only.sh -- and planning/scripts/lib/core/plan_stat_probe.sh matched on its name. PACKAGE: DEV means dev-build-only, so the prod build excluded it.
bugs.fix: Marked plan_stat_probe.sh PACKAGE: PROD and rebuilt. Every other compiler input was checked for the same mistake; it was the only one.
bugs.verification: test-portable-helpers.sh and test-duplication-ratchet.sh both pass; five stat-helper definitions and calls are back in plan-core-lib.sh. Re-marking the file PACKAGE: DEV reproduces the failure.
bugs.found_by: the both-shell run of the release commit, on both bash 5.3 and 3.2
bugs.notes: A name-substring match standing in for a marker. The marker was right in every file; the script that wrote it guessed from the filename. It also shows the release checks were not sufficient on their own: build-release.sh --list and a by-hand diff of npm pack both passed a library with a function missing, because they compare file sets and not file contents.

bugs.title: test-plan-overview fails on both macOS legs and reports nothing, so the PR is red with no diagnosis
bugs.reproduce: CI run 32726302448 on PR #3 (head f699f84). Both macOS jobs: 96 ran, 95 passed, 1 failed -- test-plan-overview, exit 1. ubuntu-latest passes all 96, and ./verify-both-shells.sh passes 96/96 on bash 5.3 and bash 3.2 on Linux.
bugs.observed: The only output under the FAIL line is the limited-run wrapper's memlimit warnings. No assertion text, no t_end summary, and no sed/awk/grep error anywhere in the full job log.
bugs.expected: Either the test passes on macOS, or it says which assertion failed.
bugs.mechanism: Confirmed by the speaking trap on CI run 32751254496: test-plan-overview.sh line 90 called timeout(9) on render-plan-overview --watch, and macOS does not ship timeout (the B6 class). The watcher died instantly of exit 127, watch.log stayed empty, grep -c exited 1 under pipefail+set -e, and the ERR trap named the exact line — the diagnosis the first half of the fix was built to produce.
bugs.fix: this session — the watch case bounds itself by polling for the second render (no timeout binary); chat/tests/test-chat.sh swaps its one timeout(5) for a read -t loop with the same ceiling; render-plan-overview traps TERM/INT so a stopped watcher exits promptly instead of deferring the signal behind its sleep child
bugs.verification: PR #3 run 32756400447: both macOS legs pass 97/97 with test-plan-overview green on macOS system bash 3.2 and the runner default bash — first macOS pass since the renderer landed. Linux unchanged.
bugs.found_by: CI on PR #3, opened for exactly this reason: 46 commits with 88 files changed had never run on BSD userland, and the branch itself had just made the macOS legs blocking
bugs.notes: Blocking because -ox removed continue-on-error from both macOS legs (T37), so this fails the PR rather than being informational. Diagnose it on a runner, not by reading: stop discarding the setup commands' output first -- capture and print it on failure -- and the cause will name itself. Worth checking the same pattern in the other new tests from this branch, since a setup command redirected to /dev/null hides a BSD failure the same way anywhere it appears. Order of work: make the test able to speak before fixing what it fails on -- capture the setup commands' output and print it on failure -- then push and read the macOS leg rather than reading the code. The same discarded-output pattern is worth checking in the other tests this branch added: test-add-work-unit-staging, test-adversarial-review-mint-order, test-adversarial-review-preamble, test-function-length-ratchet, test-installer-opencode-permissions, test-owned-roster-scaffold, test-verifier-reach-memo and chat/tests/test-chat.sh. And the flag cannot go back: making those legs blocking is what caught this.

bugs.title: The chat tests wait for a 'chat serving:' banner the detached server never prints, so every detached instance times out as not-ready
bugs.reproduce: cd src/chat && cargo build && cd ../.. && h=$(mktemp -d /tmp/t.XXXXX) && ./src/chat/target/debug/chat serve --home "$h" --bind 127.0.0.1 --port 17901 >"$h/serve.log" 2>&1 & sleep 1; case "$(cat "$h/serve.log")" in *"chat serving:"*) echo MATCH;; *) echo 'NO MATCH';; esac
bugs.observed: Prints 'NO MATCH'. The log holds 94 bytes: 'chat serving (detached): tcp 127.0.0.1:17901 pid 1146894 [endpoint given on the command line]'. The server is healthy — it binds, serves and answers clients — but the needle 'chat serving:' cannot occur in it. Both chat suites hang on this: test-chat-binary.sh:94 and test-chat-config.sh:386,417 all wait for that exact substring. test-chat-binary reports 'the server never reported serving on 17811. Its output:' followed by nothing, and test-chat-config reports FAIL (8) — every one of the eight downstream of a server that never became ready.
bugs.expected: The readiness probe recognises a server that is in fact serving, in each of the three banner forms the binary emits.
bugs.mechanism: src/chat/src/main.rs prints three different banners: line 2729 'chat serving: {} ({}), run dir {} [{}]' for the attached case, and lines 2622 and 2632 'chat serving (detached, unregistered): ...' and 'chat serving (detached): ...' for the two detached ones. The tests match the literal 'chat serving:' — with the colon immediately after 'serving' — so only the attached form is recognised, and every detached start reads as never-ready. The tests are the side that is wrong about the contract, but note test-chat-binary.sh:77-84 carries a comment explaining that the readiness probe must never be the thing under test; matching a banner's exact punctuation is the same coupling in a different place.
bugs.fix: Not fixed — every surface was deleted. chat/tests/test-chat-binary.sh, chat/tests/test-chat-config.sh and src/chat/src/main.rs went with 6bba241, "chat: ship two binaries per skill; drop src/chat; rewire CI for the rust workspace". The detached-server readiness handshake the bug is about no longer exists: chat/tests/ holds only test-chat.sh and test-chat-resolution.sh, and neither waits for a banner — readiness is the server writing server.port, which the tests poll for.
bugs.verification: The string "chat serving" now occurs exactly once in the whole of master, inside this BUGS.json entry describing the bug. No live file names it. All three recorded surfaces are absent from master's tree.
bugs.found_by: main session, diagnosing the two red tests that block Phase 1 of the 2.0.0-alpha release
bugs.notes: Filed as urgent/blocking, which distorted the register's priority ordering for as long as it sat open against deleted code. Closing it is the point of the sweep that found it: a stale entry at the top of the queue is worse than no entry, because everything below it is judged relative to it. Found by checking every open entry's surfaces against master rather than by anyone reading the entry.

bugs.title: The release-package gate rejects any prerelease version, so bumping package.json to 2.0.0-alpha turns the suite red
bugs.reproduce: for v in 2.0.0 2.0.0-alpha 2.0.0-alpha.1; do printf '%-16s %s\n' "$v" "$(printf '%s' "$v" | grep -c '^[0-9][0-9.]*[0-9]$')"; done
bugs.observed: 2.0.0 -> 1, 2.0.0-alpha -> 0, 2.0.0-alpha.1 -> 0. tests/test-release-package.sh:37-39 reads the version out of package.json and asserts that count is '1', so any version carrying a prerelease identifier fails 'package.json states a version' and the whole gate goes red.
bugs.expected: The gate accepts the versions the project actually intends to publish, prerelease identifiers included, while still rejecting a missing or malformed one.
bugs.mechanism: The pattern '^[0-9][0-9.]*[0-9]$' was written when every released version was numeric — the tag list is v1.0.0 through v1.4.2, none with a suffix — so nothing had ever exercised a prerelease. It anchors both ends and permits only digits and dots, which excludes the hyphen semver requires for a prerelease. This is a latent gate, not a regression: it has been correct for every version shipped so far and becomes wrong the first time an alpha is cut.
bugs.fix: 9e8ddc1 + 9ee5278 — release-package now validates full SemVer core, prerelease and build metadata forms, including numeric prerelease leading-zero rules and combined prerelease/build cases
bugs.verification: The gate accepts 2.0.0-alpha, 2.0.0-alpha.1, 2.0.0-alpha.1+build.7 and 2.0.0+build.7, while rejecting 2.0, x.y.z, empty, 02.0.0, 2.0.0-, 2.0.0-01 and 2.0.0-alpha..1. The release-package integration test passes from the real-disk worktree; a no-op guard mutation fails its assertions.
bugs.found_by: main session, working out the runbook for tagging 2.0.0-alpha; found before the bump rather than after, so it has never actually gone red

bugs.title: interactive-shell-input named cursor keys are case-sensitive and ignore application cursor mode
bugs.reproduce: Run mc in the wrapper, then submit key up or key UP while mc has enabled application cursor mode.
bugs.observed: Lowercase names were rejected. Uppercase cursor names were acknowledged but sent the normal cursor sequence, which mc rendered as literal input instead of moving the selected row.
bugs.expected: Named keys are discoverable without case assumptions and cursor sequences match the terminal mode requested by the active application.
bugs.mechanism: key_sequence only recognized uppercase names, and the screen parser did not retain the private cursor-mode flag set by applications with DECSET.
bugs.fix: Working tree change — normalize named keys and encode cursor keys as SS3 when application cursor mode is active
bugs.verification: Unit tests cover lowercase named keys and DECSET/DECRST application cursor mode; cargo test --locked passes.
bugs.found_by: fresh agent protocol run, subworker Gauss
bugs.notes: This was the direct blocker for navigating mc's visible file pane.

bugs.title: interactive-shell emits stale or corrupted parent-shell screen state after subprocess exit
bugs.reproduce: Start one wrapper-owned interactive Bash, launch and exit nano or mc, then observe the parent shell after the child lifecycle transition.
bugs.observed: The agent saw stale command fragments interleaved with the restored Bash prompt after nano and mc exited; the wrapper later reported child_exit but emitted a very large burst of buffered screen JSON before that lifecycle event.
bugs.expected: After a subprocess exits, the next observation is a coherent current parent-shell screen, and lifecycle ordering is explicit enough that an agent can distinguish the restored shell from stale child output.
bugs.mechanism: The PTY reader publishes each read as a screen delta while the terminal model processes redraws and alternate-screen restoration incrementally; child exit and buffered PTY bytes are not synchronized into a post-transition snapshot boundary.
bugs.found_by: fresh agent protocol run, subworker Socrates
bugs.notes: The autowrap fix addresses one renderer corruption mechanism but does not yet prove subprocess-transition synchronization is correct.

bugs.title: The registers guard and its test use the banned python3-shipped construct, so the portability gate fails on master
bugs.reproduce: ./planning/tests/test-portability-contract.sh
bugs.observed: portability: ./.github/registers-guard.sh uses banned construct 'python3-shipped' at line 101, and the same for ./.github/tests/test-registers-guard.sh at line 91. test-portability-contract FAILs, and master's ubuntu-latest leg is red with it (run 33873690073).
bugs.expected: The gate passes. python3 in a CI-only tree is either allowlisted for this rule or replaced, but master is not left red.
bugs.mechanism: The guard calls python3 for the duplicate-id check that a textual merge cannot detect, and its own comment argues CODE-STYLE.md permits python3 for development tooling. Assertion 4 of test-portability-contract scans every TRACKED script for a detectable banned construct, and .github/ carries no allowlist row, so that justification was never expressed anywhere the gate can read it. The rule's own replacement text anticipates the case: probe sites, the generated installer tables and dev-only trees carry allowlist rows.
bugs.fix: e34a7485 on fix/master-red-trio (PR #56) -- ./.github/*:python3-shipped joins the dev-only allowlist group the rule's own replacement text provides for
bugs.verification: test-portability-contract PASS. Mutation: a python3 line appended to planning/scripts/plan-env.sh, a SHIPPED file, is still reported, so the row exempts one dev-only tree rather than disabling the rule.
bugs.found_by: master CI run 33873690073, ubuntu-latest leg; reproduced locally

bugs.title: MCP adapter discards the advertised expected_revision argument; every MCP mutation dies with revision_required
bugs.reproduce: echo '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"insert","arguments":{"file":F,"text":"x","offset":0,"expected_revision":0}}}' | ai-text-editor-mcp -> revision_required; same with key 'revision' passes the guard
bugs.observed: Server receives no revision: the adapter only lifts 'revision' into the envelope; expected_revision stays in the payload where the server ignores it. Schema-faithful clients are stripped of 'revision' by validation, so no client configured against the advertised surface can mutate.
bugs.expected: The adapter accepts the key its own tool schemas advertise (or advertises the key it accepts).
bugs.mechanism: call_tool: payload.remove("revision"); the tool inputSchemas (harness-enriched) name expected_revision - two contracts, no overlap.
bugs.fix: 5dbc5da - the adapter lifts expected_revision into the envelope as well as revision
bugs.verification: cli_flow cold/recovery tests; raw tools/call insert with expected_revision now passes the guard against the new build
bugs.found_by: second agent test-drive 2026-09-05, review .Ai-EDITOR-BRUTAL-REVIEW.md

bugs.title: cached endpoint/session reuse has no liveness or generation check: every non-open command wedges after a server restart or idle shutdown
bugs.reproduce: open -f F (autostarts server), kill -9 server, then open -f F -> Connection refused (os error 111); rm the socket -> No such file or directory (os error 2); recovery needs deleting the (identity,file) session cache. Variant: restart the server, then read -f F -> session_unauthorized: the supplied session_token does not belong to a tab on this server, no recovery named.
bugs.observed: Dead-endpoint wedge persists across opens; stale-generation tokens break every non-open verb. The cli_flow killed_server test passes because it never carries a warm cache.
bugs.expected: A connect failure or token refusal on a cached endpoint re-resolves and autostarts (journal replay is already lossless); session_unauthorized names re-open as the fix.
bugs.mechanism: client::resolve forwards the cached endpoint+token without probing pid/generation; the withhold-token rule covers only method==open.
bugs.fix: 5dbc5da - liveness probes on cached and registered endpoints; execute() refreshes a stale tab token against a live server and retries once; session_unauthorized names the recovery
bugs.verification: cli_flow a_restarted_server_reports_the_journal_replay... and a_dead_server_without_a_replacement_fails_with_guidance... pass; repro that needed cache deletion now self-heals
bugs.found_by: second agent test-drive 2026-09-05, review .Ai-EDITOR-BRUTAL-REVIEW.md

bugs.title: MCP adapter discards the string expected_revision its own schema advertises; every schema-following mutation dies with revision_required
bugs.reproduce: printf two raw tools/call undo lines for a live tab against ai-text-editor-mcp over stdio, one with the revision guard as a string and one as a number; the string form refuses, the number succeeds
bugs.observed: revision_required for the string form on the shipped Sep-5 build, while the numeric form applied the undo; identical for replace — drive three could not edit through MCP at all
bugs.expected: a value that follows the published schema satisfies the guard; an unsatisfiable value is refused naming the argument
bugs.mechanism: call_tool removed expected_revision from the payload and hoisted it with as_u64(), which answers None for a JSON string; the guard is typed as string by revision_guard(). A swallowed value and a missing one are the same request to the server
bugs.fix: 3ac9b65 (PR #65, merged 4156c76) — parse_revision_argument accepts numbers and digit-strings, refuses anything else naming the value; call_tool answers unsatisfiable guards as a tool_error
bugs.verification: tests/mcp_flow.rs a_schema_following_string_revision_satisfies_the_guard drives the string form over raw stdio against a live autostarted server; removing the parser reintroduces the refusal. lib.rs unit tests pin the conversion. Runs on every cargo test --workspace leg (both triples).
bugs.found_by: third test drive, 2026-09-06 — the first MCP mutation the drive attempted
bugs.notes: B175 was closed by a test that drove the argument name but not its advertised type; that fix and B195 schema publication landed in different PRs and neither followed the other contract. Lesson for fix verification prose: argument-contract closures need a test that follows the published schema.

bugs.title: replace never checks delete_len against what is actually at the offset, so a stale length silently corrupts the buffer
bugs.reproduce: Fault-injection round trip on one PHP token, reported by the sanitairkamer session: replace(offset, delete_len=35, '=== -1') then replace(offset, delete_len=35, '=== 0'). The second delete_len was correct for the ORIGINAL token, but the first replace had left a 36-character one at that offset.
bugs.observed: The second replace deleted 35 of 36 bytes and left the orphan digit behind: the file silently became '(int) $quote->getItemsCount() === 01'. Valid PHP, wrong logic, no error, no warning, no refusal - only a subsequent read caught it. The response reported success and a new revision.
bugs.expected: A mutation cannot silently destroy content because the caller's length is stale. Two cheap guards were proposed by the reporter, either of which would have caught this: (1) an optional expected_text on replace that the server verifies at the offset BEFORE deleting, refusing by name when it does not match - the same shape as the revision guard, but for content rather than sequence; (2) the response reports the bytes actually deleted, so a caller can see what went. Neither requires line-range addressing.
bugs.mechanism: replace applies delete_len as an unchecked byte count at the given offset. The revision guard proves the DOCUMENT has not moved since the caller last read it, which is why this passed: the caller held a current revision and was still wrong, because its own previous mutation changed the length of the very text it was addressing. Nothing relates delete_len to the content at the offset, so a length that was right one revision ago truncates rather than refusing.
bugs.fix: d616bd30 — replace takes expected_text (or expected_bytes_base64 for non-UTF-8), which expected_span_bytes() reads and the handler verifies against the bytes at the span BEFORE deleting anything, refusing expected_text_mismatch with both what was expected and what is actually there. When expected_text is the only thing naming a length, its own length IS the length, so the arithmetic that got this wrong is not performed at all; a delete_len that disagrees with it is expected_text_length_mismatch. Second half: every replace answer reports the bytes it actually deleted via byte_preview(), so the damage is visible without a read.
bugs.verification: cargo test -p ai-text-editor --test cli_flow: expected_text_refuses_the_double_replace_that_corrupted_a_file replays the corruption exactly — a 35-byte comparison replaced by a 36-byte one, then the same delete_len 35 against 36 bytes with a CURRENT revision — and asserts the second call is refused naming expected_text and the buffer is byte-identical afterwards. It then runs the same call WITHOUT the guard as a control and asserts it still produces 'if (true0) {' with the deleted bytes reported as '(int) $quote->getItemsCount() === 1', so it is the guard that refuses and not some other check, and finally shows the intended edit succeeding with expected_text as the only length. Mutation: delete the 'if let Some(expected) = &expected' verification block and the refusal becomes a success, leaving the orphan digit — the test fails on both the exit status and the buffer.
bugs.found_by: sanitairkamer session 2026-09-07, hit during its own fault-injection round trip; relayed on the chat bus
bugs.notes: B226 is the addressing gap this arose from - having to recompute a byte length after every mutation is what made the stale length possible. The two are not the same fix and both are wanted: line-range or match-pair addressing removes the arithmetic, an expected_text guard catches a wrong span however it was computed.

bugs.title: folding the nick into the session key makes a saved session unreachable to any call that omits --nick
bugs.reproduce: On feat/chat-mcp-and-session-keys (PR 75), against a private server: AI_CHAT_HOME=$H chat-client-rs session set --server 127.0.0.1:$PORT --nick solo; then AI_CHAT_HOME=$H chat-client-rs send --chan "#q3" --text "no nick on this call". Same two commands with the master client as a control.
bugs.observed: PR 75: "chat-client-rs: send needs --server --nick --chan --text (or a saved session)" -- the session it just wrote is not found. Master: ":solo!solo@localhost PRIVMSG #q3 :no nick on this call". session show with no --nick likewise opens a different, empty file (h-398375cf47245be6) from the one session set wrote (h-80c958639a2070e6 for --nick parent).
bugs.expected: A saved session is what removes the need to repeat --server and --nick on every call, so a call that omits --nick finds the session that was set.
bugs.mechanism: resolve_session_key now appends "nick=" plus the nick to the harness and worktree material, and the nick comes from argv. A call that passes no --nick hashes an empty nick, which is a different key, so it opens a different file. session set stores under the nick-bearing key and every later call without --nick looks under the empty-nick one.
bugs.fix: 1267ac11 on feat/chat-mcp-and-session-keys (PR 75) - the key is h-<identity>-<nick>, so the identity half is a stable prefix and a nick-less call can find the single session its identity owns.
bugs.verification: session set --nick solo then session show with no --nick reports that session's server and nick, where before it reported an empty one. Two nicks still resolve to separate files (B271 holds) and an ambiguous identity resolves to neither. Four tests, one pinning the key SHAPE so the suffix cannot quietly go back to being hashed in.
bugs.found_by: t90-chat-mcp, verifying B271's fix at Michael's request before PR 75 merges
bugs.notes: B271 (the defect this change fixes) is genuinely fixed by it: under one CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID, --nick parent and --nick child resolve to h-80c958639a2070e6 and h-15ab5ff6b3eaee04 on PR 75 and to one key h-011bc5c0e5b7b760 on master, and a child join no longer consumes the parent unread message. The regression is the other half of the same rung: the nick is now required material and the ladder has no way to supply it from the session it is trying to open. A fix has to resolve the nick before the key -- read the saved nick from a nick-free location, or key the file on the harness id and hold per-nick state inside it. Found by t90-chat-mcp against PR 75 before it merged, which is the point of reviewing a branch rather than a release. chat/tests/test-chat.sh already covers this shape -- it sets a nick then uses send and show without one -- so the suite would have caught it; that test is currently failing on the branch for an unrelated reason (measured identically with the fix, without it, and with the pre-nick-keying client), which is the live-bus interference family B270 and B274.

bugs.title: send advances the channel cursor to the channel maximum, so it marks everyone else's unread messages as seen
bugs.reproduce: Two agents on one channel. Agent A reads to its cursor. Agent B posts. Agent A sends anything to that channel, then reads: chat-client-rs send --chan "#ops" --text "anything"; chat-client-rs read --chan "#ops".
bugs.observed: B's message is never returned by A's read. A's session cursor jumped to the channel's highest id at send time. Observed live on #ai-skills: Tschallacka posted an instruction with no @mention, this agent sent an unrelated message, and the instruction was never returned by any later read while sitting in the agent's own tail log.
bugs.expected: Sending marks nothing read that the sender has not been shown. A cursor is what the agent has SEEN, and posting is not reading.
bugs.mechanism: send (src/chat-client-rs/src/lib.rs:1277-1306) issues FETCH <chan> 0, walks every row to take the maximum id, and calls save_cursor with it. The intent is to record the id of the message just stored, which the IRC-form echo does not carry; the effect is to record the id of the LAST message in the channel, whoever wrote it. Everything another agent posted since the sender last read is skipped permanently, because read only ever returns rows after the cursor. src/chat-mcp/src/conn.rs send() takes the same maximum from LASTID and has the same effect.
bugs.found_by: t90-chat-mcp: an instruction from Tschallacka went unread because this agent sent a message after it arrived
bugs.notes: The loss is silent in both directions: the sender sees no gap, and the writer of the skipped message sees a delivered line. It is worse for an instruction with no @mention, which the mention guard also does not wake on, so nothing else compensates. A fix has to separate "what I have seen" from "what exists": either send leaves the cursor alone and read tolerates returning the senders own message, or send records only the ids it authored. B269 is the neighbouring cursor defect on the read side. Duplicate of B254, filed earlier the same day for the same defect. B254 carries the mechanism and now this entry's evidence and severity; keeping both would split one defect across two ids.

bugs.title: Declaring chat's runtimes puts python3 into the generated install.sh, which the python3-shipped gate bans
bugs.reproduce: bash planning/tests/test-portability-contract.sh   # at fa1bd62
bugs.observed: portability: ./install.sh uses banned construct 'python3-shipped' at line 417 -- see PORTABILITY.md. install.sh:417 is the generated members table: @server-runtimes) case "$platform" in *:*) printf '%s\n' python3 node perl socat ;; esac ;;
bugs.expected: Either declaring an optional runtime is allowed, or the gate says why it is not, but the suite is not red for doing the thing T39 asked for.
bugs.mechanism: e6492f6 declared the any-of group in chat/requires.tsv, and installer/build.sh generates the requirement tables into install.sh, so the literal python3 now appears in the shipped installer. The portability gate scans every tracked *.sh including the generated install.sh, and its allowlist exempts only ./chat/scripts/chat-server.sh and ./chat/tests/test-chat.sh. So the declaration the brief asked for is exactly what trips the rule.
bugs.fix: 4befd4e — exact-file allowlist row ./install.sh:python3-shipped in test-portability-contract: the generated tables NAME optional runtimes to verify and hint them, which is not requiring one; strength still decides
bugs.verification: test-portability-contract passes on both legs; removing the row restores both findings. The rule-vs-gate question itself stays open as T40.
bugs.found_by: the 5-minute watch: CI run 32728982657 showed ubuntu failing two tests rather than the one already recorded, and it reproduces locally
bugs.notes: This is T40 arriving as a blocker rather than a discussion. Do not reach for an allowlist row on install.sh: that file is generated from every skill's requires.tsv, so exempting it turns the rule off for anything any skill ever declares. The rule text is what is wrong -- it is named python3-shipped and it means do not depend on python3, while what it detects is the word appearing in a shell file. Naming an optional runtime in a fallback chain is not depending on it. Options, cheapest first: narrow the detect so it matches an invocation rather than the bare word; or scope the rule to hard requirements and let a soft or grouped declaration through; or rescope it to shipped runtime code, which is the case it was written for and which no *.sh scan can see anyway (chat/runtime/server.py has always been invisible to it).

bugs.title: A goal with no bare work-unit ids in its roster aborts validate-plan, which exits 1 with no verdict
bugs.reproduce: cp -R .plans/harden-test-reporting-and-plan-dir /tmp/rost/plan; g=/tmp/rost/plan/01-plan-dir-synonym/goal.md; grep -v '^`W[0-9]' "$g" > "$g.n" && mv "$g.n" "$g"; bash planning/scripts/validate-plan.sh /tmp/rost/plan; echo "exit $?"
bugs.observed: exit 1 with four FAIL lines and no summary at all -- no "Plan validation failed with N error(s)." and no "passed" line. bash -x ends: printf '%s\n%s\n' '' '' / grep -E '^W[0-9][0-9]+$' / sort -u / tr, then roster_ids= followed immediately by plan_validate_cleanup, which is the EXIT trap rather than the next pass.
bugs.expected: A goal whose roster names no unit is a finding or a warning, and the run still reports its verdict.
bugs.mechanism: validate-plan-propagation-lib.sh:347 assigns from a pipeline: roster_ids="$(printf ... | grep -E '^W[0-9][0-9]+$' | sort -u | tr '\n' ' ')". With both awk passes empty the printf emits two blank lines, grep matches nothing and exits 1, pipefail makes that the pipeline's status, the assignment inherits it, and set -e aborts the script -- before the summary and before every later pass. The reporter saw the WARN-only variant, which is the same abort in a plan whose earlier passes had produced no FAIL lines; the missing summary is the signature either way.
bugs.fix: this session — the roster_ids pipeline guards its grep with || true inside a brace group, the same escape every sibling assignment in the file already uses; an empty match is an answer, not an error

bugs.title: subagent worktrees are reused for new tasks, so a fresh worker inherits the previous task's stale base commit
bugs.reproduce: Launch any subagent with isolation: worktree, then in its worktree run: git log --oneline -1; git rev-list --count HEAD..origin/refactor/portability-and-installer-ox
bugs.observed: Two subagents launched within one hour on 2026-08-28 both started behind the branch tip: the webview worker by 354 commits, based on de02b9f — a tree where planning/scripts/overview-*.sh and planning/templates/ do not exist at all — and the chatfix worker by 352. Both reported it themselves and reset to the tip before reading anything. T35 records the same defect and is marked done.
bugs.expected: A worktree created for a subagent starts at the commit the launching session is on, so the worker sees the files it was sent to change.
bugs.mechanism: Established by Tschallacka, who knows the harness: old worktrees are REUSED for new tasks rather than created fresh. A worktree left behind by a finished subagent is handed to the next one, so the new agent inherits whatever commit the previous task stopped at — which is why the three today started 354, 352 and 358 commits behind rather than at the tip, and why the distances differed. My entry recorded 'Not established here' and guessed at creation; the defect is in what happens at the END of a task, not the beginning. A worktree that is cleaned up after its merge cannot be inherited stale by anyone.
bugs.fix: git-worktrees/SKILL.md § Merging the work back: removal is stated as the task's last step, covering the no-merge case (abandoned work, a checkout only ever used to look at something) as well as the merged one, with the reuse consequence spelled out as the reason; docs/README.md carries the short form. Applied to this session's six worktrees, all confirmed clean and 0 commits ahead of HEAD before removal, and their five orphaned worktree-agent-* branches deleted.
bugs.verification: Partial, and stated as such. Verified: 'git worktree list' now returns one line, the main checkout, so there is no worktree left for a next task to inherit; all six removals were preceded by a dirty/untracked count of 0 and 'git rev-list --count HEAD..<branch>' of 0, so nothing was discarded. NOT yet verified: that a subagent launched with isolation: worktree now starts at the tip. That observation needs a real launch and is the mutation that would fail without the fix — the next subagent this repo launches supplies it, and B77 stays confirmed until it does.
bugs.found_by: main session, from two independent subagent reports in one hour; both workers only noticed because their briefs told them to check
bugs.notes: Third occurrence the same day: the plancrypt worker started 358 commits behind and reset to 9be8d1a. That is three of three subagent worktrees launched in this session — webview 354 behind, chatfix 352, plancrypt 358 — so the failure rate is not intermittent, it is universal. All three caught it only because their briefs carried an explicit instruction to check the base commit, which means the current mitigation is a sentence I have to remember to write into every brief. A worker launched without it reads a tree that predates the feature it was sent to change. The fix follows from the mechanism: when a subagent finishes and its worktree has no other purpose, remove it once its branch is merged — if a merge applies at all. That closes the reuse path at the point where the worktree becomes garbage, rather than trying to detect staleness at the point where it is handed out. Cleaning up is also the cheaper half: a stale-base check has to run in every brief and be remembered by every author, while a removal happens once, by whoever did the merge and is already looking at the branch. The title carried the disproven cause ('still created from a stale commit') and was corrected in place, since bug-update.sh has no --title; register-rebuild.sh bugs reports the file stamped, sorted and sound afterwards.

bugs.title: send advances the read cursor to the channel's newest id, so messages that arrived while you were not looking are marked seen
bugs.reproduce: As nick A: have another nick post two messages. Then, without reading them, run chat-client-rs send --chan '#c' --nick A --text hi, and then chat-client-rs read --chan '#c' --nick A.
bugs.observed: The read returns nothing. The two messages were never shown to A and are already behind its cursor. Observed live on 2026-09-07: a peer agent posted a report, my own send moved the cursor past it, and the follow-up read correctly reported nothing new - so the report was only recoverable from a background tail's captured output.
bugs.expected: A send moves the SENT message's id into the cursor at most, or leaves the read cursor alone entirely. Sending is not reading, and it must not mark another nick's message as seen. The two operations share one cursor today and only one of them shows the caller anything.
bugs.mechanism: send issues FETCH <chan> 0, takes the channel's HIGHEST id from the reply and saves that as this agent's cursor (src/chat-client-rs/src/lib.rs, the FETCH block at the end of send). The id it saves is the channel maximum, not the id of the message just sent, so every send marks everything any peer posted since the last read as already seen. src/chat-mcp copies the pattern, so the adapter loses messages the same way.
bugs.found_by: hit twice in one session while coordinating with a peer agent on the bus, 2026-09-07
bugs.notes:
Rediscovered independently by t90-chat-mcp and filed as B288, now closed as a duplicate of this entry. Its evidence is stronger than the original and is the reason this is now blocking rather than major: an instruction from Tschallacka in #ai-skills was never read, because the agent sent a message after it arrived. The line sat in that agent's tail log the whole time and was permanently invisible to read.

The loss is silent in both directions -- the sender sees no gap and the writer sees a delivered line -- and it is worst for an instruction carrying no mention, which the wake guard also does not fire on. Two independent mechanisms have to fail for a message to be seen, and this defeats the one that was meant to be reliable. Attempted and reverted by aiskills, with what the attempt learned.

The fix itself is one line of deletion -- send simply stops saving a cursor, because a watermark over a shared channel cannot skip your own id without skipping the ids that interleave with it. But TWO tests encode the current behaviour, not one: chat/tests/test-chat.sh asserts the cursor advances to 2 after a send, and the per-agent isolation case uses a send to advance agent-a's #isoc cursor and asserts the result. A behaviour the suite states twice is a decision somebody made, so changing it is a decision, not a repair, and it does not belong inside an unrelated PR.

What the fix needs before it lands: a ruling on whether a send advances the reader's cursor at all. If it does not, both assertions change and a caller sees its own message in its next read -- which the local echo already printed, so the cost is a duplicate line rather than lost information. Recommended, because the alternative is what this entry records: losing a peer's message silently. SEVERITY: this entry should read blocking, not major. aiskills ran `bugs update B254 --severity blocking`, the tool reported success and dropped the field (B289). Left as filed rather than hand-editing BUGS.json, since a hand-written register is what check exists to detect. Read this as blocking until B289 is fixed and the field can be set. T107 (commit 8e4b52e0) removes the structural cause on unix: with the tail owning the connection there is exactly one process that can write the channel cursor, so a sender and a reader can no longer disagree about it. Not closed from here -- that is a claim about this entry's own reproduction, which needs running, and the Windows arm still has two writers (T111).

bugs.title: a presence tail makes every later send appear under a suffixed nick
bugs.reproduce: Hold the channel with a presence tail as nick N, then run: chat-client-rs send --chan "#ai-skills" --nick N --text hello
bugs.observed: The message arrives from N-2. Measured in #ai-skills: aiskills messages arrived as aiskills-2 and t90-chat-mcp as t90-chat-mcp-2, in both cases while their presence tail held the plain nick.
bugs.expected: A message sent under a nick is attributed to that nick. Who said a thing is the one piece of a chat message that cannot be reconstructed later.
bugs.mechanism: send opens its own short-lived connection, and the server suffixes a nick already held by another connection (B263). The two-part posture chat/SKILL.md now teaches guarantees the collision on every send, because the presence tail is holding the plain nick by design. B263 recorded the suffixing; this is the consequence the posture makes unavoidable rather than incidental.
bugs.fix: 8e4b52e0 (T107, PR 78) -- a running tail owns the session's one connection and serves send/read/names/join/leave over a control socket, so the server never sees the second registration that produced the suffix. Fixed at the client, per the ruling; the server still suffixes, which stays B263's question.
bugs.verification: chat/tests/test-chat-owner-socket.sh asserts from the CHANNEL LOG, not the sender's output: with a tail holding nick 'owner', a forwarded send arrives from 'owner'. Its mutation is permanent and in the same test -- the same send made with --no-session, which is documented to bypass the socket, still arrives from 'owner-2'. So the assertion cannot pass on a build that merely stopped suffixing, and it fails on any build where forwarding stops working. Both legs verified under the bash 3.2 floor as well.
bugs.found_by: aiskills, noticing its own messages arriving as aiskills-2 while holding a presence tail
bugs.notes:
Michael, on seeing aiskills-2 in the channel: 'why the -2 on sends... thats not how i envisioned it.' So the suffix is contrary to intent, not a tolerable side effect of the posture -- raised to urgent on that.

Two candidate fixes, and they are different bugs underneath:
(a) the CLIENT should not open a second connection for a send when it already holds one. That is the real shape: a presence tail is a live connection, and send/read/names each open another. Reusing the held connection removes the collision at the source and is what makes the posture coherent.
(b) the SERVER should not silently rename a connection. Suffixing is a guess at what the caller wanted; refusing the duplicate, or letting a nick be held by several connections of the same owner, are both more honest. B263 records the suffixing itself.

(a) is the one that fixes what Michael saw. (b) is worth deciding separately, because the suffix will keep surprising whoever hits it next. Michael, sharpening it: 'it also makes the guard hard as the send is targetted and not the tail.' The suffix SPLITS one agent's identity across two names. The presence tail holds the plain nick, which is the name a mention has to use for the guard to fire; the sends carry the suffixed nick, which is the name a peer reads and naturally replies to. So a reply addressed to what someone actually saw in the channel goes to a nick nobody is listening on, and the guard never fires.

That is worse than misattribution and is why this is now blocking rather than major: the channel looks like it is working from both ends while a reply can be silently unreachable. It also means a wider guard alternation cannot rescue it -- matching the suffixed form too would make an agent wake on its own sends, which is the self-wake fault t90 found in the step-1 example. SEVERITY: this entry should read blocking, not major, for the same reason as B254 -- `bugs update --severity` reported success and changed nothing (B289). Read it as blocking. RULING (Tschallacka, 2026-09-08): reading and sending use the same client session. The client routes a send through the live tail when one is open, and the tail replies with what the wire said. Fixed at the client, not by asking the server to stop renaming -- one owner means the server never sees the second connection that triggers the suffix. Design and in-repo precedents in T107.
