bugs.title: The bug-report skill's documented validation snippet uses IN/1, which rjq cannot parse, so it prints "BUGS.json is sound" for any file
bugs.reproduce:
echo '{}' | rjq 'if ("a" | IN("a","b")) then "yes" else "no" end'
# then run the Validating the file snippet from bug-report/SKILL.md with rjq in place of jq, against any BUGS.json
bugs.observed: rjq exits 5 with [(File { code: ... }, [("IN", Filter(1))])] and writes nothing to stdout. Every caller treats that empty stdout as the sound case. Measured against a register carrying a duplicate id and two invalid statuses: pre-push-check.sh printed "ok BUGS.json parses, ids unique, statuses known" and found nothing. jq on the same expression returns the three findings. The shipped reg_findings helper, on the same file, reports all of them.
bugs.expected: Either the snippet runs under rjq, or a runtime that cannot evaluate it fails loudly instead of reporting the register sound.
bugs.mechanism: rjq is jaq-based and jaq does not define jq's IN/1 builtin. The snippet uses it four times (parent existence, status, severity, priority). Command substitution discards the parse error to stderr and yields an empty string, and the snippet's success test is emptiness of that string -- so a runtime failure and a clean register are indistinguishable. The skill's own note that `jq -e` is wrong here because it exits 4 on empty output shows the empty-means-sound convention was deliberate; it just has no guard for the command not having run.
bugs.fix: pre-push-check.sh section 5 deletes its own copy and delegates to reg_findings, and a check that cannot run is now a failure rather than silence. bug-report/SKILL.md and todo/SKILL.md express the same rules with index(...) instead of IN/1, bind each entry with `as $e` first, and test the command status before trusting empty output.
bugs.verification: Both snippets extracted verbatim from their SKILL.md and run under rjq against copies: the real BUGS.json and TODO.json report sound (exit 0), and a register carrying a duplicate id, a dangling parent and invalid status/severity/priority yields all five findings. Before the fix the same expressions exited 5 with empty stdout, which every caller read as sound. The pre-push half was mutation-tested separately: a duplicate id in BUGS.json now yields "BUGS.json: duplicate ids" where the old check printed "ok ... ids unique, statuses known". The mutation that fails without the fix is restoring IN/1: rjq exits 5, and the added status guard turns that into an explicit failure instead of a false pass -- which is how the first attempt at this fix was caught, since `A | index(B)` evaluates B against A and a bare index(.status) dies with "cannot index".
bugs.found_by: running the skill's own validation after adding B115 and B116; it reported sound while rjq was erroring
bugs.notes: Found in bug-report/SKILL.md while validating B115 and B116, then found live in pre-push-check.sh, which carried its own jq-flavoured copy behind 2>/dev/null and || true. That gate had never fired on any machine using rjq -- which is every machine following the register contract, since reg_require_jq refuses with 69 without it. Held at blocking for that reason: a gate that always passes is worse than no gate, and this one runs before every push. All three surfaces are now fixed. The durable lesson is the shape rather than the builtin: empty output means sound ONLY if the command ran, so any check of this form has to test the status too. Went unnoticed because a passing gate looks identical either way. Since the fix, feature/ship-register-helpers replaced both documented snippets with `bugs check` and `todo check`, so bug-report/SKILL.md and todo/SKILL.md no longer carry an rjq expression to get wrong. The index(...) form and the status guard survive where they still run: reg_findings in planning/scripts/register-lib.sh, which pre-push-check.sh section 5 delegates to, and the two SKILL.md files now point at that oracle and restate why IN/1 cannot be used in it.

bugs.title: register-resolve.sh reads index stage 1 as the merge base, so during a rebase it reports no collisions and advises taking one side whole
bugs.reproduce: On a branch whose BUGS.json commits precede a commit that renumbers them, run: git rebase origin/master; resolve each earlier BUGS.json conflict with 'git checkout --ours -- BUGS.json && git add BUGS.json && git rebase --continue'; then at the renumbering commit run ./planning/scripts/register-resolve.sh BUGS.json
bugs.observed: 'register-resolve: no id collisions between the two sides; the conflict is textual only.' followed by 'take either side and re-run: git checkout --theirs -- BUGS.json', while B119 and B120 existed on BOTH sides as different entries (master: rjq-less PATH refill / pre-push per-file test runs; branch: META-LEFT omission / raw hex panic). Taking theirs as advised would have dropped master's two entries entirely.
bugs.expected: Either both collisions are reported so each gets a decision, or the tool refuses to advise because index stage 1 is not the merge base of the two sides it is comparing.
bugs.mechanism: The merge base is taken from index stage 1. That is the merge base only for 'git merge'. During a rebase, stage 1 is the parent of the commit being replayed -- a commit on the branch's own history -- so an entry the OTHER side added independently appears in the base already and reads as a modification rather than an addition. The both-sides-added test therefore never fires, and the two-sided-addition case it exists to catch is reported as textual.
bugs.fix: PR #67 (d91bb46): register-resolve.sh computes merge-base(HEAD, orig-head) from rebase-merge/rebase-apply state as the base during a rebase instead of index stage 1, and names the substitution on stderr
bugs.verification: Reproduced on 441d42d before the fix: mid-rebase second stop answered "no id collisions between the two sides; the conflict is textual only" while B50 held two unrelated entries. test-register-resolve.sh gains a rebase fixture plus merge control. Mutation named: reverting the base-selection hunk (the rebase-state branch that replaces ":1:" with merge-base(HEAD,orig-head)) fails the eight rebase assertions with the textual-only advice; the merge control passes both ways. Verified fixed on b0895a5; pre-push-check green with the npm baseline row.
bugs.found_by: pr13-rescue, rebasing PR #31 onto master 16c8c06
bugs.notes: Peer of B151: both are register-resolve.sh assuming a merge where a rebase is the other half of the same workflow. B151 is the refusal's guidance naming no available action; this one is the silent wrong answer, and it is the dangerous half -- the tool exists to stop a register merge losing bug states, and here it advises exactly that. Workaround used on pr13-rescue: install the real merge base as stage 1 before running it, with 'git show $(git merge-base origin/master <branch-tip>):BUGS.json | git hash-object -w --stdin' and 'git update-index --index-info'. With that stage 1 in place it found both collisions immediately. Went unnoticed because every test and every use so far has been a merge, where stage 1 is the merge base by definition.

bugs.title: The protocol tests connect by absolute path, so a long TMPDIR overruns sun_path and every socket test fails
bugs.reproduce: pad=$(mktemp -d); while [ ${#pad} -lt 72 ]; do pad="$pad/p"; mkdir -p "$pad"; done; TMPDIR=$pad cargo test -p interactive-shell --test protocol
bugs.observed: 8 passed; 11 failed in 30.26s, where a short TMPDIR gives 19 passed in 1.05s. Every failure reads 'socket did not appear at <110-byte path> within 30s' with 'wrapper stderr: (empty)'. A probe inside the loop printed exists=true beside 'path must be shorter than SUN_LEN', and ls showed 'srw------- socket' in that very directory during the poll.
bugs.expected: 19 passed, as with a short TMPDIR. The socket is present and connectable by name; only the absolute address is too long.
bugs.mechanism: request() and request_all() polled UnixStream::connect(dir.join("socket")). sun_path caps a Unix socket address at 104 bytes; on macOS TMPDIR is a per-user /var/folders/<2>/<28>/T/ path, run-tests.sh adds a scratch directory and each test names its own, so the address reaches about 110. The library already answers this with connect_in_directory, whose pair is bind_in_directory, and its doc comment states both ends must be relative or the shorter one just moves the failure. The tests were the third end of that rule.
bugs.fix: 14e8f5e1 -- both loops connect through interactive_shell_core::connect_in_directory, guarded by a CWD_LOCK because fchdir is process-global while this binary runs 19 tests as threads
bugs.verification: 19/19 protocol plus 19/19 library unit tests under both a short and a 74-byte TMPDIR, three parallel runs each, still 1.05s. Mutation: restoring the absolute connect fails under the long TMPDIR and reports 'last connect error: path must be shorter than SUN_LEN'. Second mutation: dropping CWD_LOCK fails 3 runs of 3 with 'Connection reset by peer' and passes with --test-threads=1.
bugs.found_by: CI, both macOS legs of run 33871455553; reproduced on Linux by padding TMPDIR alone
bugs.notes: B167 is the other half: the loop discarded the connect error and the panic blamed a missing socket, which is why the cause was looked for in the wrapper across three sessions. Fixing either leaves the other open.

bugs.title: ai-text-editor read ignores --range-start-line and --range-end-line, returning the whole file
bugs.reproduce: bin/<triple>/ai-text-editor-server start --file FILE & then: bin/<triple>/ai-text-editor open --file FILE --save-session-token T; bin/<triple>/ai-text-editor read --session-token T --range-start-line 60 --range-end-line 64
bugs.observed: The entire file comes back. Measured on a 296-line, 12787-byte file: the reply carried byte_count 13257 and the whole document in one JSON string, with "complete": true, no warning and no error. Identical with --presentation text and with the default structured presentation.
bugs.expected: Only lines 60 to 64, or a refusal naming the unsupported flag. A bounded read that silently returns everything is worse than one that refuses.
bugs.mechanism: Established in source: the CLI and MCP map --range-start-line/--range-end-line into every command's payload (bin/ai-text-editor.rs flag table), but no read path consumed those keys — only search did. read returned the whole document regardless.
bugs.fix: PR #61 (c1876f1; pre-rebase b49e4cd) - reads honour inclusive line windows on text tabs and half-open byte windows on raw, hex, and large tabs; bounds a tab cannot honour are refused with the flag named
bugs.verification: BUGS.json repro on a 296-line file returns exactly lines 60-64 over CLI, adapter, and large-tab paths; read_range_incomplete, read_range_conflict, read_range_invalid, read_range_unsupported refusals observed; tests/cli_flow.rs adds bounded_text_reads_honour_their_line_range_and_refuse_the_impossible and raw_reads_honour_a_half_open_byte_window_and_refuse_line_ranges — removing the fix fails both
bugs.found_by: using the skill for a real edit on 2026-09-04; the call spent about 7000 tokens of an agent's context returning a file it had asked five lines of

bugs.title: The skill delivery path substitutes positional parameters inside a skill body, including in fenced code blocks
bugs.reproduce: Put a shell positional parameter in a SKILL.md code block (chat/SKILL.md before 993217ae had awk index of the whole-line variable), then invoke that skill with arguments: Skill(skill: chat, args: "inspect the step-1 guard as rendered")
bugs.observed: The rendered body came back reading index(inspect, me), and the prose sentence naming the token read "The whole-line variable is inspect, spelled exactly that." The file on disk was unchanged. The substituted word was the FIRST WORD OF THE INVOCATION ARGUMENTS in all three observed cases: flowchart saw re-read, loki saw Arm, this session saw inspect.
bugs.expected: A skill body is delivered verbatim. Nothing inside a fenced code block is expanded, since a code block is by definition text the reader must receive exactly.
bugs.mechanism: Positional-parameter expansion is applied to the skill body when the skill is rendered into an agent context, and it is not suppressed inside fences. Named variables are unaffected: $NICK and $LOG survived intact in the same block, so the substitution is positional-only.
bugs.found_by: loki on the bus, from the observation that the EXPLANATORY PROSE was corrupted too; confirmed here by invoking the skill and matching the substituted word to this session's own first argument
bugs.notes:
NOT this repository's defect to fix -- the renderer is Claude Code's -- but it IS this repository's exposure, so the entry stays here and the mitigation is ours: no shipped skill body may contain a positional parameter, enforced by planning/tests/test-skill-positional-params.sh. chat/SKILL.md was the only one of 14 that had ever been exposed; the guard now uses grep, which needs none.

Why this is filed blocking rather than major even though it is upstream: it fails SILENTLY and self-justifyingly. The corrupted guard woke nobody while the agent stayed visibly present in the channel list, and the paragraph explaining the token was substituted in the same slot -- so the explanation corroborated the corruption. Two agents concluded the shipped file was broken and one concluded it had armed the guard wrong; nobody could reach the truth by reading, which is the only method available to a reader of a skill.

Reported to Anthropic through the feedback channel as well, since no fix here can stop the next skill from tripping over it.

bugs.title: A test that waits on a process it has just reported as stuck hangs instead of failing
bugs.reproduce: Make tail --mentions --mention-exit not fire (e.g. run chat/tests/test-chat.sh against a client where the mention never arrives). The test detects it, calls t_fail, and then reaches: wait "$ment_pid"
bugs.observed: The failure is printed and the script then blocks forever on the wait. Under CI this consumed three test-suite legs for over three hours each on one pull request, with no output, no exit code and no test name to identify it -- the only symptom was the absence of a result.
bugs.expected: A detected failure exits as a failure. A test may wait on a process it has killed; it must not wait on one it has just declared stuck.
bugs.mechanism: The guard and the wait disagree: the loop above bounds how long it waits for the tail to exit and reports if it did not, but the unconditional `wait` that follows has no bound and no preceding kill, so the reported-stuck process is waited on anyway. A hang is strictly worse than the failure it replaces, because the failure names itself and the hang does not.
bugs.fix: both waits now kill first: chat/tests/test-chat.sh (the mention tail) and chat/tests/test-chat-owner-socket.sh (the leave-stops-the-tail assertion, which had the same shape)
bugs.verification: test-chat.sh reached the failing assertion and exited 1 in seconds instead of hanging; with the accompanying B302 fix it exits 0. Every other wait in the chat suite was audited and each is already preceded by a kill (lines 174, 480, 646).
bugs.found_by: tracing the three-hour CI hang on PR 78 to its last executed line, which was the wait
bugs.notes: Cross-reference: B302 is the reason the mention failed; this entry is the reason the failure became a hang. Fixing either alone leaves the other -- with only B302 fixed the landmine stays armed for the next stuck process, and with only B301 fixed the test fails honestly but still fails.

bugs.title: run_cargo_one interpolated an empty wrapper, so CI ran no Rust test at all
bugs.reproduce: GITHUB_ACTIONS=1 ./run-tests.sh   (any host; the wrapper skip fires only when that variable is set)
bugs.observed:
run_one was changed to build its command as a list so that an absent layer contributes no word, because the CI skip sets wrapper to the empty string. Its sibling run_cargo_one, which runs each discovered crate, was left interpolating "$wrapper" directly and so passed an empty word as the command name.

Measured on PR 78: every one of the 86 discovered crates failed identically on all three legs, before cargo was reached.

    cargo-add-adversarial-finding    FAIL (exit 127)
        ./run-tests.sh: line 368: : command not found

The shape of the evidence is what makes it a code defect rather than an environment one: GITHUB_ACTIONS is set the same on every hosted runner, the entire shell half passed before the cargo block began, and the failing count was identical on ubuntu, macOS and the bash 3.2 floor.

Two things kept it invisible until CI. The wrapper is only dropped when GITHUB_ACTIONS is set, so no local run reaches the branch; and pre-push-check runs cargo directly rather than through run-tests.sh, so the gate that would have caught it never executes that line.

Worth recording beyond the fix: the defect was introduced by a change whose whole purpose was to make a hang report itself, and it was found in minutes precisely because the run failed loudly with a named test instead of hanging. The same commit that carried the bug carried the thing that surfaced it.
bugs.expected: Each crate runs its tests. An optional layer that is switched off contributes no word to the command.
bugs.mechanism: With wrapper empty, "$wrapper" 2G 400 -- cargo test expands to an empty first word, which the shell attempts to execute and reports as command not found, exit 127. run_one had already been converted to an argv array for exactly this reason; run_cargo_one had not.
bugs.fix: ed1f0e8e - run_cargo_one builds the same argv list as run_one, and reports through report_one so an overrunning cargo test is a TIMEOUT rather than a FAIL
bugs.verification: Both forms exercised locally with wrapper empty: the old interpolation exits 127, which is the CI failure exactly, and the list form exits 0. shellcheck and bash -n pass, and the guarded line is present in the shipped function.
bugs.found_by: a sonnet subagent reading the CI job logs, asked to name the failing step and quote the error verbatim

bugs.title: BSD awk rejects a newline inside a string, so a table cell breaks plan-content on macOS
bugs.reproduce: CI run 32394476430, job "Test suite passes on macos-latest": planning/tests/test-plan-commands.sh
bugs.observed: awk: newline in string | A | B |  — then the test failed (exit 64).
bugs.expected: The row is written as it is under GNU awk.
bugs.mechanism: plan_replace_paragraph passed the replacement text to awk with -v. A newline inside a -v assignment is what one-true-awk refuses outright, and GNU awk accepts, so a multi-paragraph or multi-line cell broke the write on macOS only.
bugs.fix: 9f41091 (codex): plan_replace_paragraph writes the replacement to a temp file and reads it in awk BEGIN instead of passing it with -v. Undocumented at the time -- attributed here by matching the change against the failure.
bugs.verification: CI run 32474258670 at a8d1285: both macOS legs pass, including test-plan-commands, which is the test that failed with "awk: newline in string" at run 32394476430. That is the first green BSD userland this branch has had. Confirmed again by run 32476867183, so the first green was not a one-off.
bugs.found_by: the macOS leg of CI, the first execution of this code on BSD userland
bugs.notes: Cannot be reproduced on this machine: it needs BSD awk. Diagnose from the CI log or a macOS runner, not by guessing here.

bugs.title: A plans-root path comparison fails on macOS, where TMPDIR carries a trailing slash and /var is a symlink
bugs.reproduce: CI run 32394476430, macos-latest: planning/tests/test-plan-env.sh line 50
bugs.observed: assertion failed: grep -Fqx "demo-plan|$plan_root/plan-description.md|$plan_root/steps". The log shows paths like /var/folders/.../T//ai-skills-tests.XmQi3B — note the double slash.
bugs.expected: The helper output holds the plan paths exactly as the test builds them.
bugs.mechanism: The test compared a path it had built literally against one the code had resolved. On macOS /var is a symlink to /private/var, so pwd -P returns the resolved form and an -Fx comparison cannot match.
bugs.fix: 9f41091 (codex): test-plan-env.sh canonicalises its temp root with tmp="$(cd "$tmp" && pwd -P)" before building the expected strings, so both sides are resolved.
bugs.verification: CI run 32474258670 at a8d1285: test-plan-env passes on both macOS legs, having failed at line 50 in run 32394476430. Confirmed again by run 32476867183.
bugs.found_by: the macOS leg of CI
bugs.notes: The trailing-slash TMPDIR was the wrong half of my guess: the double slash in the log was cosmetic, and the symlink was the whole cause. Recorded because a plausible mechanism stated alongside the real one is what sends the next reader down the wrong path.

bugs.title: BSD grep rejects an empty subexpression, so the progress fallback pattern never matches on macOS
bugs.reproduce: CI run 32394476430, macos-latest: planning/tests/test-progress-derivation.sh
bugs.observed: grep: empty (sub)expression, then FAIL: rebuild-plan-progress falls back to goal name for a bare goal.
bugs.expected: The row | 02-goal | 02-goal | is found.
bugs.mechanism: A pattern contains an empty alternation branch, which GNU grep tolerates and BSD grep refuses outright. Same family as the bre-alternation rule added today, and equally silent: the pattern matches nothing rather than erroring where it is built.
bugs.fix: The pattern is passed to check(), which greps with -E, so its pipes are escaped: a leading bare | is an empty alternation branch. One offender in the repo; the other helpers that take a pipe-leading pattern grep with a BRE, where | is literal, and are unaffected.
bugs.verification: test-progress-derivation passes, and the escaped pattern still matches the row. The unescaped form is rejected here too by ugrep (error at position 4), so the fix is strictly more portable, not merely macOS-specific.
bugs.found_by: the macOS leg of CI
bugs.notes: Candidate for a gated portability rule: an empty branch is textually detectable, unlike the general BRE-alternation case.

bugs.title: No maintainer document mentions the registers, so a change that resolves or finds a bug leaves BUGS.json and TODO.json untouched
bugs.reproduce: grep -c "BUGS.json\|TODO.json\|bug-report" planning/MAINTAINER.md CONTRIBUTING.md AGENTS.md CODE-CONTRACTS.md DEVELOPMENT.md
bugs.observed: Zero in all five. MAINTAINER.md section 4, the per-change checklist, has eight steps covering consumers, fixtures, diagrams, docs, manifest/map/skill_files registration, which tests to run, and the commit shape — and no step touching either register.
bugs.expected: The checklist names the registers: an entry closed when its defect is fixed, an entry added when one is found and not fixed in the same breath, and the version stamp refreshed.
bugs.mechanism: The registers arrived late and were documented only in their own skills. Every other obligation in the checklist has a gate that fails without it, so the checklist is a convenience for those; for the registers it is the only instruction there is, and it is silent. Nothing fails when BUGS.json is stale.
bugs.fix: MAINTAINER.md section 4 gains step 8 (update the registers) and renumbers the commit step to 9, which now also says the message names the entries it closes. The artifact map gains a row for both registers. CONTRIBUTING.md gains a bullet in the pre-PR list, and AGENTS.md says to read the relevant register before starting and update it when finished.
bugs.verification: grep for BUGS.json across the five maintainer-facing docs went from 0 hits to 4. No gate is possible -- no test can tell that a commit resolved a defect -- and each of the four places says so, so the absence of enforcement is documented rather than implied. The doc gates (duplication ratchet, mermaid accuracy, comment format, persona drift) and blast-radius still pass.
bugs.found_by: reviewing commit 9f41091 (codex, "planning: resolve bug report items"): 40 files and 789 insertions, zero changes to BUGS.json or TODO.json
bugs.notes: Written immediately after the review that found it, and the same review is the evidence: commit 9f41091 met every gated obligation and missed this one. The temptation while fixing it was to defer closing this very entry because a subagent holds BUGS.json in another worktree -- which is the same excuse the step exists to remove, so it was closed here and the conflict left to be resolved.

bugs.title: add-ui-story-links.sh could not reject an unknown work unit on bash 3.2, because its guard ran in a pipeline subshell
bugs.reproduce: nix develop --command bash32-run planning/tests/test-plan-commands.sh  # from commit 9f41091
bugs.observed: add-ui-story-links accepted an unknown related work unit. Passed under bash 5.3, failed on 3.2 only.
bugs.expected: W99 is not in the inventory, so the call refuses with exit 66.
bugs.mechanism: The validating loop was the last stage of a pipeline, so it ran in a subshell and plan_die exited that subshell rather than the script. On bash 5 set -e then aborts on the pipeline status; on bash 3.2 it does not. Isolated: `set -euo pipefail; printf a | while read x; do exit 66; done; echo CONTINUED` prints CONTINUED on 3.2 and aborts on 5.3.
bugs.fix: Split on commas with IFS and a for loop, so the guard runs in the current shell. No other guard in the repo has this shape — checked.
bugs.verification: test-plan-commands passes on both shells; before the fix it passed on 5.3 and failed on 3.2. Catalogued as the pipeline-subshell-guard rule, documentation-only because the shape spans several lines and a pipeline-while is fine when it is not guarding.
bugs.found_by: reviewing commit 9f41091 (codex) — the bash 3.2 leg of ./verify-both-shells.sh
bugs.notes: The floor earning its keep: a guard that reads correctly and does nothing is worse than no guard, and only 3.2 showed it. Codex met every gated obligation in that commit and this one had no gate.

bugs.title: Every test install wrote its throwaway --target into the real XDG config of the user, 1894 lines of it
bugs.reproduce: wc -l "${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-$HOME/.config}/tsch-ai-skills/custom-locations"
bugs.observed: 1895 lines, 120K: 1894 of them /tmp paths from test runs, one real entry.
bugs.expected: A one-off --target is not a location the user chose to remember.
bugs.mechanism: select_targets called save_custom_location on the non-interactive --target path, so every test that installed into a temp directory appended to a persistent user config file.
bugs.fix: 9f41091 (codex) removed the call. The interactive path still saves, which is where a user does choose a location.
bugs.verification: No new entries after a --target install; the interactive caller at 40-selection.sh:129 is untouched, so the feature survives.
bugs.found_by: reviewing 9f41091 - the diff removed a call, and the file it wrote to turned out to hold 120K of test debris
bugs.notes: The stale entries are gone: pruned 2026-08-21 from 1895 lines to the single live one, with a backup at custom-locations.bak. Measured before pruning: only 1 of the 1895 directories still existed, so load_custom_locations already filtered the rest with [ -d ] and the menu was never visibly wrong. The objection was the write itself, plus the fact that a leaked test root that did still exist would have been offered as an install target.

bugs.title: The per-test TMPDIR leaked for 67 of the tests, because a test setting its own EXIT trap replaces the one lib-test.sh installs
bugs.reproduce: source planning/tests/lib-test.sh; trap 'rm -rf x' EXIT; exit 0   # then look for /tmp/t.?????
bugs.observed: The root survives. 67 test files set their own EXIT trap, and six stale roots were sitting in /tmp.
bugs.expected: Each test root is removed when the test ends.
bugs.mechanism: lib-test.sh installs an EXIT trap at source time; bash keeps one EXIT trap per shell, so a test that traps EXIT afterwards silently discards it. Commit 1044857 introduced this, and the assertion written with it only covered a shell that sets no trap of its own.
bugs.fix: 9f41091 (codex): run-tests.sh exports AI_SKILLS_TEST_RUN_ID, lib-test.sh writes it into each root as .ai-skills-test-run-id, and the runner sweeps only roots carrying this run id.
bugs.verification: A run leaves no /tmp/t.????? behind. The marker keeps the sweep safe under concurrency, which was the objection behind refusing to sweep at all.
bugs.found_by: reviewing 9f41091 - its comment named the trap hazard, and the reproduction confirmed it
bugs.notes: Better than the decision recorded in T10: a run was said to be unable to distinguish its own leftovers from a concurrent run live directories. A run id distinguishes them.

bugs.title: On stock macOS the registry fallback runs a real benchmark agent with no time bound at all
bugs.reproduce: On a host with neither setsid nor timeout/gtimeout: start-worker.sh calls launch_agent isolated "${WORKER_TIMEOUT:-45m}" - mode becomes registry, no timeout binary is found, and lib-agent.sh warns and launches anyway.
bugs.observed: lib-agent.sh:140-148 prints "registry fallback cannot bound the agent to 45m" and then runs the agent unbounded, because cmd gets no timeout prefix.
bugs.expected: A worker that cannot be bounded is refused, as it was before: the setsid path still returns 69 in the same situation.
bugs.mechanism: 9f41091 added an isolated mode that degrades setsid to a registry fallback when setsid is missing, which is stock macOS. The same change turned the missing-timeout refusal into a warning for that fallback only. The two degradations compose: no process group and no clock.
bugs.fix: lib-agent.sh grew a third rung below timeout/gtimeout: in registry mode only, launch_agent parses the spec (<n>s/<n>m/<n>h, 64 on anything else) and starts _agent_watchdog as a background sibling of the agent. The watchdog polls kill -0 in one-second steps, then TERMs the ps-walked tree and escalates to KILL after 5s; wait_agent calls _agent_watchdog_stop, which kills the watchdog and its in-flight sleep. The setsid path still returns 69, and a present timeout/gtimeout still wins, so the watchdog is never used when a real bound exists.
bugs.verification: test-safeguards.sh launches fake agents with a PATH holding neither timeout nor gtimeout: a 2s-bounded sleeper and its descendant are both killed, a TERM-ignoring agent is KILLed, an agent that exits on its own is not killed and leaves no watchdog or sleep, 45x is refused with 64, a stubbed timeout binary is used with no watchdog started, and the setsid path still returns 69. Mutations that each fail exactly one of those: never starting the watchdog (the B13 regression), TERMing the pid instead of the tree, dropping _agent_watchdog_stop, TERMing the watchdog without its sleep child, one long sleep instead of the poll, accepting any spec, skipping the timeout binary, starting the watchdog even when timeout is present, and turning the setsid 69 back into a warning.
bugs.found_by: reviewing 9f41091 after being asked about the setsid fix specifically
bugs.notes: These callers launch real worker and reviewer agents that spend real tokens, so an unbounded run is the expensive failure, not an inconvenient one. The new tests in test-safeguards.sh cover the registry wiring and prove the nohup/setsid/open shims refuse, but assert nothing about the timeout path. Options: keep the refusal in registry mode too; or implement a shell watchdog (background sleep plus kill of the registered pid and its ps-walked descendants) so the bound survives without GNU coreutils. The second is more work and is the only one that makes a macOS benchmark run at all.

bugs.title: --yes did not answer the planning permission prompts, so a headless install died on a question
bugs.reproduce: HOME=/tmp/fresh bash install.sh --skill planning --target /tmp/t --yes </dev/null
bugs.observed: Create /tmp/fresh/.plans as the global plans directory? [y/N/a] install.sh: line 296: read: 3: invalid file descriptor: Bad file descriptor / Error: Interactive input is required, exit 1.
bugs.expected: --yes answers the prompt and the install completes.
bugs.mechanism: confirm() tested YES_ALL, which only the interactive "a" answer sets, and never YES, which is what --yes sets. Its help text scoped --yes to replacements, but README sells it for headless and CI use, and a flag for headless runs that stops on a question defeats itself. Separately, fd 3 is deliberately closed when there is no tty, so bash printed its own invalid-file-descriptor complaint before ask() could die with the actionable message.
bugs.fix: confirm() honours YES as well as YES_ALL, and the help line says --yes answers every prompt including the planning permission grants -- the widening is documented rather than silent, since those prompts grant agents read/write and script execution. ask() suppresses bash own read error so only the die message is shown.
bugs.verification: test-installer-noninteractive.sh: a planning install under --yes exits 0, asks for nothing, creates the plans directory and installs the skill; without --yes it exits 1 with the actionable message and no raw shell error; and a second --yes run still writes the scripts, so yes-to-everything cannot be implemented as do-nothing. Mutations: restoring the YES_ALL-only test fails the first two assertions, and removing the 2>/dev/null fails the no-shell-noise assertion. CI run 32476867183 exercises it on ubuntu and both macOS legs.
bugs.found_by: reported by Michael. I had hit the same failure earlier in the session while installing planning to a temp target and worked around it with a pipe instead of investigating.
bugs.notes: Two things I first called defects here were not. The exit code was correct all along -- my measurement read the status of a pipe. And the summary printed after the failure is deliberate: cleanup() prints it so a run that dies part-way still reports what it wrote, and says so in a comment. HOME has to be redirected to see any of this, because the prompt only appears when the plans directory does not exist, which on a developer machine it usually does.

bugs.title: verify-both-shells.sh deletes a concurrent run's live worktree, failing that run wholesale
bugs.reproduce: Start ./verify-both-shells.sh, and while it runs start a second one. The second sweeps the first worktree away.
bugs.observed: The first run reported 87 tests, 31 passed, 56 failed on its bash 3.2 leg, with errors like "cd: /tmp/verify-wt.PLtaGy/tree/planning/scripts: No such file or directory" and "/tmp/verify-wt.PLtaGy/tree/install.sh: No such file or directory". Its bash 5.3 leg, which had finished before the second run started, passed all 87.
bugs.expected: A second run leaves a live worktree alone and sweeps only leftovers.
bugs.mechanism: The startup sweep removes every registered worktree matching verify-wt.*, on the assumption that any it finds is a leftover from a killed run. It cannot tell a leftover from a live one, so a concurrent run deletes the tree the first is executing in, file by file, underneath it.
bugs.fix: already in tree (pid beside the worktree, sweep skips a live owner); verified this session, see verification
bugs.verification: Planted three registered verify-wt.* fixtures -- one whose harness.pid is a live sleep, one with pid 999999, one with no pid file -- then ran ./verify-both-shells.sh once. Output: leaving live worktree ...livefix (harness pid N), sweeping leftover ...stalefix and ...stalefix2; after the run only the live fixture remained registered. The registration-before-pid-write race cannot happen: a run registers its worktree only after its pid file exists.
bugs.found_by: the verification of c565658, which I started and then started a second one for the next commit while it was still running
bugs.notes: Same class as the test-root sweep in run-tests.sh, which codex fixed with a run-id marker after I had concluded a run could not distinguish its own leftovers from a concurrent run live directories. I wrote that reasoning down for run-tests.sh and did not apply it to my own harness. A fix is in the working tree, unverified: each run writes its pid beside its worktree and the sweep skips any whose owner is still running. Proving it means planting a worktree owned by a live process and running the sweep, which is invasive enough to want its own moment rather than being folded into another commit. Until then the rule is one verification at a time, and a wholesale failure with missing-file errors is this, not a regression in the code under test. CI cannot close this one: it runs a single suite per job, so nothing there exercises two concurrent verifications. The proof has to be local and deliberate.

bugs.title: dep_reaches memoizes every visited pair before exploring and reads the memo back as failure, so an earlier probe of a pair turns a later valid check into a false FAIL
bugs.reproduce: In one goal give two verification steps prose naming each other's unit id (W17 with W15 in its Depends-on cell, W15's step mentioning W17), then run validate-plan.sh <plan>. Isolated: source the propagation lib, populate the unit_depends/unit_type/unit_goal maps for both edges, set dep_seen=() once, and call plan_validate_propagation_reach.
bugs.observed: "W17 is a verification unit that grades W15 but has no dependency path to it" although work-unit-inventory.md lists W15 in W17's Depends-on cell. A standalone probe of dep_reaches on the same pair returned success.
bugs.expected: A pair with a satisfiable edge in either direction counts as ordered.
bugs.mechanism: dep_reaches does plan_map_has dep_seen "$key" && return 1 before exploring and then plan_map_set dep_seen "$key" 1 immediately, so the map records visited-but-not-outcome while every hit is read as known-failure. bugs.fix: 8383072 — dep_reaches keeps two maps: dep_seen marks pairs whose walk is in progress and cuts cycles, dep_failed caches only walks that completed without reaching the target; the caller clears both with plan_map_clear before each query instead of assigning an unrelated variable named dep_seen (the maps live in plan_map__dep_seen__<key> variables).

bugs.title: verify-fix-keys.sh self-certification gate cannot pass when reviewers share the coordinator's session id, so a legitimate claim reads as self-certified
bugs.reproduce: In an opencode harness: coordinator mints (or a subagent reviewer re-mints) with the shared derived session id, then the fixer claims via add-fix-claim.sh and verify-fix-keys.sh --claimed-by <session> runs — minted_by equals the claimed session for every pair, which the approval gate treats as self-certification.

bugs.expected: Either an explicit MINTED_BY is accepted as legitimate attribution, or the harness limitation is documented next to the gate so operators know the check is advisory there.

bugs.title: add-planning-bug's damaged-register guard relies on jq 1.7 empty-input behaviour, so under jq 1.6 a zero-byte register reports success
bugs.reproduce: Stub a jq on PATH that exits 0 silently when any argument equals the --arg name 'now' (planning/tests/test-add-planning-bug.sh does exactly this), then run add-planning-bug.sh on a plan with no planning-bugs.json under jq-1.6.
bugs.observed: The stubbed append writes a zero-byte register; the read-back guard jq -e on an empty file exits 0 under jq-1.6 (no input means no output, so -e never gets a false/null last output), the writer prints Recorded, and test-add-planning-bug fails its three refusal assertions. The same test passed where CI runs jq >= 1.7, whose -e exits 4 on no output.
bugs.expected: A write that produced nothing is refused with 70 naming the register and id, whatever jq version reads it back.
bugs.mechanism: The guard delegated the emptiness check to jq -e's no-output exit status, which changed between jq 1.6 and 1.7 instead of being decided by this script.
bugs.fix: add-planning-bug.sh checks the register itself before the read-back: a zero-byte result is refused with the same 70 message naming register and id. The guard no longer depends on jq -e empty-input behaviour, which differs between jq 1.6 (exit 0) and 1.7 (exit 4).
bugs.verification: test-add-planning-bug.sh fails at 885cba2 and on this branch pre-fix under jq-1.6 with three refusal assertions; it passes with the guard. Mutation: removing only the [ -s ] line reproduces all three failures under jq-1.6. The existing assertions were already mutation-hardened in B12 work; no new test needed — the seam test was right, the guard was version-dependent.

bugs.notes: Second site of the same class, not fixed here for scope: validate-plan-commands-lib.sh line ~29 answers extension registration with jq -e index() against the registry file — an empty never-executable-extensions.json would read as every extension registered under jq-1.6. That registry ships non-empty and is gate-checked elsewhere, so the exposure differs from a caller-supplied write; worth hardening if it is ever regenerated empty.

bugs.title: chat promises exchange across machines, but every server tier binds 127.0.0.1 with no way to change it
bugs.reproduce: grep -n '127\.0\.0\.1' chat/runtime/server.py chat/runtime/server.pl chat/runtime/server.js chat/scripts/chat-server.sh; then grep -n 'bind\|--host' chat/scripts/chat-server.sh
bugs.observed: server.py binds ("127.0.0.1", port), server.pl sets LocalAddr => '127.0.0.1', server.js listens on "127.0.0.1", and the socat tier uses TCP-LISTEN:...,bind=127.0.0.1. chat-server.sh has no bind or listen-address option: its only network flag is --port. Meanwhile chat/SKILL.md's description says the skill is for when agents need to exchange messages "across sessions or machines", and every client helper takes --host.
bugs.expected: Either a machine other than the server's own can reach it, or the documentation does not offer that.
bugs.mechanism: The loopback bind is hard-coded in all four tiers and no flag reaches it. --host on the client side therefore only ever resolves to a server on the same machine, or to one reachable through a tunnel that nothing in the skill sets up or mentions. The promise and the socket disagree, and the socket is right.
bugs.fix: c36bab8 — --bind ADDR sets AI_CHAT_BIND; socat option and the python3/node/perl listeners read it, status reports server.bind, and SKILL.md documents the unauthenticated-protocol caveat for non-loopback binds
bugs.verification: Contract pins cover all four runtime sites; an explicit-bind roundtrip runs on the python3 tier in test-chat.sh. A real cross-machine exchange needs two hosts and stays a documented manual step.
bugs.found_by: reading the diff of the -ox branch: the description was checked against the sockets rather than taken at its word
bugs.notes: Two ways out, and they are not equivalent. Correcting the description is the cheap one and probably the right one: the skill states it has no auth, so a loopback-only bus is a sane default and offering a listener on a routable address without authentication would be worse than the missing feature. Making the bind configurable is the other, and it should not be done without deciding what protects it -- at minimum a documented warning, and the four tiers each need the change since the address is hard-coded in each. Whichever is chosen, the cross-machine claim must not survive unqualified in the description, because an agent selecting this skill reads that line to decide whether it fits.

bugs.title: The overview counts only archived review rounds, so a plan whose review happened reports zero
bugs.reproduce: bash planning/scripts/render-plan-overview.sh .plans/reviewer-oracle-evidence-hardening --out /tmp/o.html   # then read the header and the CYCLES panel
bugs.observed: A delivered plan -- review approved, all 16 steps complete, findings 1 (0 open), 1/1 resolved -- reports review rounds 0, review depth 0/3, and a CYCLES panel reading "no review cycles recorded yet - the chart lights up after cycle 1". The same plan's adversarial-review.md carries an approved verdict and one finding row.
bugs.expected: Two rounds are always present -- the pre-implementation review and the final review -- so a plan that has been reviewed reports 2, and 3 only when a third round was actually needed. The depth ring counts against that: 2 of 2 is a complete review, not a failure against a target of 3.
bugs.mechanism: render-plan-overview.sh:153-154 sets cycles=0 and then counts '^## Cycle [0-9]' headings in adversarial-review-history.md. That file only exists once a round has been archived, which update-adversarial-review.sh does when a *new* round starts. A plan with exactly one round therefore has no history file and counts zero, and every figure derived from cycles -- the rounds count, the review-depth ring against its target of 3, and the chart -- reports as though no review occurred. The undercount is by one everywhere, and it is worst on a finished plan, where the reader concludes the work was never reviewed.
bugs.fix: this session — render-plan-overview builds one normalised cycle stream from history plus (only when no history exists) the live table, filtering placeholder rows and dropping cycles they empty; count, ring, panel and chart all read that stream, so they cannot disagree
bugs.verification: test-plan-overview pins the live-only round: one round counted, chart bar drawn, placeholder absent. Mutations: forcing cycles=0 fails the narration assertion; counting placeholder rows fails the fresh-plan placeholder assertion.
bugs.found_by: Michael, reading the delivered render: review approved and all steps complete, yet feedback and cycles empty
bugs.notes: The live round is the missing term: rounds are archived history plus the current review when one exists. Both screenshots show it -- the planning plan reports 7 findings with 0 rounds while its phase line says round 1 is open, and the delivered plan reports a resolved finding with 0 rounds. Whatever counts a round must agree with the phase line, which already says "round $((cycles + 1))" and so has the correct number in hand. Worth deciding at the same time whether review depth against a target of 3 is meaningful for a plan that needed one round and got approval; a ring reading 0/3 on an approved plan reads as a failure rather than a completed review. Corrected by Michael: the model is not "archived cycles plus the live one" but a fixed pair -- pre review and final review -- extended when the work demands another. So the count does not come from counting history headings at all; the history file says how many rounds happened beyond the pair. That also fixes the depth ring, which currently reads 0/3 on an approved plan and implies a failure: it should read 2/2 for the normal case and 3/3 when a third was needed, never a target the plan was never meant to hit.

bugs.title: An executing agent can leave the plan describing a world that no longer exists, and nothing in verification notices
bugs.reproduce: Execute any real work order under SKILL.md rules in a consumer repo: commit code for steps without calling update-step.sh in the same turn; implement an unplanned requirement and describe it in prose instead of add-work-unit.sh; deliver a step through a path outside the planned files. Then bash planning/scripts/validate-plan.sh <plan> — it passes or fails only on unrelated structural grounds, while progress.md still reads 0% and the inventory omits shipped units.
bugs.observed: Two health-app plans, cycle-15 era. order-split-api-attribute read 0% with all nine steps incomplete although the code was committed and REST-verified; EmployeeSplitSpecificationInterface and its model shipped with no unit; goal 05 of order-split-extended-rendering-v2 carried delivered work (order PDF, quote PDF) with no units at all. The executor listed every one of these as outstanding in its per-burst summaries, and the user caught the drift twice in one night.
bugs.expected: Completing work and recording it are one act. Verification must make plan-versus-reality drift visible when it is created — at the turn where code lands without its plan mutation — rather than depending on the operator reading both sides and catching it.
bugs.mechanism: The rules exist and are explicit: the progress-accuracy operating rule, §4.1.1 (dynamic scope additions are plan mutations), §2.5 (one step per unit). Nothing executes them. validate-plan checks structure before/during approval, never sync during execution; no gate connects target-repo changes to inventory, step or progress mutations; the executor summary ritual (reporting outstanding bookkeeping) made deferral feel like disclosure. Executor self-analysis names the habit: each burst optimised for visible code progress, treating the plan as a report written afterwards instead of live state mutated at the moment of discovery.
bugs.fix: this session — the freshness pass makes code-after-record drift visible at validation time (see T44); the summary-contract half lives in the execution rule that outstanding lists are mutations to perform, not disclosures
bugs.verification: test-plan-freshness: control silent, drift named with unit and dates, catch-up silent, outside-repo target skipped. Mutation inverted comparison fails the drift-named assertion.
bugs.found_by: user, health-app order-split execution sessions, August 2026 — drift caught manually twice after REST-verifying completed work
bugs.notes: Deliberate non-actions in the same session are honest decisions, not defects: W05 rewritten to what this repo controls (its trigger lives behind DownloadInvoice::execute() curling Profortool), reviews left pending to avoid self-approval. The defect is the silent drift class. Related trust surface: B34 — an overview that undercounts review rounds is the same failure family, records disagreeing with reality while looking authoritative.

bugs.title: install.sh with no --target exits 1 printing nothing at all, so a headless install fails silently
bugs.reproduce:
bash install.sh --skill git-worktrees --yes; echo "exit $?"   # exit 1, zero bytes
bash install.sh --skill git-worktrees --target "$HOME/.claude/skills" --yes; echo "exit $?"   # exit 0, installs
bugs.observed: exit 1 with 0 bytes captured from 2>&1, both with stdout on a pipe and redirected to /dev/null. The same command with an explicit --target exits 0 and prints 400 bytes ending 'Installed: /home/mdibbets/.claude/skills/git-worktrees'.
bugs.expected: either the default target is used and the skill installs, or a diagnostic names what is missing; a non-zero exit with no message is never acceptable
bugs.mechanism: Not the target logic. install.sh:3552 calls show_splash only when SKILL_SELECTION or TARGET_SELECTION is empty, which is why passing --target hides the bug. show_splash (install.sh:1077) starts with a bare 'return' guarded by a tty test on fd 3; with no tty the test fails and the bare return propagates status 1. show_splash is the last command in that then-branch, so under set -euo pipefail (install.sh:5) the script aborts there, before select_targets runs, printing nothing. Isolated proof: a function whose body is the same tty test plus bare return exits 1 and never reaches the next statement, while the same function with 'return 0' reaches it.
surfaces: installer/src (the show_splash source and its call site)
bugs.fix: this session — show_splash says return 0 on every early exit, and a --yes run with no interactive channel takes the target menu default (first listed root) with a printed note instead of dying in ask
bugs.verification: Sandboxed headless install without --target exits 0, prints the no-channel note and Installed: path. Regression pinned in planning/tests/test-installer-noninteractive.sh: exit must be 0, output non-empty.
bugs.found_by: installing the new git-worktrees skill without --target
bugs.notes: Hits every headless install that omits --target: CI, the one-liner, an agent installing for a user. Same family as B15, the non-interactive path is not exercised by the suite. A regression test should assert that a --yes install with no --target either succeeds or prints a diagnostic, and should fail if a bare return is reintroduced in show_splash.

bugs.title: chat bash-handler with_lock leaves the channel lock directory behind when the locked command fails
bugs.reproduce: Copy with_lock/bail/chan_path verbatim from chat/runtime/bash-handler.sh:38-51 into a script with set -euo pipefail, then call: with_lock '#x' failing_cmd, where failing_cmd() { return 3; }. Then ls the channel directory.
bugs.observed: Script exits 3 at the "$@" line; the following 'AFTER with_lock returned normally' line never prints; ls shows the lock still present: drwxrwxr-x 2 mdibbets mdibbets 40 '#x.log.lock'.
bugs.expected: The lock directory is removed whether the locked command succeeds or fails, as chat/scripts/chat-send.sh:70 achieves with a trap.
bugs.mechanism: bash-handler.sh runs under set -euo pipefail. In with_lock the sequence is the expanded command, then rc=$?, then rmdir. A failing command is a simple command in no conditional context, so set -e exits the shell on that line and both the rc assignment and the rmdir are unreachable. On the socat tier each connection is its own process, so the process dies holding the lock and the directory persists. Every later connection to that channel then spins LOCK_TRIES=200 times 0.05s and answers ERR lock timeout until the directory is removed by hand. Contrast chat-send.sh:70, which uses a trap and is correct.
bugs.fix: with_lock captures rc via "$@ || rc=$?" so set -e cannot abort before the rmdir; the lock directory is removed on failure paths
bugs.verification: repro verbatim: rc=3 propagates AND the lock dir is absent afterwards; chat suite green
bugs.found_by: chat-skill-developer agent (chat orientation pass, 2026-08-27)

bugs.title: chat python3 and node tiers allocate the next message id from the last log line instead of the highest, so a new message can take an id below one already stored
bugs.reproduce:
Seed a channel log with out-of-order ids, then send through each tier: printf 'MSG #t 1 100 system :one
MSG #t 7 101 a :seven
MSG #t 3 102 b :three
' > $HOME/channels/'#t.log'; then chat-send.sh '#t' 'next id?' --host 127.0.0.1 --port $P against the python3 tier, the node tier, and locally with no --host.
bugs.observed: python3 tier: MSG #t 4 ... probe :next id? -- node tier: MSG #t 4 ... probe :next id? -- local helper (awk max): MSG #t 8 ... probe :next id?. The two socket tiers produced id 4, which is lower than the id 7 already in the log.
bugs.expected: All writers allocate max(id)+1, as chat-send.sh:71, bash-handler.sh:33 and server.pl:40 do, so ids stay monotonic and gap-free as SKILL.md guarantees.
bugs.mechanism: server.py:66 is 'last = int(line.split(b" ")[2])' and server.js:50 is 'last = parseInt(line.split(" ")[2], 10) || last' - both assign the parsed id unconditionally rather than taking a maximum, so the value left in 'last' is the id of the final line, not the largest. server.pl:40 guards with '&& $1 > $last' and the awk in chat-send.sh:71 and bash-handler.sh:33 track a running max, so three of five writers are correct and two are not. Impact: SKILL.md promises the id is monotonic and gap-free and it is the cursor for every delta read, so an id below an existing one is invisible to any reader whose --since is already past it, and it collides on a second occurrence. Trigger is any log whose lines are not in ascending id order - a merged or restored log, or a hand edit.
bugs.fix: server.py parses only well-formed MSG lines and keeps a running max; server.js takes max instead of the last line's id
bugs.verification: seeded out-of-order log (ids 1,7,3): next send takes id 8 through the python3 tier; local helper already agreed
bugs.found_by: chat-skill-developer agent (chat orientation pass, 2026-08-27)

bugs.title: chat server.py append dies on a log line it cannot parse, dropping the client connection with no error reply
bugs.reproduce: Put a non-MSG line in a channel log and send through the python3 tier: printf 'MSG #t 1 100 system :one\n# hand-added note\n' > $HOME/channels/'#t.log'; then on one connection send NICK probe, PRIVMSG #t :does this survive, PING, QUIT.

The node tier on the identical log answers MSG #t 2 ..., PONG and OK bye.
bugs.expected: An unparseable log line is skipped (as server.js:50 does by testing startsWith('MSG ')), or at worst answered with an ERR line; the connection is not silently dropped.
bugs.mechanism: server.py:64-68 iterates every line of the channel log and calls int() on the third space-separated field with no 'MSG ' prefix test and no try/except. Any line that is not a well-formed MSG raises ValueError, or IndexError if it has fewer than three fields. Handler.handle catches only ConnectionResetError and BrokenPipeError (server.py:164), so the exception escapes, the handler thread dies, and the socket closes without any reply. server.js:69 and :50 guard with a startsWith('MSG ') test and a '|| last' fallback, which is why node survives the same input. Note python3 is the first tier chat-server.sh selects, so this is the default runtime.
bugs.fix: append skips non-MSG and malformed lines instead of raising; handler no longer dies on hostile logs

bugs.title: the node rung of overview-serve serves nothing: page, state and sections routes all return empty
bugs.reproduce: bash planning/tests/test-overview-serve.sh
bugs.observed: Three failures, all on the node rung: '/state.json equals the extractor' got '' against a full expected document; '/ serves the artifact' output did not contain '<!DOCTYPE html>'; '/sections slices identity-panel' output did not contain 'id="identity-panel"'. The python3, perl and socat rungs pass in the same run. Reproduced at commit 54ee970, before the B51-B59 batch and before any change of mine, so it is pre-existing rather than a regression from either.
bugs.expected: The node rung serves the same three routes as the other rungs, which is what makes it a rung: the test asserts identical output across all four.
bugs.mechanism: overview-server.js prints the port with console.log(port) where port is a NUMBER. Node applies util.inspect colouring to a non-string argument whenever colour is forced, so with FORCE_COLOR set in the environment (FORCE_COLOR=3 here, alongside COLORTERM=truecolor) the port line is written as ESC[33m35115ESC[39m even though stdout is a file, not a TTY. test-overview-serve.sh reads it with head -1 into the URL, so every request goes to a malformed host and all three routes return nothing. Proven: node -e 'console.log(8080)' emits ESC[33m8080ESC[39m here, while env -u FORCE_COLOR node -e 'console.log(8080)' and node -e 'console.log(String(8080))' both emit a bare 8080. Invoking the server directly and reading the port by eye serves all three routes correctly (page 200 with 181335 bytes, state 200 with 172956), so the rung itself works and only the port line is unparseable. Environment-specific in trigger; the defect is a server printing a number through a colourising API on a machine-read channel.
bugs.fix: console.log(String(port)): node applies util.inspect colouring to a NUMBER argument whenever FORCE_COLOR is set (main's box: v24.18.0 with FORCE_COLOR=3, honoured even for non-TTY stdout), so the port file carried ANSI escapes and every URL built from it failed to connect — status 000, no server-side error, which is why the rung looked empty on that host only. The test now also rejects a non-digit port line loudly with the raw bytes dumped
bugs.verification: reproduced on node 22 with FORCE_COLOR=3: bare number prints ESC[33m8080ESC[39m, String() prints clean; served under FORCE_COLOR+COLORTERM the rung answers state 200; mutation (reverted String()) fails the test with 'unparseable port line: ESC[33m...'
bugs.found_by: main session, from the full suite: 106 ran, 104 passed
bugs.notes: ox does not reproduce on node v22.16.0 with no FORCE_COLOR set, which is consistent: the colouring is forced by the environment rather than the node version. Fix is String(port) or process.stdout.write, so the port line cannot be decorated whatever the environment says.

bugs.title: chat-send.sh's socket path lets a message body forge any nick, because newlines are not sanitised before the protocol printf
bugs.reproduce:
bash chat/scripts/chat-register.sh '#injtest'; body=$(printf 'first line from aiskills
NICK ox
PRIVMSG #injtest :this line claims to be from ox
'); bash chat/scripts/chat-send.sh '#injtest' "$body" -n aiskills --host 127.0.0.1 --port 7717; bash chat/scripts/chat-read.sh '#injtest' 0
bugs.observed: Two messages are stored from one send. Reproduced here verbatim: 'MSG #injtest 2 ... aiskills :first line from aiskills' followed by 'MSG #injtest 3 ... ox :this line claims to be from ox'. The send passed -n aiskills; message 3 is attributed to ox. A message body can forge any nick on the channel. A plain two-line body is silently truncated instead — the second line becomes a protocol command rather than text, exit stays 0, and the acknowledgement looks like success.
bugs.expected: A message body is data. Whatever it contains reaches the channel as one message attributed to the sending nick, or the send is refused.
bugs.mechanism:
chat-send.sh has two paths that disagree about sanitisation. The direct-append path runs the text through tr '
' '  ' before writing the log line. The socket path does printf 'NICK %s
PRIVMSG %s :%s
QUIT
' with the raw body, so every newline in it is a command boundary on the wire and every following line is parsed as a protocol verb. The safe path is the one callers were told not to use: B65 made --host mandatory for a message to reach subscribers at all, which routes every well-behaved caller through the unsanitised path.
bugs.fix:
fccb430 — chat-send.sh now collapses newline and carriage return to a space once, just after validation, so the socket path and the direct-append path share one sanitisation. The socket path no longer interpolates a raw body into 'NICK %s
PRIVMSG %s :%s
QUIT
'. Sanitise was chosen over refuse: refusing a body containing a newline would break the common legitimate case (an agent relaying a diff, a file excerpt, command output or a quotation — B75's own surface), and collapsing is exactly what the direct append has always done, so the two paths now agree on already-documented behaviour. Server side, a PRIVMSG rejection buys nothing against this defect because the newline IS the frame delimiter — by the time a handler sees the PRIVMSG the forged NICK is already a separate, indistinguishable, well-formed command; the python and node rungs were instead hardened to strip CR as well as LF so a bare CR cannot corrupt a stored line (the bash rung already did, perl collapses all whitespace). chat/SKILL.md now states that one message is one line.
bugs.verification:
New chat/tests/test-chat-injection.sh sends a body of 'honest line
NICK impostor
PRIVMSG #inj :forged line' as nick 'sender' on both paths and asserts one stored message, attributed to the sender, whole body on one line. Mutation: restore the pre-fix split sanitisation (drop the shared 'text=$(printf %s "$text" | tr 
 "  ")' and put the tr back inside the direct-append printf only). Observed under that mutation: FAIL 'socket path (python3): one send stored 2 messages, expected 1' and 'a body forged the nick impostor', with the log showing 'MSG #inj 2 ... sender :honest line' and 'MSG #inj 3 ... impostor :forged line'. Unmutated the test passes on this bash and on the bash 3.2 floor via bash32-run. The fixed client was also exercised against all four rungs (python3, node, perl, socat): each stores one message attributed to the sender.
bugs.found_by: the webview subagent, reproduced independently by the main session on #injtest

bugs.title: relaying untrusted text into chat is an injection vector while B74 stands
bugs.reproduce: Any agent that pastes text it did not author — a file excerpt, a diff, command output, a quote from a user — into chat-send.sh with --host
bugs.observed: Not yet observed in the wild. It follows from B74: a body's newlines become protocol commands, so whoever wrote the relayed text chooses what else gets sent and under whose nick. The main session has relayed reviewer reports, diff excerpts and command output into this channel repeatedly today, any of which could have carried a crafted line.
bugs.expected: Relaying a quotation into a channel cannot cause anything but that quotation to appear, attributed to the relaying agent.
bugs.mechanism: Same as B74 — unsanitised newlines in the socket path — but the exposure is what makes it worth its own entry: the attacker need not have chat access, only the ability to get text in front of an agent that will quote it. That is a much larger surface than the channel's own participants, and it is the reason B74 is high rather than minor.
bugs.fix: fccb430 — closes with B74. The relay surface existed only because chat-send.sh's socket path let a newline in the body become a command boundary; with the body sanitised on both paths before it reaches the wire, text an agent did not author can no longer forge a nick, whatever it contains.
bugs.verification: The B74 reproduction IS the relay case: the forgery body is exactly the pasted-text shape (a first honest line followed by attacker-authored lines). test-chat-injection.sh asserts on both paths that such a body produces one message attributed to the sending nick, and fails with the forged 'impostor' line under the mutation that restores the pre-fix split sanitisation. bugs.title: chat-watch.sh never advances its cursor, so every poll re-emits the same messages
bugs.reproduce: timeout 20 bash chat/scripts/chat-watch.sh '#aiskills' --since 64 --host 127.0.0.1 --port 7717 | awk '{print $3}' | sort | uniq -c
bugs.observed: Each message id is emitted once per poll for as long as the watcher runs: ids 65 and 66 each appeared 4 times in 20 seconds. Identical in local mode without --host, so it is not the socket path. Armed as a Monitor it re-delivered the same message repeatedly until the watch was stopped by hand — the first arming flooded the session with roughly a dozen copies of one message before it was noticed.
bugs.expected: Each poll prints only messages newer than the last one printed, which is what the helper's own contract says: 'using FETCH since-id so no message is missed and no message is double-read; each poll prints new messages only'.
bugs.mechanism: The since-id used for each fetch is the value the watcher started with rather than the highest id it has emitted, so every round re-requests the same window. The step-down cadence makes it worse rather than better: on a quiet channel the interval grows to 60s and the same backlog is re-emitted at each step, and any new message resets the cadence to 5s, so an active channel re-emits its whole window every five seconds.
bugs.fix: fccb430 — chat-watch.sh no longer puts --since into read_args. chat-read's argument parser is last-wins, so appending the ORIGINAL --since after the per-poll --since made every poll re-request the window the watcher started with; the starting id now lives in the cursor and nowhere else. A second mechanism was hiding behind the first: the cursor was advanced to id + 1 on the stated belief that FETCH is '>= since'. It is not — every tier's FETCH is '> since', matching the local awk '($3 + 0) > s' — so id + 1 would have silently skipped the very next message once the first bug was fixed. The cursor is now the highest id printed, taken as a max rather than from the last line so an out-of-order log cannot rewind it. The stale '>=' comment was corrected.
bugs.verification: New chat/tests/test-chat-watch-cursor.sh watches a channel across several polls on both the local and the socket path and asserts every id exactly once, plus a message that arrives mid-run delivered exactly once and not skipped. Two mutations, both run. (1) Put --since back into read_args: FAIL 'local watch: ids re-emitted (id x count): 1x3 2x3 3x3' and 'socket watch (python3): ids re-emitted: 1x4 2x4 3x4 4x2'. (2) Set cursor=$(( id + 1 )): FAIL 'socket watch (python3): emitted ids [1 2 3], expected [1 2 3 4]' — the mid-run message skipped. Unmutated the test passes on this bash and on the bash 3.2 floor via bash32-run. bugs.title: the fix-key session id falls back to a guessable value built from the pid, the whole second and bash's $RANDOM
bugs.reproduce: PATH=/usr/bin:/bin bash -c 'unset -f openssl; id="$(printf "%s-%s-%s" "$$" "$(date +%s)" "$RANDOM$RANDOM")"; printf "%s\n" "$id"'   # the arm mint-fix-keys.sh's new_session_id took whenever openssl was absent
bugs.observed: The id is three guessable fields joined by hyphens: the process id, the current time truncated to a whole second, and two draws of bash's $RANDOM. On Linux the pid space is 4194304 by default and is usually far smaller in practice; the second is known to anyone who knows roughly when the review ran; $RANDOM is a 15-bit value from a PRNG seeded per shell, giving 30 bits across the two draws. A reader who can see the fixes.md timestamps can enumerate the space.
bugs.expected: The session id comes from the OS CSPRNG or the helper refuses. It names the secret directory that gates approval, so it must not be derivable from information a claimant already has.
bugs.mechanism: new_session_id ran 'openssl rand -hex 8' and, on any failure, fell through to 'printf %s-%s-%s "$$" "$(date +%s)" "$RANDOM$RANDOM"'. The guard after it only checked the result was non-empty, which the fallback always is, so the weak arm was indistinguishable from success. openssl was declared a soft requirement, so a machine without it took the weak arm silently on every mint. The same script's session secret had a matching pair — 'openssl rand -hex 32' with a '/dev/urandom | od' fallback — but that one degraded to another CSPRNG rather than to a guessable value, which is why only the id is this entry.
bugs.fix: new_session_id calls plan_random_hex 8, which is the shipped plan-crypt binary (/dev/urandom on unix, BCryptGenRandom on Windows) or, without it, /dev/urandom read directly and length-checked. There is no third arm: without a CSPRNG the helper exits 69 and mints nothing. The session secret moved to plan_random_hex 32 in the same change, which also fixed a width inconsistency — 'openssl rand -hex 32' produced 64 hex chars but its 'head -c 64 /dev/urandom' fallback produced 128, against a comment in both scripts asserting the secret is always 64.
bugs.verification: planning/tests/test-plan-crypt.sh section 6: two draws must differ, 64 consecutive draws must all be distinct, the width must be exactly 2 chars per byte, every character must be hex, and mint-fix-keys.sh must contain no $RANDOM expansion outside a comment. Mutation: replacing plan_random_hex's body with a constant ('printf ab' repeated) makes it report 'two session ids came out identical: abababababababab' and '64 draws are all distinct: expected 64, got 1'. A second mutation in the Rust source — random::fill returning a zeroed buffer instead of reading the OS — fails two cargo tests, draws_differ_and_are_not_zero and odd_lengths_are_filled. Starved-PATH run with no plan-crypt and no digest tool exits 69 rather than improvising.
bugs.found_by: plancrypt, while replacing the openssl calls in the fix-key helpers with a compiled binary
