Reproduced verbatim on this machine. Nothing is wrong with the server, and the message offers no recovery. With the parent present the same open succeeds, the tab starts empty and save writes the file, as SKILL.md promises - so the two cases differ only in the parent directory and only one of them says so.
bugs.expected: open detects the missing parent and uses the wording save already uses for the identical condition, which is excellent: 'the parent directory <dir> does not exist - create it and save again, or close the tab to discard the buffer'. And it is never reported as failed-to-start: the server is fine, the path is not.
bugs.mechanism: the autostart path reports any server-launch failure as failed-to-start and passes the child's stderr through verbatim; the server's own resolve step reports the ENOENT without distinguishing an absent leaf (legitimate, a new file) from an absent parent (unusable). save already has the good message for this condition, so the wording exists and is simply not reached from open.
bugs.fix: d616bd30 — autostart_server() in src/ai-text-editor/src/client.rs checks the parent directory before spawning anything, so a path problem is never routed through the failed-to-start message. Two steps, per Michael's revised expectation: the refusal names the missing directory in the wording save already uses for the identical condition and creates nothing, and acknowledge_create_parents (CLI --acknowledge-create-parents, the --acknowledge-force-save family's shape, carried on ResolveRequest and declared in the MCP schema) creates the chain recursively and opens the tab.
bugs.verification: cargo test -p ai-text-editor --test cli_flow: open_under_a_missing_parent_names_the_directory_not_the_server asserts the refusal names 'parent directory' and the directory itself and does NOT contain 'failed to start', then adds only the parent and drives the same open through an insert and a save to a written file — so the control proves the directory was the whole difference. Mutation: delete the parent check and the refusal reverts to 'server for <path> failed to start: ... cannot resolve <path>', failing both the positive and the negative assertion.
bugs.found_by: sanitairkamer session 2026-09-07, relayed on the chat bus and reproduced here
bugs.notes: MICHAEL'S RESOLUTION, 2026-09-07, which supersedes the wording-only expectation above: the editor should CREATE THE PATH RECURSIVELY, after the agent has been explicitly asked to verify the path for typos. So the fix is two-step, not a better message: (1) open refuses with the missing parent named and asks the caller to confirm the path is not a typo, (2) an acknowledged retry creates the directory chain and opens the tab. The wording save already uses is the right text for step 1; the acknowledgement flag belongs with the other safety acknowledgements (--acknowledge-force-save, --acknowledge-large-edit), which is the established pattern for 'I meant this'. Silent mkdir -p is NOT wanted - a typo would then quietly build a directory tree nobody asked for, which is exactly what the verify step exists to prevent.

bugs.title: the git-worktrees skill prescribes a worktree location the EnterWorktree tool does not use, and warns against the one it does
bugs.reproduce: Read chat of the rule: awk on ~/.claude/skills/git-worktrees/SKILL.md section 'Where worktrees live', then compare with the actual path EnterWorktree creates: git worktree list in this repository.
bugs.observed: SKILL.md: 'Agent worktrees go under ~/.config/tsch-ai-skills/worktrees/, one named directory each ... Never /tmp ... and a worktree under the repository itself confuses the repo's own filesystem scans and cleanup tools.' Meanwhile every worktree in use sits under the repository: git worktree list reports /home/mdibbets/git/ai-skills/.claude/worktrees/{registers,fix-drive5-batch,agent-a4c12403322e18fc2,fix-b111-source-shipped}, which is what the EnterWorktree tool creates.
bugs.expected: The skill states the location that is actually used, or states the exception explicitly. As written an agent following the skill puts its worktree somewhere no other agent or tool looks, and an agent following the tool is violating a documented rule for a stated reason - so one of the two is wrong and nothing says which.
bugs.mechanism: Documentation predating the harness's own worktree support: the section was written for worktrees an agent created by hand with git worktree add, where the author chose a central location on purpose. EnterWorktree creates them under the repository's .claude/worktrees/ instead, and the skill was never reconciled with it.
bugs.found_by: Michael 2026-09-07, asking whether the skill already specified the main-agent/subagent division; checking it surfaced this instead
bugs.notes: Correcting the surfaces field, which was mistyped on filing: the file is git-worktrees/SKILL.md at the repository root (the skill is tracked here and installs to ~/.claude/skills/git-worktrees/). Verified present: /home/mdibbets/git/ai-skills/git-worktrees/SKILL.md. B232 and B233 are the other two gaps in the same file, kept separate because each has its own fix and closing one leaves the others: B232 is the missing main-agent/subagent division, B233 the session-wide pin hazard. This entry is the wrong location. B234 depends on how this resolves: if worktrees are to live under the tsch-ai-skills config directory as this skill says, the installer has to create and permit that directory (it currently grants only the plans and planning-tmp paths, Read/Edit and no Write). If instead the in-repo .claude/worktrees/ location that EnterWorktree creates is blessed, B234 becomes unnecessary. Decide the location here first.

bugs.title: the git-worktrees skill never says worktrees are for subagents while the main agent works in the main checkout
bugs.reproduce: Search the skill for the division of labour: awk 'tolower($0) ~ /main checkout|main agent|subagent|coordinator|main session/' git-worktrees/SKILL.md
bugs.observed: Two hits, neither stating it: the description's 'a risky change kept off the main checkout' and 'that you want the main checkout untouched'. The skill covers one-worktree-per-agent, disjoint scopes, branch naming and the concurrent-sweep hazard, but never says who is entitled to a worktree.
bugs.expected: The skill states the division Michael gave on 2026-09-07: worktrees are for the SUBAGENTS; the main agent works directly in the repository checkout. Without it the reasonable reading is that every agent isolates, including the coordinator - which is what I did, and it broke a running subagent (see B233).
bugs.mechanism: Documentation omission. The skill is written from the point of view of a worker deciding how to lay out parallel work, and never addresses the coordinator's own position, so it reads as advice to everyone equally.
bugs.found_by: Michael 2026-09-07: 'You can work in the ~/git/ai-skills directory. worktrees is only for the subagens, not the main agent', then 'didn't the worktree skill specify that?' - it did not
bugs.notes: B231 (the prescribed location contradicts what EnterWorktree creates) and B233 (the pin is session-wide) are the other two gaps in this file. B233 is the consequence of this omission going unstated, so the two are worth fixing in one pass even though they close separately.

bugs.title: nothing warns that the worktree isolation pin is session-wide, so entering one breaks every subagent already working in another
bugs.reproduce: With a subagent working in .claude/worktrees/<its-own>, call EnterWorktree from the main session for an unrelated task. Then have the subagent run any Bash command in its own worktree.
bugs.observed: Every command the subagent runs is refused: 'This session is isolated in the worktree .../fix-b111-source-shipped ... refusing to run it in the shared checkout (.../fix-drive5-batch)'. Observed live on 2026-09-07: the ai-editor-drive-5 agent lost git access mid-batch and one edit was refused mid-write. It cannot recover on its own - EnterWorktree back to its own path appears to succeed while Bash keeps refusing, and ExitWorktree answers 'cannot be called from a subagent with a cwd override'. A pre-push-check run in that state also measures the WRONG working tree and reports PASS for a branch it never examined.
bugs.expected: The skill warns that the pin is session-wide rather than per-agent, so a coordinator must not enter a worktree while a subagent holds one, and states the recovery: ExitWorktree with action keep from the main session releases the pin, after which the subagent re-issues EnterWorktree with its own path. It should also tell a stranded subagent NOT to repoint another agent's worktree to unblock itself.
bugs.mechanism: The isolation pin is session state, and a subagent shares its parent's session, so the guard resolves one pin for all of them. The skill's parallel-agents section assumes each agent's isolation is its own, which is true of the worktrees themselves but not of the pin that decides which one the guard permits.
bugs.found_by: hit live on 2026-09-07 while picking up a second bug alongside a running subagent; the subagent reported it correctly and refused to work around it
bugs.notes: B232 is the omission that made this reachable - nothing said the coordinator should stay in the main checkout. B231 is the third gap in the same file. All three want one editing pass over the skill's parallel-agents guidance.

bugs.title: the installer grants no permissions on the worktrees directory the git-worktrees skill tells agents to use, and grants Edit without Write anywhere
bugs.reproduce: Read what planning_permission_step actually grants: awk on install.sh for planning_permission_step and claude_permissions. Then compare with the location git-worktrees/SKILL.md prescribes.
bugs.observed: The grant covers exactly three paths - ${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-$HOME/.config}/tsch-ai-skills/plans, ${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/planning-agent, and <root>/planning/scripts - and the rules written are 'Read(<plans>/**)', 'Edit(<plans>/**)', 'Bash(<scripts>/**:*)', 'Read(<scripts>/**)', 'Read(<tmp>/**)', 'Edit(<tmp>/**)'. So: nothing covers tsch-ai-skills/worktrees, which is where git-worktrees/SKILL.md tells every agent to put its checkout; there is no Write rule anywhere, only Edit, so CREATING a file in any granted directory still prompts; and the whole step runs only inside main's planning branch, so an install that does not select planning grants nothing at all.
bugs.expected: If worktrees are to live under ${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-$HOME/.config}/tsch-ai-skills/worktrees, the installer creates that directory and grants Read, Edit AND Write on it, independently of whether the planning skill was selected, so an agent can create and edit files in its own checkout without a prompt per file.
bugs.mechanism: planning_permission_step (install.sh) hardcodes the three planning paths and is called only from main's planning branch; claude_permissions/opencode_permissions receive exactly those three and emit Read/Edit/Bash rules with no Write. Nothing in the installer knows about the worktrees location, because that location is documented in the git-worktrees skill rather than declared anywhere the installer reads.
bugs.found_by: Michael 2026-09-07, asking whether the installer should be granting read/write on the tsch-ai-skills config directory so worktrees there are editable without prompts
bugs.notes:
SCOPE WARNING for whoever implements this: grant the worktrees subtree specifically, NOT tsch-ai-skills/**. That directory also holds the chat home (channel logs, server.crt/server.key), the editor's private metadata and session registry, and on a shared install the installed binaries. A blanket Write there would let any agent overwrite the server's TLS private key or the binaries it is itself running - so the rule set should name .../tsch-ai-skills/worktrees/** and nothing above it.

BLOCKED ON B231, and should be implemented together with it. If B231 resolves the other way - worktrees stay under the repository at .claude/worktrees/, which is what EnterWorktree actually creates - then this grant is unnecessary, because the repository checkout is already the agent's working directory and already permitted. So the location decision comes first and this entry follows it. Filing it now so the permission half is not forgotten once the location is settled.

bugs.title: test-review-lifecycle writes about 6G into a hardcoded /tmp directory, so the suite can exhaust a tmpfs machine
bugs.reproduce: export TMPDIR=$HOME/.config/tsch-ai-skills/tmp; resource-limited-testing/scripts/limited-run.sh 6G 400 -- ./run-tests.sh   # then, while it runs: du -sh /tmp/* | sort -rh | head
bugs.observed: /tmp/reviewer-lifecycle-goal03.HsLHzX reached 6.0G, and TMPDIR was exported to a real-disk directory throughout, so the export did not redirect it. On this workstation /tmp is tmpfs, so that is 6G of RAM: free reported 473Mi free and 6.7Gi shared with the run in progress. test-review-lifecycle itself FAILED with exit 137 (SIGKILL) - the 6G cgroup ceiling from limited-run.sh, which counts tmpfs pages against the scope that allocated them. The directory was still present and full AFTER the test died, so a failed run leaks the whole 6G until something removes it. test-ai-text-editor failed in the same run and PASSES in isolation, so it was collateral of the pressure rather than a defect of its own.
bugs.expected: The test writes its scratch under TMPDIR (or the repo's chosen scratch root) so an operator can put it on disk, and it removes it on failure as well as on success. A single test should not be able to allocate 6G of RAM on a machine whose /tmp is tmpfs, and it should not be able to fail the suite under the memory cap the repo's own resource-limited-testing skill documents as the preset for a large suite.
bugs.mechanism:
benchmark/planning/setup-benchmark.sh:98-107, copy_workspace_for_publication(): it tars the whole workspace with ONLY .env exclusions (.env, .env.tmp.*, */.env, */.env.tmp.*) and no exclusion for target/, .git/, node_modules/ or bin/. So it copies the entire Rust debug build tree. Measured: the destination grows from 276 KB to 5,479,476 KB in about eight seconds, and the largest files are target/debug/rjq at 51M and target/debug/deps/rjq-720c42d65ed1153c at 51M, under contract-fixture/integration/testing/current-<ts>-adapter-test-<pid>/source/.

test-review-lifecycle.sh is the caller, not the cause: it makes the destination with a hardcoded mktemp -d /tmp/reviewer-lifecycle-goal03.XXXXXX at line 142 (so TMPDIR cannot redirect it) and drives setup-benchmark.sh at line 548. The size comes from the harness's copy.

That combination is why this is invisible until it bites: the volume depends on whatever the developer's local target/ happens to hold, so a fresh CI checkout with no debug build copies almost nothing while a working machine copies gigabytes.
bugs.found_by: a suite run after the machine had already been rebooted once for an out-of-memory crash, 2026-09-07
bugs.notes:
This is very likely the cause of the out-of-memory crash that forced a reboot on 2026-09-07, and the attribution matters because the first diagnosis was wrong. Agent scratch in /tmp was blamed and cleaned up first - roughly 20 logs and two 200KB install.sh copies, about 640KB total. That is three orders of magnitude too small to matter. This single test directory is 6G. Anyone reading the earlier /tmp-hygiene guidance should know it was necessary housekeeping but not the fix.

Two consequences worth acting on separately from the fix:
1. The documented preset is the problem's detector, not its cause. resource-limited-testing's table names 6G/400% for a large suite, and this test needs about 6G on its own, so the suite cannot pass under its own recommended cap while this stands.
2. It leaks on failure. The 6G tree was still there after exit 137, so a killed run leaves it until a reboot or a manual rm. A trap that removes the directory would at least bound the damage. CORRECTION to this entry's earlier note, from reading the source rather than inferring: the test is NOT careless about cleanup. Line 143 is trap 'rm -rf -- "$tmp"' EXIT. The leak happens because the memory cap SIGKILLs the process and an EXIT trap cannot run on SIGKILL - so the cap that stops it filling RAM is exactly what stops it reclaiming the space. Confirmed by measurement: exit 137, and the 5.5G tree was still present until an external cleanup removed it.

MEASURED EVIDENCE, replacing the earlier estimate: peak 5,479,476 KB, reached in about 8 seconds from 276 KB. Every sample recorded the two 51M rjq binaries in target/debug.

FIX DIRECTION: add target/, .git/ and node_modules/ to copy_workspace_for_publication's exclusion list. Note the blast radius is wider than this test - setup-benchmark.sh is the real harness, so every benchmark run copies the target tree too, which is a silent cost on any machine with a warm build.

bugs.title: insert accepts delete_len and ignores it, so an insert asked to delete first is answered as a success
bugs.reproduce: Over MCP or NDJSON: insert --file F --offset N --text T --delete-len 5 --expected-revision R
bugs.observed: The delete_len is accepted by the protocol-wide key check, never read by the insert handler, and the call answers success with a new revision. A caller that asked for 'delete five bytes, then insert' got a plain insert and no way to tell the difference.
bugs.expected: Refused by name, with accepted_keys, as B237's per-verb declaration now does. delete_len belongs to replace; on insert the span is empty, so the argument can only be a caller error - and answering success to a partially-performed instruction is the worst available outcome.
bugs.mechanism: The unknown-argument check was one protocol-wide list (B237), so a key any verb reads passed for every verb. delete_len is read by replace's handler and simply absent from insert's, which made an accepted-and-ignored argument indistinguishable from an honoured one.
bugs.found_by: surfaced by B237's fix: binding the per-verb key table to both the server door and the adapter schemas, editor-batch agent 2026-09-07

bugs.title: endpoint_for_file abandons XDG_RUNTIME_DIR for a machine-global /tmp directory once the socket path passes 96 characters
bugs.reproduce: Set a long TMPDIR/XDG_RUNTIME_DIR - the length this repo now mandates for scratch is enough - then autostart an editor server and look for its .endpoint record.
bugs.observed: The record lands in a machine-global /tmp/tsch-ai-skills-editor instead of the configured runtime dir. In the cli_flow suite EVERY endpoint record went there, so the suite escaped its own isolation and the harness sweep was reading an empty directory for all 38 tests - the larger half of the ~173 leaked servers swept by hand on this machine.
bugs.expected: A configured runtime dir is honoured, or the fallback is loud rather than silent. Two agents on one box must not share an endpoint namespace, and on a multi-user machine a shared 0700 directory is one two users would fight over.
bugs.mechanism: src/ai-text-editor/src/transport.rs endpoint_for_file(): when the path it would build reaches the 96-character sun_path limit it falls back to /tmp/tsch-ai-skills-editor. The mandate for a long scratch TMPDIR and this fallback are each reasonable alone and jointly broken - the longer the configured dir, the more certain the fallback fires.
bugs.found_by: editor-batch agent while writing B239's test, 2026-09-07; raised as its Q3

bugs.title: a response key with no verbosity tier panics the connection thread, and the caller sees only "the server closed the connection without answering"
bugs.reproduce: On the T99 branch feat/t99-verbosity-ladder: ai-text-editor cursor -f FILE -a home -p structured, or any cursor command. In the suite it presents as cli_flow::unknown_options_are_refused_before_anything_is_sent failing.
bugs.observed: ai-text-editor: the server at unix:/.../<key>.sock closed the connection without answering (endpoint unix:/.../<key>.sock). No error frame, no code, no message, nothing on the servers stderr the client keeps - the log is deleted on a successful start. Indistinguishable from a crashed or wedged server, and there is nothing in it that names a key, a verb, or verbosity.
bugs.expected: A key nobody has classified is loud in a way that names itself. The debug_assert was put in deliberately as the safety net for exactly this - an unclassified key is kept at every level so production fails safe rather than silently dropping a field - but a debug_assert inside the request handler takes the connection thread down with it, and the assert text never reaches the caller. It should be caught before the handler runs, or reported as a refusal frame naming the key.
bugs.mechanism: src/ai-text-editor/src/verbosity.rs, tier(): debug_assert!(false, "response key `{key}` has no verbosity tier") on the None arm. It is reached from handle() while a payload is being filtered, inside the per-connection thread that `serve` spawned, so the panic unwinds that thread and the socket closes with no frame written. The cursor verbs own response keys (line, column, visual, wrap_width, range) are the unclassified set that fires it: they are the ANSWER of the cursor verb, so line and column want tier 0 and the wrapped-view fields tier 2. Release builds do not assert at all, so the symptom exists only in debug - which is to say only in the test suite and only for whoever is developing it.
bugs.fix: The cursor verbs own response keys are classified: `line` and `column` at tier 0, because a cursor position is the ANSWER of the cursor verb and not metadata about one - the same reason a reads `text` is tier 0 - and the wrapped-view fields `visual`, `wrap_width` and `range` at tier 2, being needed only when navigating a wrapped view. The fail-safe is deliberately unchanged: an unclassified key is still kept at every level and still trips the debug_assert, because a key that is merely more verbose than intended costs tokens while one that silently vanishes at the default level is a correctness bug in whatever depended on it.
bugs.verification: The whole cli_flow file at the new default no longer produces the symptom; before the fix the search for "no verbosity tier" in a test run returned the cursor keys, and after it returns nothing. The classification itself is pinned by verbosity::a_verbs_own_result_survives_the_lowest_level and the end-to-end ladder test cli_flow::the_verbosity_ladder_shortens_the_answer_without_dropping_the_guard. NOT closing the underlying shape: a debug_assert inside the request handler still takes the connection thread down with no frame written, so the next unclassified key will present the same way. That is recorded here rather than fixed, because moving the check out of the handler is a design change and this entry was about a specific unclassified set.
bugs.found_by: the safety net firing for real while measuring T99s blast radius; filed on the coordinators instruction that the symptom be recorded prominently, because nobody debugging a closed connection blind would guess an unclassified response key
bugs.notes: STATUS CORRECTED from fixed back to confirmed, same reason: the fix is on feat/t99-verbosity-ladder, commit 674f532a, which has not merged. Its fix and verification text stand as recorded. Close on merge.

bugs.title: an unmarked request was served by whichever tab a no-file call cached first, so a read after opening a second file could answer from the first
bugs.reproduce: In one agent workspace: open file A, then open file B, then issue a request with no file, endpoint or tab marker - a plain read.
bugs.observed: The read is answered from A. The per-(identity,file) client cache had stored A's session token for the identity-only lookup, so a call naming nothing resolved to whichever tab happened to be cached first rather than the tab most recently opened. It answers successfully and reports A's content, so a caller has no signal that it read the wrong document.
bugs.expected: An unmarked request resolves to a defined tab - the session's focused tab, which open sets - or is refused. Silently answering from a different document than the caller last opened is the failure mode a revision guard cannot catch, because the answer is internally consistent: A's content with A's revision.
bugs.mechanism: Found while implementing T98 (a session carries a focused tab): the focus made the ambiguity visible because there was previously nothing that DEFINED which tab an unmarked request meant. The identity-only path in the client cache resolved to a first-cached token; with several tabs open in one workspace, 'first cached' and 'most recently opened' diverge. Fixed by T98's focus, which open now sets, and every response names the tab it answered so a caller can see it.
bugs.found_by: editor-batch agent while implementing T98, 2026-09-07; reported in its final summary and unfiled until now
bugs.notes: Filed by the coordinator from the agent's closing report rather than by the agent, so it exists independently of whether T98's branch lands. Related but distinct: B178 was cached endpoint reuse with no liveness or generation check - that was a dead endpoint being reused; this is a LIVE tab being the wrong one. Same cache, different failure.

bugs.title: the prescribed mention tail is one-shot, so every wake opens a window in which the agent is off the bus and a mention reaches nobody
bugs.reproduce: Hold the posture chat/SKILL.md prescribes: chat-client-rs tail --chan "#c" --nick worker --mentions --mention-exit --no-session. It exits on the first mention. Send a second mention before the agent has re-armed.
bugs.observed: Nothing holds the nick between the exit and the re-arm, so the second mention wakes nobody. The agent is also absent from every other clients nick list for that window - B255 recurring on every single wake rather than once. And because the wake IS the only prompt to read, an agent that is idle rather than mid-task never learns the mention happened: there is no later signal that distinguishes "no mentions" from "a mention arrived while I held no connection".
bugs.expected: An agent told to be reachable stays reachable. Either the tail keeps listening across a mention - the exit is what creates the hole - or something re-arms it without the agent having to remember, whether a supervised restart or a tail that reports the mention and continues.
bugs.mechanism: src/chat-client-rs: --mention-exit terminates the tail on the first matching message by design, so a harness can treat the process exit as the wake signal. The re-arm is then left to the agent, and chat/SKILL.md prescribes appending a literal "RE-ARM NOW" reminder to the wake output precisely because that is unreliable - which is an admission that the posture is unsafe by default. --no-session mitigates the CONSEQUENCE (the cursor is untouched, so a read after waking still returns the spool) but not the cause: the wake itself is lost, and only an agent that happens to read anyway recovers it. Distinct from B263, where a HELD tail suffixes a later send, and from B255, where an agent holds no tail at all; this is the gap the prescribed remedy leaves open on every wake. Frequency is not hypothetical: aiskills reported forgetting to re-arm four times in one session and said the bus went silent each time with nothing to show it.
bugs.found_by: sanitairkamer, which noticed its own tail was momentarily down and pointed out this is a separate defect from the nick suffix; the two were entangled because the tail being down is what made B263s control possible
bugs.notes: FOUND-BY CORRECTED: this entrys found_by credits sanitairkamer with pointing out the exit window, and sanitairkamer has since said plainly "that is NOT what I meant... I never raised the exit window". The defect is real and it confirmed as much, but the provenance was mine - I filed it after misreading its message, and it is the second of two things I read wrong there. Recording it rather than quietly editing the field, because a register that credits a peer with a claim it disclaimed is worse than one with an ugly note. PREMISE CORRECTED AGAIN, and this time it exonerates the entry rather than the provenance. B266 explains why I read sanitairkamers messages wrong three times: its sends were truncated at the first newline, so the halves of its messages I was guessing at had been silently discarded before they reached the channel. My guesses were at missing text, not ambiguous text. That does not make this entry wrong - sanitairkamer confirmed the exit window is real - but the found_by correction above stands, and the reason for the misreading is now known and filed.

bugs.title: the mention filter matches the nick as a substring, so a nick that is a prefix of another gets false wakes and the longer nick misses its own
bugs.reproduce: Hold chat-client-rs tail --chan "#c" --nick bob --mentions and have someone say "@bobby ping". Inverse: hold --nick editor-batch-2 and have someone say "@editor-batch ping".
bugs.observed: The first wakes bobs tail, which was never addressed. The second wakes nothing, though @editor-batch is the prefix of the nick holding the tail. Live in #ai-skills: my tail holds `editor-batch` and every mention of `@editor-batch-2` (the nick B263 makes my own sends arrive under) wakes it.
bugs.expected: A mention of @bobby is not a mention of @bob. The filter should match the nick as a whole token - bounded by the start of the text or a non-nick character on each side - so neither a prefix collision nor a suffixed sibling changes who is woken.
bugs.mechanism: src/chat-client-rs/src/main.rs, both filter sites, each a bare substring test: line 1429 in local_read, `if !line.contains(&format!("@{}", nick))`, and line 1746 in tail, `.map(|text| text.contains(&format!("@{}", nick)))`. Neither checks what follows the nick, so "@bob" matches inside "@bobby", and neither checks the whole nick is present, so a tail for "editor-batch-2" does not match "@editor-batch".
bugs.found_by: sanitairkamer, which named it as the other half of its controlled measurement after I twice read its message as something else; confirmed from the source rather than from the wire
bugs.notes:
TWO things that make this more than a filter tidy-up.

(1) Its own test cannot see it. local_read_mention_filter_matches_only_the_named_nick (src/chat-client-rs/src/main.rs ~2457) asserts bob, carol and dave against "@bob"/"@carol" - three nicks where none is a prefix of another, so the substring behaviour is invisible to it. The test is named for the property it does not verify: add "@bobby" to its log and ask for "bob" and it would bite. This is the trap aiskills named earlier in the same session, a test asserting a weaker rule than its name claims.

(2) It currently MASKS B263, so the order of the fixes matters. B263 makes an agents one-shot sends arrive as N-2 while its tail holds N, so peers naturally address @N-2 - and only this substring behaviour delivers those to the tail holding N. Fix the matcher first and cross-agent addressing breaks for every agent holding a tail, because @editor-batch-2 would stop waking editor-batch. B263 has to land first, or the two have to land together. LIVE EVIDENCE, and a third consequence: the filter has no SENDER check either, so an agent wakes on its own messages.

Observed just now. My tail holds `editor-batch`. It woke on a PRIVMSG whose sender was `editor-batch-2` - my own send - because my prose about this very bug contained the literal string "@editor-batch". The tail is a separate connection from the send, so the server relays my own message to it correctly per RFC; nothing server-side is wrong and this is not B249, which is fixed and was about a standard client double-rendering its own lines.

Why it is not merely amusing: it burns a wake and a full re-arm cycle, and with B264 that cycle is a window in which a real mention reaches nobody. So a self-wake can cost a genuine message. B263 makes it worse rather than better - because the agents sends arrive under N-2, the tail cannot recognise them as its own even by comparing nicks.

Recorded here rather than as its own entry because it is the same filter missing a second check: a mention is a message addressed to you BY SOMEONE ELSE, and the filter tests neither the token boundary nor the sender.

bugs.title: send silently truncates a multi-line message at the first newline while printing the whole of it locally, so the sender believes it arrived
bugs.reproduce: chat-client-rs send --chan '#c' --nick n --text $'first paragraph\n\nsecond paragraph', then read the channel back with chat-client-rs read --local --chan '#c'.
bugs.observed: The channel stored only "first paragraph". Everything from the first newline on is gone, and the sending client printed the COMPLETE text to its own stdout as its success line, so nothing about the call looks wrong. Measured by sanitairkamer across four of its own messages: msg 97 stored 415 characters of about 1900 sent, msg 108 stored 257 of about 1900, and 102 and 105 likewise - each cut exactly at its first paragraph break. My own msg 34 in the same channel is the same defect: I sent an intro plus two numbered questions in separate paragraphs and only the intro stored.
bugs.expected: Either the newline is rejected with a named refusal - a PRIVMSG is one line by construction, so a multi-line text is a caller error the client can see before it writes anything - or the text is split into one PRIVMSG per line. What must not happen is the current behaviour: most of the message discarded, no error, and a local echo of the full text that tells the sender it succeeded.
bugs.mechanism: src/chat-client-rs/src/main.rs:1053, `write_line(&mut tls, &format!("PRIVMSG {} :{}", o.chan, o.text))`, with write_line appending CRLF and writing the lot. An embedded newline in o.text therefore terminates the IRC line early: the server reads "PRIVMSG #c :first paragraph" and then tries to parse the remainder as a command of its own, which it discards as unknown. o.text is never validated or escaped. Two things hide it: line 1093 prints the full o.text locally as the senders own echo, so the caller sees what it meant to send rather than what left; and the write result is discarded with `let _ =`, so nothing is reported even when the write itself fails.
bugs.found_by: sanitairkamer, which measured it across four of its own messages after five exchanges had been built on text I never received. I hit it MYSELF at the start of the same session - my msg 34 - noticed the symptom, worked around it by writing one line per send, and did not file it. Michaels standing rule is that a finding goes in the register when it is noticed, and this is the cost of not doing that: my three successive misreadings of sanitairkamers messages were guesses at text that had been silently discarded, not at anything ambiguous.
bugs.notes: A LATENT SECOND LIMIT, not the cause here but adjacent: an IRC line caps around 512 bytes including the prefix and CRLF, and sanitairkamer was sending about 1900 characters. Its messages were cut at the paragraph break rather than at 512, so the newline is what bit first and the length limit has not yet been observed to bite - but a single-line message long enough would meet it, and the same discarded write result and full local echo would hide it exactly as well. Worth checking when this is fixed: splitting on newlines alone would turn one silent truncation into another.

bugs.title: insert silently clamps a negative offset to 0 and writes at the top of the file
bugs.reproduce: Open any multi-line file, then: insert --file F --expected-revision R --offset -1 --text placeholder
bugs.observed: The call succeeded, reporting {"offset":0,"bytes_written":11}, and "placeholder" was inserted at byte 0 -- ahead of the first line. No warning, no error, and the response named offset 0 rather than the -1 that was passed.
bugs.expected: A negative offset is refused as an argument error naming the offending value, the way a non-numeric offset would be. If "end of document" is wanted as a sentinel it has to be documented and tested, not arrived at by accident -- and it would then have to append, which is the opposite end from where the clamp lands.
bugs.mechanism: The offset is accepted as a signed integer and clamped into range rather than validated, so any negative value collapses to 0. The response then reports the clamped value, so the caller's own log agrees with the wrong write.
bugs.fix: 24ca6c4c on fix/worktrees-tmpdir-chat-relay - verbs::is_count_key() declares the keys read as a non-negative integer, and the server refuses any present-and-invalid one at the door, beside B237's unknown-argument door. Not yet merged.
bugs.verification: On the MCP surface that produced it: offset -1 answers argument_out_of_range naming offset and -1, isError true, and the file is unchanged; a legal offset 9 still inserts there; 50 lib tests, fmt and clippy clean. Mutation: disabling the door restores {"offset":0,"bytes_written":11} and the silent write at byte 0, the defect's observed behaviour verbatim.
bugs.found_by: aiskills, hit live while inserting helpers into chat-client-rs on 2026-09-07
bugs.notes: Hit by hand: I passed --offset -1 intending "append at end", which the schema does not define, and the edit landed at byte 0 instead. Undo recovered it cleanly. The dangerous shape is that a clamp turns an out-of-range argument into a SUCCESSFUL write somewhere else in the file, and reports the clamped offset as though that is what was asked -- so nothing in the response distinguishes it from a correct call. An agent that did not re-read would not notice; I only did because the insert was visibly at the top of the file. Note the relation to the per-verb argument door: that door validates WHICH keys a verb accepts, not whether a value is in range, so this class of defect can exist behind a fully exhaustive door. The CLI was never affected - it already refused --offset -1 in argument parsing, which is why this only ever showed up through MCP, where the JSON reaches the server untouched. Worth knowing before reproducing it: the obvious CLI repro does not reproduce it. The fix covers all fourteen count keys rather than offset alone, since every reader shares the .and_then(Value::as_u64) shape that cannot tell an out-of-range value from an absent one.

bugs.title: a skipped test is reported as PASS, so a suite can be green while running nothing
bugs.reproduce: Run a test whose preconditions are absent, e.g. on a host with no timeout(1): chat/tests/test-chat-broadcast-stall.sh; or via the runner: ./run-tests.sh and read the summary line for it.
bugs.observed: The test prints "SKIP chat broadcast stall: no timeout(1) ..." to stderr, then calls t_end, which prints "test-chat-broadcast-stall.sh: PASS". run-tests.sh records it as PASS in the summary, identical to a test that ran every assertion.
bugs.expected: A skip is its own outcome and is reported as one -- a SKIP column in the summary and a count in the epilogue -- so a green run states how many tests actually executed. A test that did not run must never be summarised with the word PASS.
bugs.mechanism: The skip paths do `printf SKIP >&2; t_end; exit 0`, and t_end has exactly one success wording: it prints "<test>: PASS" whenever the findings count is zero. It cannot distinguish "asserted everything and found nothing wrong" from "asserted nothing at all", because a skip records no finding. run-tests.sh then judges by exit status alone, and a skip exits 0.
bugs.found_by: aiskills, while diagnosing why the macOS bash 3.2 leg failed test-chat-broadcast-stall while macos-latest passed it
bugs.notes: Found while diagnosing a different failure, and it cost real time: macos-latest reported test-chat-broadcast-stall as PASS while the macOS bash 3.2 leg failed it, and "PASS" was consistent with two very different stories -- the test ran and passed, or the test skipped for want of timeout(1), which stock macOS does not ship. Ruling the second out needed the raw job log rather than the summary, because the summary cannot express the difference. Note the interaction with the skip being LOUD on stderr: the authors did the right thing at the test end (the comment in test-chat-broadcast-stall.sh calls it "a loud SKIP, not a failure"), and the runner then flattens it back to PASS, so the loudness is lost exactly where the decision is made. Related to the evidence gap fixed in lib-test.sh on fix/worktrees-tmpdir-chat-relay: both are cases of CI reporting less than it knows.

bugs.title: read returns nothing forever once a channel cursor is 0, because 0 is read as no cursor
bugs.reproduce: H=$(mktemp -d); mkdir -p "$H/channels"; P=44311; AI_CHAT_HOME="$H" AI_CHAT_BEACON_PORT=$((P+1)) AI_CHAT_BIND=127.0.0.1 chat-server-rs "$P" & sleep 1; AI_CHAT_HOME="$H" CHAT_SESSION_ID=reader chat-client-rs join --server 127.0.0.1:$P --nick reader --chan "#newchan"; AI_CHAT_HOME="$H" CHAT_SESSION_ID=poster chat-client-rs send --server 127.0.0.1:$P --nick poster --chan "#newchan" --text "first thing said here"; AI_CHAT_HOME="$H" CHAT_SESSION_ID=reader chat-client-rs read --server 127.0.0.1:$P --nick reader --chan "#newchan"; echo "rc=$?"; AI_CHAT_HOME="$H" CHAT_SESSION_ID=reader chat-client-rs session cursor "#newchan"; cat "$H/channels/#newchan.log"
bugs.observed: join prints "joined #newchan (resuming after id 0)" and the cursor is 0. read prints nothing and exits 0, the cursor is still 0, and the log holds "MSG #newchan 1 1788810945 poster :first thing said here". Every later read repeats it, so the message is never returned by read at all.
bugs.expected: read prints the stored MSG line and advances the cursor to 1. A cursor of 0 recorded by join means "seen nothing yet", so the delta is the whole channel.
bugs.mechanism: read_delta reads the cursor through Session::cursor(), which returns 0 both for a recorded 0 and for a channel with no entry, and only uses it when cur > 0. At 0 it leaves --since empty, asks LASTID for the channel end and fetches after that, so everything already stored is skipped. Nothing is printed, so max_id stays 0 and no cursor is written back: the state that caused the skip survives, and the next read skips again. join on an empty channel is what records the 0.
bugs.found_by: T90 (src/chat-mcp): the adapter inherited the same rule and its own regression test caught it
bugs.notes: Session.cursors is a map, so cursors.get(chan) already separates a recorded 0 from an absent entry; src/chat-mcp/src/conn.rs read() uses exactly that. tail has the same cur > 0 shape at its LASTID fallback and needs checking against this. No test covers a read on a channel joined while empty. chat/tests/test-chat.sh:308-310 already documents this behaviour and works around it -- "a join to an EMPTY channel seeds the cursor to 0, which read cannot tell apart from having no cursor at all" -- by seeding the channel with a message before the joins. The suite therefore tiptoes around the defect rather than covering it. RULING (Tschallacka, 2026-09-08): yes -- tail backfills from a RECORDED cursor. A recorded position is replayed; only an absent one starts at the channel's current end, so the history gate that stops an old channel dumping its whole log is unchanged. The tail change in 6986dd3e is therefore necessary but not sufficient: it made tail read cursor_recorded, and tail never FETCHes, so a message posted between join and the tail starting is still lost. Verified by reproduction on 2026-09-08 -- join an empty channel, post one message, tail prints nothing. Stays confirmed until tail replays. T107 makes it structural. T107 makes the tail the only cursor writer, which removes the two-writer half of this. The unresolved half is unchanged: tail still never FETCHes, so 'backfills from a recorded cursor' is still not something it does. Stays confirmed.

bugs.title: a Claude Code subagent gets its parent's chat session, so it shares the parent's nick and rewrites its cursors
bugs.reproduce: In a Claude Code subagent, with no --session: chat-client-rs session show; then compare with the same command in the parent session. Also: printf %s "$CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID" in the subagent, against the subagent id the harness uses for its own scratchpad and task paths.
bugs.observed: The subagent printed session=h-323712af0e4a99f0 source=harness, file .../sessions/h-323712af0e4a99f0.json, nick=aiskills -- a nick it never set, belonging to the parent session. CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID was 1de1736f-ae05-4cef-88a4-cecdf6e96510, the PARENT session id, while the subagents own id was a2409594-7374-4f1c-896e-55476c23b77d. A join from the subagent then wrote "#ai-skills": 118 into the parent session file.
bugs.expected: A subagent resolves a session key of its own, so it has its own nick and its own cursors. The parent session file is not written by an agent that never opened it.
bugs.mechanism: HARNESS_ID_VARS takes CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID, and Claude Code exports the TOP-LEVEL session id into a subagents tool calls; the subagent id is exported nowhere in the environment. Every rung below is then unreachable, so parent and subagent hash the same material and open the same sessions/<key>.json. join seeds the cursor to the channel end, so the subagents join silently advances the parents cursor past everything it had not read.
bugs.fix: 52a6e63b on fix/worktrees-tmpdir-chat-relay - resolve_session_key folds the nick into the harness, worktree and shared rungs; explicit is left alone. Not yet merged.
bugs.verification: A subagent nick and a parent nick under one CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID resolve to different keys, each stable across invocations; the same nick under two harness ids stays separate, so a nick alone cannot claim a session; both inferred rungs split by nick; an explicit --session id does not. Mutation: dropping the nick from the harness material fails the subagent test with 'one harness id and two nicks must not share a session file'. 45 tests, fmt clean.
bugs.found_by: t90-chat-mcp: a subagents first join landed in the main sessions file
bugs.notes: Both surfaces state the refuted claim: the HARNESS_ID_VARS docblock and SKILL.md rung 2 both say CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID is "one per session and per subagent". The measurement that established the rung was taken across sessions, not between a session and its own subagent. A fix has to find an id the harness exports per subagent, or add a rung below the harness one that separates them; until then --session is the only separation, and the docs should say so. Measured while fixing: there is exactly one claude process on this machine and every subagent's shell is its child, so a process tree cannot separate a subagent from its parent and no thread id reaches the spawned client. That rules out identifying an agent from the pid tree; the nick is the only discriminator available, which is why it is folded in alongside the harness id rather than replacing it.

bugs.title: the chat suite's broadcast-delivery assertion needs openssl, which the dev flake deliberately does not declare
bugs.reproduce: nix develop --command bash -c "command -v openssl"; then read flake.nix packages (no openssl entry, and a comment stating it is deliberately absent) against chat/tests/test-chat-broadcast-stall.sh:222 and chat/tests/test-chat.sh:66.
bugs.observed: openssl resolves to /nix/store/d4vvjf2zix40pq13w778cz4hkyna90ii-openssl-3.6.3-bin/bin/openssl inside the dev shell, which declares no openssl: it is on PATH only through another package closure. flake.nix says openssl is excluded on purpose. With it gone, test-chat-broadcast-stall.sh prints "SKIP chat broadcast stall: no openssl or mkfifo - broadcast delivery was not asserted" and passes.
bugs.expected: Every tool the chat suite needs is declared in the flake, so the assertions run because the shell provides them and not because an unrelated closure happens to. The flake is the source of dev tooling.
bugs.mechanism: chat-client-rs consumes no broadcast -- it FETCH-polls and discards PRIVMSG -- so the only thing in the suite that proves a broadcast reaches a subscriber is an openssl s_client speaking the wire by hand. flake.nix omits openssl on the grounds that plan-crypt owns digests now, which is about openssl as a hashing fallback and does not cover its use as a TLS client. Nothing declares the second use, so it survives only while some other package propagates openssl-bin.
bugs.fix: 77de7201 on fix/b272-flake-openssl — pkgs.openssl declared in the dev shell, with the digest-fallback half of the old exclusion comment kept for rjq
bugs.verification: Measured in the same shell both ways: with the line, nativeBuildInputs carries openssl-3.6.3-dev; with it removed, nativeBuildInputs carries no openssl while command -v openssl still resolves into the store, which is the transitive path this closes. The broadcast test itself was NOT run: it announces on the live beacon port (B274) and this machine has a live bus.
bugs.found_by: t90-chat-mcp, on Michael's report that the chat skill is not using the flake
bugs.notes: Nothing shipped calls openssl any more: plan_sha256_hex.sh and plan-context-lib.sh both record it as removed from the digest chain, and the only remaining call site is lib-test.sh t_sha256, third behind sha256sum and shasum. So declaring it in the flake cannot mask a plan-crypt defect, which is what the exclusion was protecting. ps is a second undeclared tool the chat tests use (ps -o state=, ps -o time=), but it is in the base system on every platform the flake targets and nixpkgs procps is Linux-only, so it is not the same class and is left borrowed.

bugs.title: the membership guard cannot pass: names lists open connections, join creates none
bugs.reproduce: From the main checkout: ./target/release/chat-client-rs join --chan '#ai-skills' --nick nitpick-probe --session nitpick-probe, then ./target/release/chat-client-rs names --chan '#ai-skills' --nick nitpicker --session nitpicker. Control: start 'tail --chan #ai-skills --nick nitpicker --session nitpicker' in the background, wait 3s, run names again.
bugs.observed: join prints 'joined #ai-skills (resuming after id 164)' and exits 0, and names does not list the nick, on that run or any later one. The nick appears in names within 3s of a tail starting and disappears when the tail ends. send works throughout, so messages land while the nick is absent from names.
bugs.expected: Either names lists a nick that has joined regardless of whether a connection is currently open, or the membership check the profile prescribes is written against something that a short-lived client can satisfy.
bugs.mechanism: names reports the connections the server currently holds, not the channel's joined set. Every chat-client-rs invocation except tail is short-lived, so it holds a connection only for the length of the call. The guard added to .agents/profiles/nitpicker.md in f66a9199 says 'if your nick is not in the list, rejoin' and 'if the command fails at all, the server is down'. For an agent that is not blocked inside a tail the first condition is permanently true and join cannot clear it, so the until-loop spins against a command that always exits 0; the second condition never fires because names succeeds. The guard therefore reports a healthy, reachable agent as absent, and its recovery path cannot terminate.
bugs.fix: The guard was in the wrong document, not the server: .agents/profiles/nitpicker.md prescribed "join, then check names; rejoin if absent" as the liveness check, but join/names/read/send all close their connection before the reply is read, so a nick can never appear in names from a one-shot call -- only a held tail connection does (AGENTS.md: "only a running tail holds the connection that keeps a nick in the channel list"). Corrected the step-1 guard and the wake-loop guard in nitpicker.md to check pgrep -x chat-client-rs, and replaced the unreachable-server retry (a join loop that always exits 0, so it could never detect anything) with chat-client-rs discover --wait 3.
bugs.verification: Manual: pgrep -x chat-client-rs correctly reflects whether a tail is running, unlike names (confirmed live in this session -- a nick vanished from names within seconds of its tail ending, matching the reproduction). No server-side change; the previous behavior (names reflects open connections only) is correct per AGENTS.md and left untouched.
bugs.found_by: nitpicker

bugs.title: chat/SKILL.md blesses a detached & for the presence tail while its own rule below forbids one
bugs.reproduce: Read chat/SKILL.md: the copyable line at :201 ends in a bare "&", :234 calls that "the exception to the rule below", and the rule below at :277 says "Start it as a tracked background task, never with a detached &".
bugs.observed: The document gives an agent a copyable command that its own rule forbids, and then names it an exception without saying why the stated harm does not apply.
bugs.expected: One instruction. The presence tail is started as a tracked background task like every other long-lived process, or the exception states plainly why the harm at :277 does not reach it.
bugs.mechanism: The exception was written for the wrong reason: that the tail must outlive the turn. The harm :277 names is not about lifetime - a detached tail is invisible to the harness AND advances the channel cursor, so it consumes messages a later read then skips as already seen. :283 records that happening here. Both halves apply to a presence tail exactly as much as to any other.
bugs.found_by: nitpicker, reviewing 8e67302a and f66a9199 in #ai-skills

bugs.title: the nitpicker profile restates the chat posture chat/SKILL.md owns, and restates the wrong half
bugs.reproduce: Compare .agents/profiles/nitpicker.md:56-66 with chat/SKILL.md:196-236.
bugs.observed: The profile teaches tail --mentions --mention-exit as THE wait for a pseudo-daemon whose whole job is staying visible in the channel. chat/SKILL.md:229-232 already says that form is the one-connection shorthand whose cost is that presence ends the moment it fires, to be kept for a short errand.
bugs.expected: The profile references the mechanism rather than restating it, and where it must name a form it names the two-part one. MAINTAINER 1.2: shared facts live in exactly one place, docs reference and never duplicate.
bugs.mechanism: Written in 8e67302a before chat/SKILL.md carried the two-part posture, and not revisited when f66a9199 added it. A second copy of a mechanism drifts from the first, and this one drifted immediately: it kept the half that costs presence for the agent that most needs presence.
bugs.found_by: nitpicker, reviewing its own profile in #ai-skills

bugs.title: an mcp-mode install copies the adapter binary but registers it with no agent
bugs.reproduce: Read the generated install.sh for any MCP registration: awk on install.sh and installer/src/*.sh for mcpServers, "mcp add", mcp_servers or .mcp.json returns nothing. Then read ai-text-editor/SKILL.md for a registration instruction: none. install.sh --skill ai-text-editor --integration mcp and install.sh --skill chat --integration chat=mcp both take the same path.
bugs.observed: No installer part writes an MCP server entry to any agent configuration, and no SKILL.md tells the user to. The mode copies ai-text-editor-mcp or chat-mcp into the skill directory and stops there. test-installer-integration-mode.sh asserts which binaries land and nothing about reachability.
bugs.expected: After an mcp-mode install the bridge is callable: either the installer registers it in each agent configuration it already edits, or the install prints the exact per-agent registration step. A mode whose artifact nothing is configured to run is not installed.
bugs.mechanism: install.sh chooses WHICH binary to copy by mode (integration_file_allowed) and removes the other mode's binary on a switch (remove_stale_integration_binaries) -- that half works. What is missing is the step after: nothing writes an MCP server entry into any agent config, so the adapter lands on disk and no agent knows it exists. 70-permissions.sh already edits ~/.claude settings and opencode.json through rjq, so the machinery is there and was never extended; codex needs TOML, which rjq cannot write.
bugs.fix: 8e4271b5 on feat/b284-mcp-registration — installer/src/72-mcp-registration.sh registers the adapter through each agent's own CLI after the install loop, and removes a registration this installer owns when the skill is no longer in mcp mode
bugs.verification: planning/tests/test-installer-mcp-registration.sh PASS under bash 5 and under the bash 3.2 floor (bash32-run). It stubs claude, codex and opencode and asserts on argv. Mutation: dropping the 'claude mcp remove' line fails it with 'claude was not asked to remove before adding'. The CLI behaviours it encodes were measured against the real binaries in an isolated HOME: claude mcp add on an existing name exits 0 without updating the command, codex overwrites in place, and opencode mcp add NAME -- PATH registers non-interactively and writes the global config.
bugs.found_by: t90-chat-mcp, starting the chat MCP harness wiring; the premise that the editor bridge already registers itself does not hold
bugs.notes: Three config shapes, not one: Claude Code takes mcpServers in ~/.claude.json or a project .mcp.json, opencode takes an mcp block in opencode.json, and codex takes [mcp_servers.<name>] in ~/.codex/config.toml. The first two are JSON the installer already edits with rjq; the third is TOML and needs either a writer or a printed snippet. SCOPE CORRECTED. The entry first read as though --integration only picked a binary and did nothing else. It also cleans up: measured on a real target, --integration skill installs chat-client-rs and chat-server-rs, then --integration mcp leaves chat-mcp and chat-server-rs with chat-client-rs removed. Michael's toggle-with-mutual-cleanup was implemented and is not what is missing; registration is. aiskills endorsed the wider claim without checking it, having asserted the opposite in the same conversation.

bugs.title: toggling an mcp-mode skill back to skill mode leaves every registered MCP entry pointing at a deleted binary
bugs.reproduce: In an isolated HOME and target: install.sh --skill chat --integration chat=mcp --target T --yes, then install.sh --skill chat --integration chat=skill --target T --yes, listing T/chat/bin/<triple>/ after each. An agent config registering the adapter names <skill root>/bin/<triple>/chat-mcp, which is the path the second install removes.
bugs.observed: after mcp:   chat-mcp chat-server-rs / after skill: chat-client-rs chat-server-rs. The adapter binary an mcp registration points at is gone, and nothing tells the agent whose config still names it. The registration is by hand today, so nothing in the repository knows it exists to clean it up.
bugs.expected: A mode switch that removes an artifact either removes the registrations that name it, or says plainly that it has just invalidated them and how to undo that.
bugs.mechanism: remove_stale_integration_binaries deletes the other mode binary on a switch, which is correct for disk hygiene, and a registration is a reference to that path held OUTSIDE the installer, in each agent config. Nothing connects the two, so the toggle is silently destructive to a reference it cannot see.
bugs.fix: 8e4271b5 on feat/b284-mcp-registration — installer/src/72-mcp-registration.sh registers the adapter through each agent's own CLI after the install loop, and removes a registration this installer owns when the skill is no longer in mcp mode
bugs.verification: planning/tests/test-installer-mcp-registration.sh PASS under bash 5 and under the bash 3.2 floor (bash32-run). It stubs claude, codex and opencode and asserts on argv. Mutation: dropping the 'claude mcp remove' line fails it with 'claude was not asked to remove before adding'. The CLI behaviours it encodes were measured against the real binaries in an isolated HOME: claude mcp add on an existing name exits 0 without updating the command, codex overwrites in place, and opencode mcp add NAME -- PATH registers non-interactively and writes the global config.
bugs.found_by: aiskills raised the lifecycle question on B284; t90-chat-mcp measured the toggle in an isolated HOME and target
bugs.notes: B284 is "nothing registers the adapter"; this is "a registration that exists does not survive a toggle". They are the two halves of one lifecycle and the order matters: writing registrations without removing them on toggle-away adds a second thing that dangles instead of fixing the first. Live today for the editor, which Michael registered by hand in all three configs pointing into the skill root.

bugs.title: bugs update silently ignores --severity, so a severity change reports success and does not happen
bugs.reproduce: bugs update B254 --severity blocking --priority urgent --mechanism "..."; bugs show B254
bugs.observed: It prints "Updated B254" and exits 0. severity is unchanged. Passing --severity alone prints "bugs: nothing to set for B254; name at least one field to change", which shows the flag is consumed and contributes nothing.
bugs.expected: Either --severity sets the severity, or it is refused by name the way any other unknown option is. A flag that is accepted, reported as an update and then dropped is the worst of the three.
bugs.mechanism: update parses a fixed set of settable fields -- title, status, fix, verification, reason, priority, mechanism, append-note -- and severity is not among them. The argument parser does not refuse the unknown flag, so it falls through and the write proceeds with whatever else was named, reporting success for the fields it did change.
bugs.found_by: t90-chat-mcp, noticing B254 still read severity major after aiskills said twice that it was blocking
bugs.notes:
Consequence beyond the tool: aiskills reported B254 and B283 to Tschallacka as blocking, twice, on the strength of an "Updated" that had changed nothing. Both still read major. A register is read by severity at triage, so a silently dropped severity is a defect being triaged at the wrong level for as long as nobody re-reads the entry.

Until this is fixed, a severity is only settable at `bugs add` time, which means correcting one requires filing a new entry or editing BUGS.json by hand -- and a hand edit is exactly what `bugs check` exists to catch.

bugs.title: test-chat-broadcast-stall fails on the macOS bash 3.2 leg without a change that could explain it
bugs.reproduce: Open a PR based on master at d641acf2 and read the 'Test suite passes on macOS system bash 3.2 (portability floor)' leg. Seen on PR #77 run 34216364984 job 102028941573. Locally: nix develop --command bash32-run chat/tests/test-chat-broadcast-stall.sh
bugs.observed: test-chat-broadcast-stall FAIL (exit 1), 'the subscriber never received a message, so it was not a connection the server was servicing:' with sub.out empty. The arming wait is 60 iterations of sleep 0.5, so the subscriber produced nothing for 30 seconds.
bugs.expected: The subscriber tail prints the opener's 'subscriber-armed' message within the 30 second wait, or the failure names something the change under test could have caused.
bugs.found_by: CI on PR #77, whose diff touches only the portability scanner, tony-the-pony and one test -- nothing that reaches chat
bugs.notes: Two live hypotheses, neither confirmed. (1) A timing flake: the same test passed on PR #76's macOS 3.2 leg from the same base d641acf2, and the arming wait is a fixed 30s poll on a shared runner. (2) An interaction with the B269 tail change merged in #75: the subscriber IS a tail, the test's own comment says it receives the message through tail's poll of the channel log, and 6986dd3e changed where tail starts -- a recorded cursor is now honoured whatever its value. That makes the test's dependence on tail's starting id load-bearing, which it was not when the test was written. Do not close this as a flake without re-running it several times on that leg, and check hypothesis 2 first because it is the one that would also be wrong in production. A re-run of job 102028941573 was queued 2026-09-08 and its result is the next evidence. EVIDENCE 2026-09-08: the re-run of the failed macOS 3.2 leg passed, and PR #77 is now 18/18 green with no change to the branch. That is one clean re-run on the same commit, which supports the timing-flake hypothesis and weakens the B269-tail one, but it is a single observation -- the entry still asks for repeated runs on that leg before closing, because a test that fails once in N is exactly the shape that gets dismissed and then blocks a merge at the worst moment. Keep it open until it has been seen to pass several times, or until someone reads the arming wait against tail's start position and rules the interaction out on the code. Additional evidence 2026-09-09: 5 independent CI runs of the macOS bash 3.2 leg (PRs #80-84, unrelated content, current master base) all PASS on test-chat-broadcast-stall, 0 failures. Combined with the 2026-09-08 clean re-run already recorded, this is 2 separate observation sessions with zero reproductions on 6 total runs. Strongly supports the timing-flake hypothesis over the B269-tail-interaction hypothesis; code reading (chat-client-rs tail(), non---local path) confirms the socket tail prints PRIVMSG lines directly via live push as they arrive over the connection, not only via a FETCH poll as the tests own comment claims -- so if the B269 interaction were real it would need JOIN to lose a race with the very next send on a fresh channel, which 6/6 clean runs argue against. Not closing: the entry itself asks for it to stay open until seen passing several times OR ruled out on the code, and "several" plus a code reading that weakens but does not eliminate hypothesis 2 is closer to that bar but I am not the one who gets to decide it is cleared.

bugs.title: A forwarded join makes the owner a member of a channel its tail never prints
bugs.reproduce: With a tail owning the session on #a: chat-client-rs join --chan "#b"   (forwarded to the owner), then have a peer post in #b
bugs.observed: The owner sends JOIN #b on its connection, so the server counts it as present in #b and relays #b traffic to it. The tail loop filters PRIVMSG on its single --chan, so every #b line is read off the stream and dropped. The agent is in the member list of a channel it cannot hear, and its #b cursor never moves.
bugs.expected: Either the join is followed -- its messages printed and its cursor kept -- or it is refused. Being a silent member is the one outcome that misleads the peers who can see the nick in NAMES.
bugs.mechanism: serve_join (T107) writes JOIN on the owner connection, but the tail loop was written for exactly one channel and compares against o.chan. Membership therefore became a property of the connection while listening stayed a property of the loop, and the two diverged the moment join could be forwarded.
bugs.fix: d7c12ec5 (T112) -- a tail follows a SET of channels and serve_join adds to it, so a channel the owner is a member of is a channel the tail prints. Membership and listening are now one decision in one place instead of two in two.
bugs.verification: chat/tests/test-chat-owner-socket.sh asserts on the TAIL'S OWN OUTPUT, the only place that distinguishes following from merely joining: a forwarded join, then a peer posting into that channel, then the message appearing in the tail's log. The send must come from a PEER because the server deliberately does not echo a PRIVMSG to its sender (B249), so a test that posted to itself would assert on traffic that is never pushed -- that mistake was made first and caught by the test failing. Mutation: disabling the push in serve_join fails three assertions, including this one.
bugs.found_by: aiskills, writing serve_join for T107 -- noted in the code and in conversation and NOT filed at the time, which is the process failure this entry also records

bugs.title: The interactive-shell grant does not cover an availability probe, so checking for the wrapper prompts
bugs.reproduce: With the installer grants in place (PR #76 section 13a), have an agent check whether the wrapper exists: command -v interactive-shell interactive-shell-input
bugs.observed: A permission prompt: "Do you want to proceed?" with "Ask rule Bash(bimport:*) overrides auto mode for this command." The probe is not covered by the installed grant, so an agent asking "is this tool here?" is interrupted before it can find out.
bugs.expected: An availability probe of a binary the installer just granted runs without a prompt. Whether a tool EXISTS is not a privileged question, and the grant already permits executing it.
bugs.mechanism: installer/src/70-permissions.sh grants Bash(<root>/interactive-shell/bin/**:*) -- the wrapper by PATH. A `command -v interactive-shell` is not that string, so no allow rule matches and the decision falls through to whatever ask rule does. The grant covers running the tool and not asking after it.
bugs.found_by: Tschallacka, screenshot of the prompt during an availability check
bugs.notes:
SECOND HALF, and the sharper one: the prompt in the screenshot fired on an ask rule for bimport, which was one of THREE names in a single command -v. So a compound probe is gated by the strictest rule among its arguments -- batching availability checks converts a permitted probe into a prompt, and the denial names a rule for a binary that was not the one being looked for, which is what makes it hard to read. That is Claude Code's matching, not this repo's, but it decides how the grant must be written: grant the probe SHAPE, and probe one binary per command rather than batching, so one unrelated ask rule cannot gate the rest.

Why it matters beyond the annoyance: a prompt on an availability check is precisely how a tool gets skipped rather than used, which is the failure PR #76's grant exists to prevent (see the interactive-shell description work and headless-is-not-a-smaller-interactive). A blocked probe reads to an agent as 'not available'.

bugs.title: ci-scope returns full on almost every commit, because the file that registers a new file is treated as able to alter every crate
bugs.reproduce: On a branch whose only source change is one crate: ./.github/ci-scope.sh --base origin/master   (measured 2026-09-08 on fix/chat-skill-two-postures, whose diff touched src/chat-client-rs plus one added test)
bugs.observed: scope=full, reason="install.sh changed, which can alter every crate". Re-running with install.sh removed from the change set: scope=full, reason="installer/src/50-manifest.sh changed, which can alter every crate". Both files changed only because ONE test filename was added to skill_files().
bugs.expected: A crate-scope decision narrowed to the crates a change can affect. Adding a filename to a manifest list cannot alter any crate, and install.sh is a generated artifact whose agreement with its sources CI already proves in a dedicated job.
bugs.mechanism: Two rules fire. install.sh is regenerated by installer/build.sh from installer/src/NN-*.sh, so any installer edit rewrites 232KB of generated content and matches the "install.sh changed" rule. And 50-manifest.sh is where every new file must be registered, so it matches the "installer/src changed" rule on any commit that adds a file. The selector is therefore disabled by the very act of adding a test -- which is the commit shape this repository sees most often.

bugs.title: test-chat.sh used the nick-suffix bug as its mention fixture, so fixing that bug broke the test
bugs.reproduce: Run chat/tests/test-chat.sh with a client where one session owns one connection (T107), on a host whose TMPDIR is short enough for the control socket to bind
bugs.observed: FAIL: mention was not surfaced: []. The tail --mentions --mention-exit never saw the message and never exited.
bugs.expected: A mention from another agent wakes a tailing agent. That is the feature, and it does not depend on how the sender is connected.
bugs.mechanism: The test sent the mention from the WATCHERS OWN state dir, and its comment said so: "the sender auto-suffixes on nick-in-use". It worked only because the send opened a SECOND connection that the server renamed (B283) -- the message therefore arrived as another party. T107 gives one session one connection, the send is performed on the tail own connection, and the server deliberately does not echo a PRIVMSG to its sender (B249), so the tail never saw it.
bugs.fix: the mention now comes from a separate peer state dir and nick, which is what the feature actually promises and holds on both sides of T107
bugs.verification: test-chat.sh exits 0 and the mention assertion passes. The fixture no longer depends on the owner socket being active, so it cannot regress with the socket path length again.
bugs.found_by: the hang investigation: the last trace line before the wait was the mention assertion failing
bugs.notes:
Cross-reference: B301 is why this presented as a three-hour hang rather than a two-minute failure.

WHY IT WAS INVISIBLE LOCALLY, which is the part worth keeping: the owner socket only binds when its path fits the unix address limit. A CI runner TMPDIR is short (~/work/_temp), so the socket bound, forwarding was active, and the mention never arrived. This workstation TMPDIR is long, so serve() declined to own, every verb opened its own connection exactly as before T107, and the test passed. The same commit therefore passed here and hung on all three CI legs, and the difference was a path length. Moving the socket to XDG_RUNTIME_DIR (short by construction, and what interactive-shell and ai-text-editor already use) is what made it reproduce locally within a minute.

bugs.title: A subagent that holds a presence tail leaves it orphaned, so its nick stays present with nobody reading
bugs.reproduce: Spawn a subagent whose brief tells it to hold presence per chat/SKILL.md Posture A, let it finish, then run: chat-client-rs names --chan "#ai-skills" and ps -eo pid,ppid,args | grep chat-client-rs
bugs.observed:
A subagent told to hold presence starts a background tail, and that tail is not stopped when the subagent finishes. It is reparented and keeps the connection, so the nick stays in the channel with nobody behind it.

Measured 2026-09-08 on #ai-skills. The nitpicker subagent completed; more than an hour later `names` still listed nitpicker, and its tail was pid 590403 with ppid 2475 -- reparented away from the claude process 4876 that had spawned it. The parent session's own tail, pid 586192, correctly still showed ppid 4876.

Why it matters more than an idle process: presence is how agents decide whether a peer can be reached. The chat skill says so plainly -- "is that peer listening right now?" is what `names` answers, and a nick that is present but unattended is the one answer that cannot be recovered from. A mention addressed to it is delivered to a connection nobody reads, and the sender has no way to tell that from a slow reply. The skill already warns about the same silence for a detached `&`; this is the same failure arriving through a different door, because it is the AGENT that ended rather than the shell.

What is missing is the symmetric half of a rule the skill already states. It says whatever runs the tail must notice when the tail exits. Nothing says what stops the tail when the RUNNER exits, and for a subagent that is the common case: the agent is finished the moment it reports, while its background task has no reason to stop.
bugs.expected: A tail stops when the agent that started it is done, or the skill says how to stop it and whose job that is. A nick in names means somebody is reading.
bugs.mechanism: The tail is a background process of the subagent. Nothing links its lifetime to the agents: when the agent reports and ends, the process is reparented and keeps its TLS connection, and the server has no reason to drop a live connection. The skill covers the tail exiting unnoticed; it does not cover the runner exiting first.
bugs.found_by: Tschallacka, noticing nitpicker in the channel while it was not among the active agents

bugs.title: The documented renders sort ids as strings, so item 10 lands between item 1 and item 2
bugs.reproduce: jq -r 'def prank: {urgent:0,high:1,normal:2,low:3,someday:4}[.priority]//5; def srank: {blocking:0,major:1,minor:2,cosmetic:3}[.severity]//4; [.bugs[]] | sort_by(prank, srank, .id)[] | .id' BUGS.json
bugs.observed: B2 B10 B13 B3 B4 B5 B7 B8 B9 B11 B12 B6 B1 - B10 sits between B2 and B3. The todo queue renders T13 T14 T15 before T21, and T5 T6 after T31.
bugs.expected: Numeric order within a priority band: B2 B3 B4 B5 B6 B7 ... B13.
bugs.mechanism: Seven snippets across the two SKILL.md files sort with sort_by(rank, .id) or sort_by(prank, srank, .id), where .id is a string, so jq compares byte-wise and "B10" < "B3". jq has no natural-sort builtin.
bugs.fix: def idkey: [(. | scan("[0-9]+") | tonumber)?, .]; added beside the existing rank defs in all seven snippets across both SKILL.md files, and every sort_by now passes (.id | idkey). Ids stay free-form, so nothing had to be renumbered and the commit messages that reference T30 and B8 still resolve. The id row in both field tables says why the def is there, so it does not get removed as noise.
bugs.verification: The documented snippets were extracted from SKILL.md and run verbatim against the real registers: top-level normal tasks read T1 T2 T3 T4 T5 T6 T13 T14 T15 T16 T17 T21 T23 T24 T26 T27 T30 T31, and a sub-task renders under its parent. Mutation: dropping idkey from one snippet gives T1 T13 T14 T15 T16 T17 T2 T21 ... T3 T30 T31 T4 T5 T6. A first mutation probe looked green because within the high band the ids happen to sort identically either way -- the normal band is where it shows.
bugs.found_by: a bug report written against 1.4.2 by an earlier session (bug-report-old-version.md), re-verified against the current registers
bugs.notes: Live, and it produced misleading output all through this session without being noticed - every register render printed above is in the wrong order. Two candidate fixes. Zero-padded ids make lexical sort correct with no snippet change, but require renumbering ids that commit messages already reference (T30, B8), because a mix of T5 and T05 sorts wrong anyway. A derived key - def idkey: [(. | scan("[0-9]+") | tonumber)?, .] - keeps ids free-form and is the only option that also respects the skills own T1 -> T1a convention, placing a child immediately after its parent in a flat render; length-then-lexical looked cheaper but drifts T1a to the end. Its stated cost, a def copied into seven snippets, is already the pattern in these files: the rank and prank/srank defs are duplicated across all of them today, so this adds no new kind of debt.

bugs.title: bugs/todo update accept --title, ignore it, then refuse saying no field was named

bugs.title: bug-add.sh --mechanism produces invalid JSON when the mechanism text contains a double quote
bugs.reproduce: BUGS_JSON=/tmp/probe.json bash planning/scripts/bug-add.sh --title probe --reproduce probe --observed probe --expected probe --mechanism 'the value is "quoted" here'
