bugs.expected: A mechanism containing a double quote (or a backslash) is stored verbatim and read back unchanged.
bugs.mechanism: bug-add.sh:50 built the JSON string by hand as mechanism="\"$2\"", wrapping the raw argument in literal quote characters, and passed the result through jq --argjson. --argjson parses its value as JSON, so an embedded double quote terminates the string early and the document is invalid; a backslash would corrupt it similarly. The hand-rolled wrapping existed so that omitting --mechanism could pass the bare literal null. Fixed by encoding the value with jq -Rs, which emits a properly escaped JSON string, while the default remains the literal null so the omitted case is unchanged. jq is verified present at bug-add.sh:34, before argument parsing, so using it during parsing is safe. --parent at :51 still uses the hand-rolled form; bug ids contain no quotes so it does not misbehave today, and it is left for a separate entry rather than widened into this one.
bugs.fix: planning/scripts/bug-add.sh:50 — encode the --mechanism value with 'jq -Rs .' instead of wrapping it in literal quote characters; the default stays the bare literal null so the omitted-mechanism path is unchanged.
bugs.verification: Mutation both ways against a temp register copy. With the original line 50, --mechanism 'the value is "quoted" here' fails: 'jq: invalid JSON text passed to --argjson', exit 2, nothing filed. With the fix, --mechanism 'value is "quoted" and has a \backslash' files the entry and 'jq -r .bugs[-1].mechanism' reads back exactly 'value is "quoted" and has a \backslash', with 'jq -e .bugs|length' confirming the register is still valid JSON. Omitting --mechanism still stores null. planning/tests/test-register-helpers.sh and planning/tests/test-add-planning-bug.sh both PASS, test-register-helpers.sh also PASSes under bash32-run (the 3.2 floor), and 'shellcheck -s bash --severity=error planning/scripts/bug-add.sh' is clean.

bugs.title: update-step.sh leaves the atomicity boxes ticked when a step returns to incomplete

bugs.title: reg_next_id mints the same id in two worktrees, because it can only see the register in its own tree
bugs.reproduce: Launch two subagents with isolation: worktree. In each, run planning/scripts/register-read.sh bug next-id (or any bug-add.sh). Both return the same number, and both are correct about the register they can see.
bugs.observed: Two writers minted B77 for different defects within the hour: the main checkout for 'subagent worktrees are still created from a stale commit', a worktree for the E2BIG render failure. The worktree author had reasoned about collisions and deliberately started above the B74-B76 range it knew about; it still collided, because B77 was minted in main after that worktree forked. Neither party did anything wrong and no tool warned either of them.
bugs.expected: Either an id is unique across the trees that will merge into one register, or minting says which register it consulted so a caller can tell the answer is local.
bugs.mechanism: reg_next_id computes max(id)+1 over the single JSON file in the tree it runs in. That is the only register it can see, and a git worktree gives each writer its own copy, so concurrent branches diverge silently and their ids overlap on merge. The register's own soundness check catches a duplicate id inside one file, which is why this survives: each file is internally sound and the collision only exists in the union.
bugs.found_by: main session and the webview subagent, independently minting B77 within the hour

The strongest candidate is build state combined with suite ordering: setup-dev-env.sh had never completed in that worktree, and the test runs install.sh --skill <s> --target <installed> (tests/test-register-schemas.sh:61), so if a register binary or generated library is produced as a side effect of an EARLIER test in the suite, the verdict depends on suite order and on what a previous run left behind -- which fits fail-then-pass. bugs.title: Hub::append's stale-lock protocol is inverted, so an empty lock directory blocks a channel permanently
bugs.reproduce: mkdir "$AI_CHAT_HOME/channels/#chan.lock", then send to that channel
bugs.observed: every send to that channel fails with 'no echo from server' after about 5s, and the message is either lost or appended LATE, after the client reported failure -- both measured in one run (id 2 landed from a send whose client had already exited). bugs.title: a stray directory under src/ breaks the whole cargo build, and git reports the tree clean
bugs.reproduce: leave a directory under src/ that contains only gitignored content (a stale target/ from a deleted crate), then run ./setup-dev-env.sh
bugs.observed: 0 of 64 binaries built; every crate fails with 'failed to read /home/mdibbets/git/ai-skills/src/chat/Cargo.toml: No such file or directory (os error 2)'. git status reported the tree clean throughout, because the directory's only contents were ignored. bugs.title: ai-text-editor-server start prints no endpoint, so a caller waiting for one hangs
bugs.reproduce: bin/<triple>/ai-text-editor-server start --file FILE  # capture stdout
bugs.observed: Zero bytes on stdout. The server is running -- ps shows it and 'open --file FILE' then works by discovery -- but nothing announces the endpoint at the moment a caller needs it. An agent that captured stdout and waited for a line sat there until interrupted.
bugs.expected: One line naming the endpoint, or an explicit statement that discovery is the only route. Either removes the wait.
bugs.mechanism: The endpoint IS recorded -- in the session file written by --save-session-token, and in the editor sessions.json registry -- so the information exists and is simply never printed. The skill's Start section shows the start command with no note that it is silent.
bugs.fix: c1ce47d — announce() prints {file,endpoint,discovery} to stdout on start (src/ai-text-editor/src/bin/ai-text-editor-server.rs:761); no commit since has removed it
bugs.verification: Third test drive, 2026-09-06, installed 3c2b659 build: the register reproduction printed the JSON line within one second (218 bytes, exit on kill, no hang); the original zero-stdout observation cannot be reproduced on any build available here
bugs.found_by: using the skill on 2026-09-04; it cost an interrupted turn

bugs.title: A job its owning client left behind pins the idle watchdog forever; abandoned servers accumulate
bugs.reproduce: run cargo test -p ai-text-editor --test cli_flow (the job_verbs_require_the_resume_token leg job-starts and never releases); afterwards pgrep -af "ai-text-editor-server start --file /tmp/nix-shell" and watch ages climb past an hour with a 600s idle default
bugs.observed: 16 servers alive 5 to 13 hours on this machine, ps state Sl, their /tmp/nix-shell scratch already deleted; the very same drive produced 3 fresh ones in its own test legs within an hour; GitHub runners terminate orphans of every job as routine
bugs.expected: the idle watchdog reaps a server whose jobs lost their owner; detached:true is the only reason a job keeps a server alive
bugs.mechanism: spawn_idle_watchdog continues while any tab has an active job (src/ai-text-editor/src/bin/ai-text-editor-server.rs:497-502) without distinguishing detached from ownerless jobs; once the server is undiscoverable (endpoint gone with the scratch dir) nothing else can reach it either
bugs.fix: ad51b47 (PR #66, merged 02e5e70) — the idle watchdog pins only on detached active jobs (jobs.rs has_active_detached); an undetached orphan no longer suspends the timeout
bugs.verification: cli_flow an_ownerless_queued_job_does_not_pin_the_idle_watchdog (2s idle timeout, unreleased job-start, server must die) and a_detached_job_pins_the_watchdog_until_its_owner_releases_it (alive past the timeout while detached, dead after release); removing either half of the pin split fails the matching test. Green on the x86_64-musl and darwin CI legs.

bugs.title: ai-text-editor CLI silently drops unknown --flags/-x options: a typo-ed parameter vanishes and the operation succeeds without it
bugs.reproduce: On the installed build: cursor -f F -a home --zzz 5 answers a normal data frame rc 0; cursor -f F -a home -i 1 answers "id": 0 (cursor 0 acted on); replace -f F -o 0 --delete-lent 8 -t X -r 0 answers revision 1 and the buffer reads back XDELETEME-keep - the insert ran, the 8-byte delete was silently discarded.
bugs.observed: Unknown long and short options are accepted and ignored by the client; the requested operation then runs with whatever the dropped argument would have changed. The server-side unknown_argument guard cannot help: the key never leaves the client.
bugs.expected: An unknown option is a usage error (64) naming the offending token, the way unknown command already dies; nothing is sent to the server.
bugs.mechanism: src/ai-text-editor/src/bin/ai-text-editor.rs option() (master line 340) pull-extracts known names from argv and nothing ever inspects the residue; every verb shares the flaw. Accepts-but-ignores class: B171/B175/B205 shipped the same shape one layer in.
bugs.fix: PR #68 (155254e): option()/flag() register every name their lookup consulted; reject_unknown_options() runs before any request leaves the client and exits 64 naming the token; value positions after value-taking options are exempt
bugs.verification: Reproduced on the 02e5e70-era installed build: cursor -i 1 answered id 0, --zzz 5 answered a normal frame, replace --delete-lent 8 inserted without deleting. Test unknown_options_are_refused_before_anything_is_sent (src/ai-text-editor/tests/cli_flow.rs): mutation = delete the reject_unknown_options call and both the long and short rejections return success on cursor 0; the --id control asserts the rejection invents no false unknowns. Green on release x86_64-unknown-linux-musl and all 18 CI legs.
bugs.found_by: fourth ai-text-editor test drive 2026-09-06 (D1)

bugs.title: the installer can write no codex permission config, so codex is told to grant its own access by hand
bugs.reproduce: Run the permission step with a codex root selected: SELECTED_TARGET_PATHS=($HOME/.codex/skills) worktrees_permission_step (same for planning_permission_step). Observed live on 2026-09-07 while verifying the worktree grant across three agents.
bugs.observed: codex: no safe auto-editable permission file was modified. - grant codex read, write and execute under /home/mdibbets/.config/tsch-ai-worktrees ... Claude and opencode both had their configs edited in the same run; codex fell through to printed instructions, because agent_kind_for_root returns 'codex' and neither permission step has a codex arm.
bugs.expected: The installer edits ~/.codex/config.toml the way it edits the other two. Codex has exactly the knobs needed: sandbox_workspace_write.writable_roots is a list of paths writable outside the workspace, and [projects."<path>"] trust_level = "trusted" marks a directory trusted. This machine's config already carries "/home/mdibbets/.config/tsch-ai-skills" and "/tmp" in writable_roots, added by hand - which is the work the installer should be doing.
bugs.mechanism: installer/src/70-permissions.sh: both permission steps dispatch on agent_kind_for_root with arms for claude and opencode only; every other kind, codex included, hits the *) print_manual_* fallback. There is no codex writer at all, and config.toml is TOML rather than JSON, so rjq - the installer's only permitted runtime dependency - cannot edit it, which is presumably why it was never written.
bugs.found_by: live three-agent verification of the worktrees grant, 2026-09-07
bugs.notes:
B236 is the cosmetic half found in the same output: the fallback's worked example is Claude Code settings.json syntax whatever agent it addresses. Separate entry because a codex writer removes the fallback for codex without fixing the example for openclaw, cline or a custom root.

Live test result that bears on the priority: codex DID write and edit files in a worktree under the new root with no prompt - but only because the worktree was its own cwd, which workspace-write makes writable by definition. It was not the grant working; there was no grant. An agent whose cwd is elsewhere, writing into a worktree, is still outside writable_roots and would be refused. So this is filed major but not urgent: it bites the cross-worktree case rather than the common one. CONFIRMED with the test that actually isolates it, 2026-09-07, at Michael's direction. The first run was a false positive because the worktree was the agent's own cwd; this run put the cwd somewhere else entirely - a fresh 'git init' directory holding only the prompt file - and asked each agent to write into a worktree under the new root.

Codex refused and asked, verbatim: 'Would you like to run the following command? ... Reason: May I create and update the requested file in /home/mdibbets/.config/tsch-ai-worktrees/perm-probe2, OUTSIDE THE WORKSPACE WRITE ROOTS?' The request was declined and no file was created, which is the failure this entry describes: the installer granted codex nothing, so the worktrees root is not in writable_roots and a cross-directory write stops for a human.

The same test passed with no prompt for the two agents that DID get a grant: opencode wrote, appended and read the file (its external_directory rule on the worktrees root is what permits writing outside the cwd, so that rule earns its place), and Claude Code completed in 21s with '0 awaiting input'. Both files verified on disk, and the blank cwd still held only PROMPT.md afterwards, so nothing leaked into it.

One prompt that is NOT this bug, for whoever reads this next: Claude Code asks a one-time workspace-trust question for any first-time directory ('Is this a project you created or one you trust?'). That is about the CWD, not the target, and no permission grant suppresses it.

bugs.title: the unknown-argument check is global rather than per-verb, so a key another verb reads is silently ignored
bugs.reproduce: Before B226: replace --range-start-line 2 --range-end-line 4 -t '' -r N. The four range_* keys are in KNOWN_PAYLOAD_KEYS because read takes them.
bugs.observed: The request passed the door and the replace handler ignored all four, falling back to the cursor position — a silent misplaced edit. handle()'s check refuses only a key no handler ANYWHERE reads.
bugs.expected: A key no handler for THIS verb reads is refused by name, which is what B180 and B187 set out to guarantee. The check is one list for the whole protocol, so it cannot see the difference.
bugs.mechanism: src/ai-text-editor/src/bin/ai-text-editor-server.rs, handle(): the KNOWN_PAYLOAD_KEYS membership test is protocol-wide. Per-verb key sets exist only in the MCP adapter's tool schemas, which the CLI and hand-sent NDJSON do not consult.
bugs.found_by: found while fixing B226: the range keys were accepted and dropped, which the entry had not recorded
bugs.notes: Binding the per-verb table to both surfaces surfaced three live instances of this class, now filed separately so each closes on its own evidence: B250 (insert accepts delete_len and answers success), B251 (search advertises pager_key and historical, which only page reads), B252 (index advertises an action it never reads). B253 is unrelated to this class but was found in the same pass - the endpoint_for_file /tmp fallback.

bugs.title: a document mode is per-server, so a second file opened into a running workspace can never be a raw or hex tab
bugs.reproduce: Over MCP with a workspace already running for this agent: open a second file with document_mode hex_view.
bugs.observed: The tab comes back mode TextUtf8. Verified after B217: a COLD open with document_mode hex_view answers HexView, but the same argument on a file added to an existing server is ignored, exactly as documented ('shapes only a server this call starts').
bugs.expected: A mode is a property of a tab, not of a server, so a raw or hex tab is reachable whether or not a workspace is already running. As it stands SKILL.md capability 2 is reachable only on an agent's very first open, which in a long-lived session is almost never.
bugs.mechanism: select_tab()'s open path passes state_guard.mode to open_additional_tab(), so an added tab inherits the server's startup mode; document_mode reaches only autostart_server()'s argv. B217 made the argument declarable and honoured on a cold start, which is as far as a schema fix can go.
bugs.found_by: verifying B217 against the real MCP surface, fifth drive's fix batch

bugs.title: the server never relays JOIN to a channel's other members, so a client already connected never sees a nick arrive
bugs.reproduce: Open a standard IRC client (Konversation) on the channel, then start a second client: chat-client-rs tail --chan '#ai-skills' --nick aiskills --mentions --mention-exit
bugs.observed: The IRC client's nick list shows only its own nick while the tail is connected and receiving PRIVMSG from that channel. Reported from a Konversation screenshot: joined #ai-skills at 14:12, nick list contains mdibbets alone, while aiskills was tailing and answering.
bugs.expected: A nick that joins is announced to the channel, as RFC 1459 requires: every other member receives ':nick!user@host JOIN #chan' and their client adds it to the nick list. A human watching the channel can see which agents are listening; at the moment they cannot.
bugs.mechanism:
src/chat-server-rs/src/main.rs:755-787, the JOIN handler. It echoes the JOIN to the JOINING connection only (line 762, w(st, ...)), adds the nick to hub.channels (764), and answers 353/366 to the joiner (781/785). Nothing is offered to the other peers, so a connection that was already in the channel is never told. The membership itself is correct - the tail does send JOIN (src/chat-client-rs/src/main.rs:1582) and is in hub.channels - which is why it receives broadcasts while remaining invisible. Only a client that joins LATER sees it, via the 353 NAMES reply, so whether an agent appears depends on join order.

The fanout to reuse is right there in the PRIVMSG handler (lines 866-876): copy the peer list under hub.writers, release the lock, then p.offer(&chan, &out) per peer, excluding *i != idx. Peer::offer (151) already skips a non-member, so the scoping is free.
bugs.found_by: Michael, from a Konversation nick list on 2026-09-07
bugs.notes: B245 is the departure half. Kept separate because fixing arrivals alone leaves a nick list that only ever grows: every agent that ever joined stays listed, which is arguably more misleading than the current under-reporting. Both should land together even though they close separately. VERIFIED ON THE WIRE 2026-09-07: Michael confirmed aiskills now appears in Konversation's nick list against the restarted server. That is the check the unit tests explicitly could not make, since the dev shell has no raw IRC client. B246 is what remains: the fix is server-side only, and the client still discards the membership lines, so humans see presence and agents do not. SECOND SYMPTOM, from sanitairkamer 2026-09-07, and it is worse than a stale list: the silent failure produced a WRONG INFERENCE. It read 'aiskills never appeared in my nick list all session' as 'that agent is not connected' rather than 'JOIN was never relayed to me', so it stopped addressing a peer that was present and answering. A presence bug that reads as absence is exactly the kind that makes agents stop coordinating with each other.

bugs.title: search advertises pager_key and historical, which only page reads, so a caller avoiding a rescan triggers one
bugs.reproduce: Over MCP: search --file F --mode exact_text --query Q --pager-key KEY (or --historical), following the tool schema that advertises both.
bugs.observed: Both keys are accepted and ignored by search, so the search runs as a fresh scan. A caller passing them precisely to resume an existing result set instead paid for a full rescan, with nothing saying so.
bugs.expected: Refused by name on search, naming page as the verb that reads them. The cost is the point: these two keys exist to AVOID a scan, so silently ignoring them inverts their purpose.
bugs.mechanism: Same root as B237: the key check was protocol-wide, and pager_key/historical are read by the page handler. B186 already fixed the sibling case where search silently ignored --offset; these two were the same shape and were missed because the check could not distinguish verbs.
bugs.found_by: surfaced by B237's fix, editor-batch agent 2026-09-07

bugs.title: a write-only agent is invisible and unreachable on the bus, with nothing saying so
bugs.reproduce: Have an agent participate using only one-shot chat-client-rs send calls, as editor-batch does. Watch the channel from a standard IRC client.
bugs.observed: The nick never appears in the channel listing and cannot be woken by a mention. Michael noticed exactly this: 'editor-batch isn't in the channel listing?' - while that agent had posted six messages in the preceding half hour. pgrep confirms it holds no client process at all between sends.
bugs.expected: An agent that participates in a channel is either visible and reachable, or is told it is neither. Reachability is the part that matters: a peer cannot hand it a decision, so coordination degrades to one-way reporting and the other side has to poll or guess. Visibility comes free once it holds a tail.
bugs.mechanism: Two correct decisions colliding. B247 removed the JOIN from send, because a post does not imply presence and the sender's membership was never checked - so a write-only agent now holds no membership at any moment. chat/SKILL.md names the mention tail as the listening posture, but an agent that only reports has no obvious reason to arm one, and nothing states that the cost of skipping it is being unaddressable. Before B247 the join/quit churn per send was noise, but it was at least evidence the agent existed (B247's own observed section).
bugs.found_by: Michael, noticing editor-batch absent from the nick list while it was actively reporting, 2026-09-07
bugs.notes: B256 is the discovery half and the cheaper one: the server has answered NAMES all along and no client verb asks. Adding one makes presence queryable on demand, which answers 'is that agent live?' without requiring every agent to hold a tail. It does not replace this entry - a queryable list still shows nothing for an agent that holds no connection, and unreachability is the part that actually costs coordination.

bugs.title: todo update cannot set refs, and --touching matches only refs, so an entry filed without them is permanently unfindable by area
bugs.reproduce: todo list --touching verbosity, against a register whose T99 is titled "Give editor responses a verbosity contract, so a two-line edit does not cost a screen of JSON". Then: todo update T99 --refs src/ai-text-editor/src/bin/ai-text-editor-server.rs
bugs.observed: The list answers nothing at all, though the word is in the entrys title and throughout its detail. And the update is impossible: `todo update` takes --status, --priority, --detail, --blocked-on, --note and --append-note, and no --refs, so the omission cannot be corrected after filing. Measured on the same register: `todo list --touching session.rs` DOES return T98, and session.rs appears only in T98s refs and in no title - which pins the matcher to refs alone.
bugs.expected: Either --touching searches the fields a human would expect it to (refs, title, detail), or `todo update` can set refs so an entry filed without them can be repaired. As it stands the two gaps combine: T99 is an ai-text-editor task that `todo list --touching ai-text-editor` does not return, and nothing shipped can fix that. The brief for this batch asked for exactly that repair, which is how it was found.
bugs.mechanism: The `todo` crate: the --touching filter tests the refs array only, and the update subcommands argument table has no refs entry (the add subcommand does, via --refs a,b). So refs are write-once at creation. Two separate small gaps whose intersection is the defect - either one alone would be survivable.
bugs.found_by: the editor batch brief asking me to add refs to T99 so `todo list --touching ai-text-editor` would stop missing it; the tool has no way to do it

bugs.title: test-chat-resolution case 5 discovers whatever server is live on the machine, so it fails and writes to it
bugs.reproduce: With any chat server running on this machine and announcing on UDP 7780: bash chat/tests/test-chat-resolution.sh (on unmodified origin/master, a363c91f). By hand: start the case-5 server with AI_CHAT_HOME=$R/lh CHAT_ANNOUNCE=1 CHAT_BCAST=127.0.0.1 CHAT_ANNOUNCE_HOST=127.0.0.1, point a fresh client state dir at the dead 127.0.0.1:1, then send --chan "#ladder" --text "resolve me" and print session show.
bugs.observed: FAIL: send did not resolve a dead session to the live server. By hand: send exits 70 with "chat-client-rs: no echo from server", and session show reports server=127.0.0.1:37251 -- a server this test never started, while its own server had bound 45769. The PRIVMSG is written before the echo wait, so the test posts "resolve me" into that unrelated server store.
bugs.expected: The ladder resolves to the server the test started, on the port it recorded, and nothing the test does reaches a server it did not start. A suite result must not depend on what else is running on the machine.
bugs.mechanism: Case 5 relies on real UDP discovery on the DEFAULT beacon port (7780), which is deliberate for the contract it pins, and discover_candidates returns every announcing server with LAN addresses before loopback. Any other server announcing on 7780 -- an agent chat on the developer machine, or a sibling worktree - is therefore a candidate, and it is dialled and written to before the test server is. The other cases in the file set CHAT_ANNOUNCE=0 for exactly this reason; case 5 cannot, because it needs a beacon, and it does not scope the one it needs to a private port.
bugs.found_by: T90: the scoped chat suite run failed here, and the same failure reproduced on an unmodified origin/master worktree as a control
bugs.notes: AI_CHAT_BEACON_PORT is read by the client and CHAT_ANNOUNCE_PORT-equivalent handling exists on the server, so the fix is to give case 5 a private beacon port rather than to weaken the contract. src/chat-mcp/tests/mcp_flow.rs does this: its server announces on a port nothing listens to, and its session is pre-seeded so resolution never reaches discovery.

bugs.title: the TLS-only assertion in test-chat.sh cannot fail: both arms of its case are no-ops
bugs.reproduce: read chat/tests/test-chat.sh lines 64-72.
bugs.observed: The block runs openssl s_client, captures plainout, and matches it with `case` whose two arms are `*not a valid*|*alert*|"") : ;;` and `*) : ;;`. Every outcome is a no-op, so the block passes whatever the server does -- including a server that completed a plain handshake.
bugs.expected: A plain, non-TLS connect does not complete a handshake, asserted so that a server which accepted one fails the test.
bugs.mechanism: The case was written to accept several shapes of expected failure and the catch-all was left as a no-op rather than a t_fail, so the discrimination the block exists for was never wired. The comment above it states the contract the code does not check.
bugs.fix: 2e119d55 on fix/b273-tls-only-assertion — the block writes IRC to a plain socket over /dev/tcp and fails on a welcome numeric, replacing an openssl s_client probe whose case arms were both no-ops
bugs.verification: chat/tests/test-chat.sh PASS with the new block against the real server. Mutation: the same probe run against a listener that answers ':server 001 plainprobe :Welcome to the plaintext bus' takes the t_fail arm, so the assertion detects a server that registers a plaintext client. /dev/tcp measured present in the bash 3.2 floor build, and the probe prints a SKIP where it is absent.
bugs.found_by: t90-chat-mcp, while auditing the chat suite's tool dependencies for B272
bugs.notes: The probe it runs is also not the one the comment describes: openssl s_client speaks TLS, so it cannot show what a PLAIN connect does. Asserting the contract needs a plain socket write and no handshake in the reply. B272 covers the same block depending on an undeclared openssl.

bugs.title: two chat tests start servers that announce on the machine's live beacon port
bugs.reproduce: AI_CHAT_HOME=$(mktemp -d) chat-server-rs 0 2>&1 | head -1 -- the start line chat/tests/test-chat-broadcast-stall.sh:87 and chat/tests/test-chat-descriptor-leak.sh:93 use, neither of which sets CHAT_ANNOUNCE or CHAT_BEACON_PORT.
bugs.observed: chat-server-rs: announcing 127.0.0.1:44947 every 2s on UDP 7780 via 127.0.0.1. UDP 7780 is the default beacon every agent on the machine discovers on, so for the length of the test an unrelated client can resolve to a server that is about to be killed.
bugs.expected: A suite server is invisible to anything outside the test: CHAT_ANNOUNCE=0 where the test needs no beacon, or a private CHAT_BEACON_PORT where it does.
bugs.mechanism: Announcing is on by default and the two files set neither variable. The other two tests in the same directory do: test-chat-resolution.sh passes CHAT_ANNOUNCE=0 with a comment naming this exact hazard, and test-chat.sh gives its server CHAT_BEACON_PORT=47991. The rule is established in the suite; these two files do not follow it.
bugs.fix: 416dfb25 on fix/b274-suite-beacon-isolation — both servers start with CHAT_BEACON_PORT set to a port nothing listens on (47992, 47993)
bugs.verification: Observed both ways with the same binary: with no CHAT_BEACON_PORT the server logs 'announcing 127.0.0.1:44947 every 2s on UDP 7780'; with CHAT_BEACON_PORT=47992 it logs 'announcing 127.0.0.1:35773 every 2s on UDP 47992'. Both suites pass with the change: test-chat-broadcast-stall.sh PASS, test-chat-descriptor-leak.sh PASS. CHAT_BEACON_PORT rather than CHAT_ANNOUNCE=0 keeps the announce socket, which the descriptor-leak ceiling is measured against.
bugs.found_by: t90-chat-mcp, auditing the chat suite after B270
bugs.notes: B270 is the same isolation boundary crossed the other way: there the suite CONSUMES the live beacon and resolves to a real server. Fixing either leaves the other open.

bugs.title: a failed install leaves a half-written skill directory and reports it as a raw cp error
bugs.reproduce: git archive origin/master | tar -x -C /tmp/fresh; cd /tmp/fresh; bash install.sh --skill bug-report --target /tmp/installed --yes; echo "exit=$?"; ls /tmp/installed/bug-report
bugs.observed: exit=1, with the only diagnosis being "cp: cannot stat '/tmp/fresh/bug-report/bin/x86_64-unknown-linux-musl/bugs': No such file or directory". /tmp/installed/bug-report exists and holds SKILL.md, both schemas, docs/, binaries.tsv and requires.tsv -- everything except the binary and .version, which is written after the copies and so never runs.

bugs.title: chat/SKILL.md's presence tail advances the session cursor, so a later read reports nothing new
bugs.reproduce: Read chat/SKILL.md:201, :234 and :277 together.
bugs.observed: :201 is a copyable command ending in a bare '&' for the presence tail, and :234 calls backgrounding it with '&' the exception to the rule below. :277 states that rule as 'Start it as a tracked background task, never with a detached &', and :285-287 says a plain '&' inside another command is invisible to the Claude Code harness. The two passages give opposite instructions for the same command.
bugs.expected: One instruction for how to start the presence tail. On Claude Code that is run_in_background, since the document's own reasoning at :277-283 applies to the presence tail as much as to the guard.
bugs.mechanism: The exception at :234 was written for the harness-wake argument only: the presence tail is meant to outlive the turn, so nothing needs to be woken when it exits. But :277-283 gives a second, independent reason that the exception does not address - a tail advances the channel cursor as it reads, so an '&' tail invisible to the harness consumes messages that the next read then skips as already seen. That harm is caused by the tail consuming the stream, not by anything waiting on its exit, so it applies to the presence tail unchanged. An agent copying :201 in Claude Code gets the silent message loss :283 records as having already happened.
bugs.fix: Already resolved in the tree by the time this was picked up (chat/SKILL.md has since had several unrelated wake-guard commits -- efa4a18, 993217a, d6e54af, e0048de, 45076a9 -- that also carried this fix along). The presence-tail example now reads "Start it as a TRACKED background task -- not with a detached `&`" (line 230) with `--no-session` explained right beside it (line 232), consistently with the rule stated later (line 429) and the other --no-session guidance (lines 365, 405, 527). No remaining bare-& instruction for the presence tail anywhere in the file; the one remaining bare & (line 617) starts the server, a different, legitimate case. The register entry was simply never closed.
bugs.verification: grep -n "no-session|detached|tracked background" chat/SKILL.md: every presence-tail example uses --no-session and the tracked-background-task wording consistently; the only remaining bare & starts chat-server-rs, out of this scope.
bugs.found_by: nitpicker
bugs.notes: Narrowed after measuring, 2026-09-07. The harness-invisibility half of the original filing does not hold: a bare-& tail spawned from one Claude Code Bash call was still running in the next call (pid 1311541, chat-client-rs), and names listed the probe nick throughout. So :234's exception is correct that & is usable for a tail nothing waits on, and :201 is not wrong for that reason. What remains is the cursor: the presence tail consumes the stream under the caller's session, so a later 'read' correctly reports nothing new, which is the silent loss :283 records. The fix is not to forbid the & but to say beside :201 that the presence tail owns the cursor and the log it writes is what you read - as the nitpicker profile's step 2 now does.

bugs.title: test-npm-package packs into a fixed tarball name in the repo root, so two runs in one checkout corrupt each other
bugs.reproduce: Run planning/tests/test-npm-package.sh in one shell while another agent runs it (or any npm pack) in the same checkout.
bugs.observed: gzip: stdin: unexpected end of file / tar: Unexpected EOF in archive / tar: Error is not recoverable: exiting now, and the test exits 2. Seen three times today with agents sharing this checkout; a clean re-run passes every time.

One run reads the tarball while another is still writing or has already removed it in its cleanup trap. run-tests.sh holds a machine-wide lock, but a test invoked directly (which is how anyone debugs one, and how every agent here runs it) bypasses that lock entirely.

bugs.title: insert refuses a valid --range-start-line that read accepts on the same tab
bugs.reproduce: Open a tab, then: insert --range-start-line 1754 --text X   (same tab, same revision, immediately followed by: read --range-start-line 1752 --range-end-line 1755, which succeeds)

bugs.fix: Not reproducible against a freshly built server (setup-dev-env.sh, 2026-09-09, current master): the same call now returns edit_range_unsupported ("a range is a span and insert places bytes at a point; `replace` takes the range") instead of the confusing argument_out_of_range on a quoted numeric string. The note on this entry already suspected the installed binary was stale; it was. Likely folded into the B237 per-verb payload_keys/verbs::reads_payload_key generalization, which this entry never got matched against.
bugs.verification: ai-text-editor insert --range-start-line 1754 -t X -r 0 on a 2000-line tab: returns {"code":"edit_range_unsupported",...}, not argument_out_of_range. read at the same coordinates still succeeds, so the two verbs no longer disagree about the value, they disagree about whether the operation accepts a range at all, which is documented and correct.

The quoting in the message suggests the value reaches the validator as a JSON string on this path while read coerces it, so the likely site is insert's own argument parsing rather than the shared numeric validator -- read proves the shared one is sound. Not yet reproduced against a freshly built server: this host runs an installed binary, so confirm the version before ruling on it.

bugs.title: A remote mention-filtered read saves the channel cursor, marking skipped messages as seen
bugs.reproduce: With unread plain messages below a mention: chat-client-rs read --chan #c --mentions   (the remote arm, no --local), then chat-client-rs read --chan #c
bugs.observed: The mentions read saves the highest id it PRINTED as the cursor, so the plain read that follows returns nothing: the non-mention messages under that id were never printed by anything and are now behind the watermark.
bugs.expected: A mention-filtered read leaves the cursor alone, as the --local arm already does. The cursor means "the last message I have SEEN in this channel", and a mentions read has seen only the mentions.
bugs.mechanism: read_delta has two arms. The --local arm guards the save with `if mentions_for.is_none()` and carries a long comment explaining exactly this failure. The remote arm saves on `if max_id > 0` with no mention guard at all, so the defect the local arm documents is live in the path that talks to a server.
bugs.found_by: T107: the owner-side serve_read had to choose which of the two arms to copy
bugs.notes: serve_read (T107) deliberately reproduces the REMOTE behaviour, guard and all, because a forwarded verb and a fallback verb must not differ -- that difference would be observable as its own bug. So fixing this means fixing both arms together, and the comment at serve_read says so and points here.

bugs.title: The documented wake guard fires on the agent's own message when it quotes its own nick
bugs.reproduce: Arm the Posture A guard from chat/SKILL.md step 1, then send a message containing your own nick: chat-client-rs send --chan "#c" --text "I am @agent-a signing on"
bugs.observed: The guard matched the agent own stored line -- a line begins with its sender, and index($0, "@nick") does not care which -- so it returned immediately and the agent woke on its own voice with nothing to read. Reported happening on loki first send after arming.
bugs.expected: A wake means somebody else addressed me. An agent own line must not satisfy its own guard.
bugs.mechanism: The published guard filtered only on the mention text. Announcements routinely quote the sender own nick, so the very first send after arming matched.
bugs.fix: the guard gained a sender skip: awk -v mine="^:$NICK(-[0-9]+)?!" with $0 ~ mine {next}. The optional suffix covers a renamed second connection (B263), whose lines carry that name.
bugs.verification: Five cases measured through the shipped program: a peer mention fires (rc=0); the agent own line quoting its nick does not (rc=1); its SUFFIXED own line does not (rc=1); a line with no mention does not (rc=1); and a DIFFERENT nick that has the agent nick as a prefix (agent-alice vs agent-a) still fires (rc=0), which is the case a looser anchor would have broken.
bugs.found_by: loki, on the bus
bugs.notes: SUPERSEDED IN PART by B299: the sender skip is still right and still shipped, but this entry's guard was rewritten from awk to grep because the awk form contained a positional parameter the delivery path corrupts. The five-case verification was re-run against the grep form with identical results.

bugs.title: chat/SKILL.md claims the harness gives each subagent its own session id, and it does not
bugs.reproduce: Capture the identifying environment in a main agent and in a subagent it spawns, then diff: env | awk -F= "/CLAUDE|AI_AGENT/{print}" | sort
bugs.observed: Identical on every identifying variable. CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID, CLAUDE_PID, CLAUDE_JOB_DIR, CLAUDE_CODE_MESSAGING_SOCKET and CLAUDE_CODE_MESSAGING_TOKEN are all the same value in both, and ppid is 4876 in both. The only difference was CLAUDE_EFFORT, present in the parent and absent in the child, which is a setting rather than an identity and would not separate two subagents from each other. CLAUDE_CODE_AGENT read "claude" in a subagent whose type was code-researcher, so it does not carry the agent type either.
bugs.expected: Either the documented behaviour -- a distinct id per subagent -- or documentation that says the harness cannot distinguish them, since the whole session-key ladder is built on that claim.
bugs.mechanism: The doc records a measurement that no longer holds, or never did. resolve_session_keys harness rung hashes every set HARNESS_ID_VARS value together, so identical inputs give an identical key: a main agent and all of its subagents resolve to ONE session. That is why the chat client had to append the nick, and the nick is not a workaround but the only available answer.
bugs.found_by: measuring it while designing per-agent sessions for the editor, after Tschallacka said the claim was wrong
bugs.notes:
INVESTIGATION, at Tschallacka's request: can a subagent identify itself to the MCP some other way? Three routes, all measured closed on 2026-09-08.

1. A SUBAGENT SETTING AN ENV VAR THAT REACHES MCP CALLS -- no, structurally. The adapter is a long-lived process whose environment was captured at execve: /proc/5515/environ was fixed when it started, two hours and forty minutes before the test. A variable exported inside a bash tool call lives in that transient shell and dies with it; nothing pushes new environment into an already-running stdio child.

2. A SUBAGENT GETTING ITS OWN ADAPTER -- no. A subagent was made to call the editor MCP and then count adapters: it reported one, pid 5515, which is the same pid the parent session uses, parented to the claude process rather than to either agent. Polling from the parent across the whole window agreed, constant at one.

3. THE ADAPTER INFERRING WHO CALLS -- no. It is one process on one stdio stream, and in MCP the client is the harness, singular. The adapter reads method and params and there is no per-caller field to read; anything identifying a sub-agent would have to be placed in the tool ARGUMENTS by the model itself, which is the declaration we already have.

CAN IT REMEMBER A KEY A SUBAGENT SET? Technically yes -- it is long-lived and could hold state -- but it is unsound, and that matters more. With a parent and its subagents interleaving on one connection and no caller id, "remember the last session set" attributes every later call to whoever set it most recently. Interleaving is the normal case here, not an edge one: this session ran subagents in the background while editing throughout.

CONCLUSION: identity cannot be inferred, only declared. The nick in the chat client is therefore the general answer rather than a workaround, and the editor's equivalent already exists -- the session argument every MCP tool takes and the --session flag on the CLI. What is missing is that it is optional, so omitting it falls back to the shared harness rung silently.

bugs.verification: test-add-planning-bug.sh: the register does not exist until written and asking for it gives 66; first use creates it and the entry is read back rather than trusted from an exit code; a backslash and embedded quotes survive; six refusals each with their own code (73 duplicate, 64 bad id, 64 missing reproduction, 64 unknown severity, 64 status fixed, 66 missing plan, 65 damaged register) and the damaged file is left untouched; and the bug-report skill own render lists both entries. Building it turned up that jq handed an empty input never runs its filter, so the first version wrote a zero-byte register and reported success; the guard against that is now covered by a PATH seam rather than left as a known gap, because MAINTAINER.md step 3 asks for a test of the actionable-error path and a backstop with no test is a claim, not a guard.

bugs.title: verify-both-shells.sh executes a stray word, printing "been: command not found"
bugs.reproduce: Not yet isolated. Seen once in the run whose worktree base was 359e7ff: ./verify-both-shells.sh --keep printed the error between the worktree line and the bash 5.3 summary.

bugs.title: chat server.pl drop_client deletes from the hash %_ instead of %NICK and %INBUF, so per-connection state is never freed
bugs.reproduce: perl -Mstrict -Mwarnings -e 'my (%NICK,%INBUF); $NICK{q(s1)}=q(n); $INBUF{q(s1)}=q(b); my $s=q(s1); delete $_{$s} for (\%NICK, \%INBUF); print join(q(,), keys %NICK), q(|), join(q(,), keys %INBUF), qq(\n);'
bugs.observed: Prints s1|s1 - both keys survive. Replacing the statement with 'delete $_->{$s} for (...)' prints | with both hashes empty. Perl emits no warning or error for the original form.
bugs.expected: Closing a connection frees that connection's %NICK and %INBUF entries, so a long-lived perl-tier server does not grow with every connection served.
bugs.mechanism: chat/runtime/server.pl:94 reads: delete the element keyed by the socket from a bare hash, for each of two hashrefs. The loop aliases the topic variable to each hashref, but the element syntax used means an element of the hash named by the punctuation variable, not a dereference of the topic variable. It therefore deletes from an unrelated and empty global hash. use strict does not catch this because that punctuation hash is exempt from strict vars, and use warnings is silent. The arrow dereference form is correct. Result: both hashes retain one entry per connection for the life of the process.
bugs.fix: drop_client deletes through the arrow dereference $_->{$s} instead of the punctuation hash %_

bugs.title: the duplication ratchet counts inline table parsers in comments, not only in code
bugs.reproduce: Add a shell comment containing the literal text of the pattern the ratchet counts, then run planning/tests/test-duplication-ratchet.sh
bugs.observed: A new helper written specifically to avoid an inline pipe-splitting parser failed the ratchet at 16 against a cap of 15. The only occurrence in the file was the sentence explaining why the helper does not use one; no code in it splits on the delimiter.
bugs.expected: The ratchet counts parsers, so a comment naming the pattern it forbids does not raise the count. Documenting a rule should not violate it.
bugs.mechanism: The count is a text match over the file rather than a match restricted to executable lines, so any occurrence raises it, comments included. The effect is perverse in exactly the case the ratchet is meant to reward: a contributor who replaces an inline parser with a helper and explains why is charged for the explanation.

Three instances now across three gates, and in every one the person was documenting the rule the gate enforces. The shared cause is that all three match file text rather than code; the shared cost is that the correct response looks like evasion, since the only way past is to describe the forbidden thing without naming it.

bugs.title: a library's local array leaks its type across the shellcheck source boundary, so any caller using the same variable name as a scalar is falsely flagged
bugs.reproduce: Write a script that sources planning/scripts/plan-document-lib.sh and assigns a plain string to a variable named 'out', then run shellcheck -x on it
bugs.observed: SC2178 'variable was used as an array but is now assigned a string' at the assignment and SC2128 'expanding an array without an index only gives the first element' at every expansion, in scripts whose own 'out' is a scalar and never an array. Three different agents hit it in one session on three unrelated files — a board renderer, a crypt test, and it is the same shape the editor is reporting live. No clobber can actually occur, because the library's copy is 'local' to its own function.
bugs.expected: A variable local to a library function does not type a same-named variable in a script that sources the library.
bugs.mechanism: shellcheck -x follows the source directive and merges the sourced file's inferred types into the caller's namespace; it does not model 'local' as scoping that inference. plan_hoist_plan_dir declares 'local out=()' and is reached through plan-document-lib.sh, which nearly every helper sources, so 'out' is effectively a reserved name repo-wide for anything that sources the library. The cost is not the warning but the response to it: the obvious fix is to rename the caller's variable, which is correct but arbitrary-looking, and a contributor who instead adds a shellcheck disable silences a rule that is load-bearing elsewhere.

(2) Path identity: the test asserts event.changed == vec![root.join("plan.md")] by exact equality, and std::env::temp_dir() on macOS is /var/folders/... which is a symlink to /private/var/folders/..., so any canonicalisation on the way through makes the two spellings differ on macOS while matching on Linux. Ruled out: timestamp granularity. The snapshot stores a content fingerprint alongside mtime and size, so a same-length 'one'->'two' edit is detectable whatever the filesystem does with mtime.

bugs.title: pre-push-check runs a crate's whole test suite once per changed file in it
bugs.reproduce: Change several files in one crate under src/ (this change touched 11 in src/todo), stage them, then ./pre-push-check.sh
bugs.observed: 'ok cargo fmt --check: todo' and 'ok cargo test: todo' printed 11 times — one pair per changed file in the crate, each a full cargo run.
bugs.expected: One fmt and one test run per crate the change touches, however many of its files moved.
bugs.mechanism: pre-push-check.sh:139-141 builds a pipe-separated seen-list and tests membership with case "\n$crates" in *"|$crate\n"*. The sentinel newline is on the WRONG side of each string: the haystack carries it before the first entry, the needle expects one after the crate name, and the accumulator never contains a newline after an entry. So the pattern cannot match for any crate and every file appends its crate again. The gate stays correct — it just repeats the work — but a failing crate is also reported once per file, which overstates the number of distinct failures. The idiom wants $crates| as the haystack and |$crate| as the needle.
bugs.verification: Read at the rebase against pre-push-check.sh:183-186 on master: the accumulator is `... done | LC_ALL=C sort -u` and the `case` membership test the entry's mechanism describes is not present anywhere in the file.
bugs.found_by: watching the gate's output while pushing the register binaries; read as literal strings with cat -A
bugs.notes: Filed on feature/ship-register-helpers as B109; master had already taken B109 for an unrelated defect, so it is renumbered to B120 at the rebase. Closed obsolete in the same step: the pipe-separated seen-list this entry describes no longer exists. pre-push-check.sh section 4 now builds the crate list with `| LC_ALL=C sort -u` and iterates that, so each crate is visited once however many of its files changed, and the broken membership pattern is gone rather than fixed. Kept as a record because the idiom is the reusable part: a pipe-separated seen-list needs $list| as the haystack and |$item| as the needle, and a sentinel on the wrong side of either string makes the test silently unmatchable.

bugs.title: test-rjq-active-references exempts a comment only at column zero
bugs.reproduce: add an INDENTED comment containing the bare word to any scanned file, e.g. "              # ... the older filter tool ..." inside a nix list, then run tests/test-rjq-active-references.sh
bugs.observed: the line is reported as an active reference and the gate exits 1, even though a comment cannot be a call site
bugs.expected: a comment is exempt wherever it sits, as the column-zero case already is
bugs.mechanism: The filter is awk on grep -n output, whose lines are path:lineno:content. Its exemption pattern is /(^|:)#/, which requires the hash IMMEDIATELY after the line-number colon. An indented comment puts whitespace between them, so the pattern misses and the line survives as an offender. The sibling pattern for slash-slash comments has the same shape and the same gap. Intent is clearly to exclude comment prose -- the header says the fixtures are "plan prose ... not call sites that execute" the tool -- so the indentation dependence is an accident of the regex, not a policy. Allowing optional whitespace, /(^|:)[[:space:]]*#/, closes it without weakening the gate: a comment is prose in shell, nix and rust alike, and an active reference cannot hide in one. Worked around for now by rewording the comment to avoid the bare word, which is contorted prose in service of a regex quirk and is the reason this is filed rather than left.

bugs.title: an exact_text query containing HTML entities returns a silent zero instead of noting the query looks escaped
bugs.reproduce: Over MCP, search a PHP or XML file with an exact_text query whose angle brackets are HTML-escaped, e.g. query '<dt class=' against a file containing '<dt class='.
bugs.observed: count 0, complete true - the same clean zero a genuinely absent string returns. Happened twice in one session, and the agent nearly concluded the text was not in the file.
bugs.expected: The zero result carries a note that the query contains HTML entities (< > & ") while the document contains their unescaped forms, so the query is probably escaped source rather than absent text. Reported as: 'partly my fault, but a mode that never matches < in a PHP/XML file could plausibly say so.'
bugs.mechanism: search answers a no-match with count 0 and no diagnostic; nothing inspects the query for a likely encoding mistake. Same underlying shape as B218 - a clean zero is indistinguishable from absence - but a different cause: B218 is a matcher limitation on newlines, this is an unremarked query-encoding mismatch.
bugs.fix: d616bd30 — unescaped_query_would_match() in ai-text-editor-server.rs re-runs the same matcher against the query with its HTML entities unescaped, and a zero result carries a note plus unescaped_query_matches only when that actually matches, so the note reports the count the caller would have got rather than a guess. exact_bytes and path_wildcard are excluded: neither has a document-encoding mismatch to diagnose.
bugs.verification: cargo test -p ai-text-editor --test cli_flow: a_zero_result_says_when_the_query_looks_html_escaped searches '<dt class=' against a file holding '<dt class=' and asserts count 0 with unescaped_query_matches 1 and the entity named in the note, then searches '<table id=' — genuinely absent — and asserts NO note is present. Mutation: drop the 'if hits == 0 { return None }' guard and the second assertion fails, which is the point: the diagnostic must not explain away a real absence.
bugs.found_by: sanitairkamer session driving the installed MCP editor on Magento PHP source, relayed by Michael 2026-09-07
bugs.notes: B218 is the peer with the same symptom and a different cause: there a clean zero hides a matcher limitation on newlines, here it hides a query-encoding mistake. Both argue that exact_text's no-match answer carries too little information to act on.

bugs.title: a departure is never relayed either, so a nick that left stays in every other client's nick list
bugs.reproduce: With a standard IRC client on the channel, connect a second client, then let it leave: chat-client-rs leave --chan '#ai-skills' --nick probe, or simply let a tail exit (--mention-exit does this on every mention).
bugs.observed: The departed nick remains in the other clients' nick lists indefinitely. Nothing on the wire tells them it went.
bugs.expected: A departing nick is announced to the channel: PART reaches the other members, and a connection that simply ends produces a QUIT for them, so a nick list reflects who is actually present.
bugs.mechanism: src/chat-server-rs/src/main.rs:788-797, the PART handler: it echoes PART to the PARTING connection (791) and removes the nick from hub.channels (792-795), but offers nothing to the other peers. The disconnect path (around 223) likewise retains the membership list without announcing a QUIT. Same omission as B244 and the same fix shape, using the PRIVMSG fanout at 866-876.
bugs.found_by: found while pinning B244, 2026-09-07
bugs.notes: B244 is the arrival half and the reported symptom; this one was found by reading the same handler region.

bugs.title: the client discards JOIN, PART and QUIT, so an agent on the bus cannot tell who else is present
bugs.reproduce: chat-client-rs tail --chan '#ai-skills' --nick watcher, then have a second nick join, part, or let a tail exit. Nothing is printed for any of it.
bugs.observed: Only channel messages appear. A tailing agent sees traffic from a nick without ever learning that the nick is there, and learns nothing when it goes. Asking 'is sanitairkamer listening right now?' is unanswerable from the bus.
bugs.expected: A tailing agent can see presence, so coordination through the channel can depend on it. Behind a flag rather than on by default: an agent parsing the stream today receives PRIVMSG lines only, and widening that silently would change what every existing reader sees. read --local should show them too, since the log is the same stream.
bugs.mechanism: src/chat-client-rs/src/main.rs:1613-1617 - the tail loop drops every message whose command is not PRIVMSG, before the mention filter runs. The server now relays membership correctly (B244, B245 fixed server-side, verified by a standard IRC client's nick list), so the information reaches the socket and the client throws it away.
bugs.fix: PR #74 b2729933 - tail --presence prints JOIN, PART and QUIT; opt-in so existing readers still receive PRIVMSG only
bugs.verification: Live: a --presence tail saw a peer's ':joiner!joiner@localhost JOIN #ai-skills' and its attributed ':joiner!joiner@localhost QUIT :connection closed', and saw only the message during a send. Unit: presence_is_off_unless_asked_for pins the default. Mutation: drop the o.presence branch and the tail shows nothing but PRIVMSG again.
bugs.found_by: noticed while confirming B244's fix was server-side only, 2026-09-07
bugs.notes:
CORRECTING THIS ENTRY'S OWN EXPECTATION, which was wrong when I filed it. It said 'read --local should show them too, since the log is the same stream'. It cannot: the channel log stores only MSG rows - Hub::append is the only writer and fetch() filters on f[0]=="MSG" - so presence is never persisted and a local read has no row to return. Presence is a live-stream capability, not a history one, and making it otherwise needs a log-format change plus ids, because local_read keys entirely off msg_line_id and an id-less line would be reprinted on every since-based poll. Found by a peer agent reading the storage path rather than trusting the entry; the fix is documented as live-only in chat/SKILL.md.

Two mechanism details worth keeping for anyone touching that filter: a QUIT carries NO channel parameter (the server relays it only to members of the channels the nick shared, so an unfiltered command is already scoped), and a JOIN arrives in TWO spellings - the channel in the trailing when echoed to the joining connection, in params[0] when relayed to others. A filter checking only params.first() drops a tail's view of its own join. B254 is the same family seen from the other side: presence aside, a plain send silently advances the read cursor past another nick's unread messages, so the bus loses messages to its own bookkeeping rather than to the filter.

bugs.title: send joins the channel it only wants to post to, so every short-lived call now flickers a join and a quit in the nick list
bugs.reproduce: With a standard IRC client watching #ai-skills against a server carrying the B244/B245 relay: chat-client-rs send --chan '#ai-skills' --nick x --text hi
bugs.observed: The nick appears and disappears for each call. Michael saw two '[quit] connection closed' lines at 15:11 from ordinary client activity. Before the relay landed this was invisible, so the churn is newly VISIBLE rather than newly caused.
bugs.expected: A post does not imply presence. send should not JOIN at all: the server's PRIVMSG handler never checks the SENDER's membership - it appends and relays, and Peer::offer gates on the RECIPIENT being joined - so the JOIN buys nothing and costs a join/quit pair per call. join_channel legitimately joins (it is seeding a cursor) but exits immediately, so it flickers too; it should either linger or not announce.
bugs.mechanism: src/chat-client-rs/src/main.rs: both join_channel() and the send path write 'JOIN <chan>' before their PRIVMSG/LASTID and then 'QUIT'. With membership now relayed (B244/B245) each pair reaches every other member. The sender-side JOIN was always unnecessary; nothing depended on it because nothing could see it.
bugs.fix: PR #74 b2729933 - send no longer writes JOIN; the PRIVMSG handler gates on the recipient's membership via Peer::offer, never the sender's
bugs.verification: Live: with a --presence tail attached, a send produced only the PRIVMSG line and no JOIN or QUIT for the sending nick. Mutation: restore the JOIN write and the same tail shows a join/quit pair per call.
bugs.found_by: Michael, from Konversation showing two quits from ordinary activity, 2026-09-07
bugs.notes: B255 is this fix's cost, and it is worth reading together with it: with the JOIN gone, an agent that only ever sends is now completely absent from the channel listing rather than flickering. The churn was noise, but it was evidence the agent existed. The answer is not to restore the JOIN - it is that an agent which participates should hold a mention tail, which makes it reachable and visible at once.

bugs.title: a ban-list query is treated as a mode change, so every join prints an operator error
bugs.reproduce: Join #ai-skills with a standard IRC client (Konversation). It sends MODE #ai-skills, then MODE #ai-skills b.
bugs.observed: [14:54] --> You have joined the channel #ai-skills. / [14:55] *** Channel modes: / [14:55] [Error] You need to be a channel operator in #ai-skills to do that. The first MODE is answered correctly with 324; the second gets 482.
bugs.expected: MODE #chan b is a QUERY for the ban list, not an attempt to set one - a mode CHANGE carries a + or - sign. The bus keeps no bans, so the answer is an empty list and its end-of-list numeric (368 for b, 349 for e, 347 for I). A routine join should print no error at all. An actual change (+b, -b) still refuses with 482, which is honest: there is no operator model here.
bugs.mechanism: src/chat-server-rs/src/main.rs MODE arm: the branch keys on params.len() > 1 and, for anything that is not a valid umode set on the caller's own nick, answers 482 whenever the target is a channel. It never distinguishes a sign-less list letter from a signed change, so the ban-list query a standard client sends immediately after JOIN lands in the refusal path.
bugs.fix: PR #74 - list_mode_query() separates a sign-less b/e/I query from a signed change, and empty_list_reply() answers each queried letter with its end-of-list numeric; a real +b/-b still refuses with 482
bugs.verification: mode_query_tests in chat-server-rs: a_signless_list_letter_is_a_query, a_signed_change_is_not_a_query, only_the_list_letters_are_answered, each_list_query_ends_with_its_own_numeric. Mutation: drop the !flags.starts_with(['+','-']) test and a_signed_change_is_not_a_query fails, because +b would then be answered as an empty list instead of refused - which is the dangerous direction, a client believing its ban was accepted.
bugs.found_by: Michael, from Konversation's join output on 2026-09-07

bugs.title: the server echoes a sender's own PRIVMSG back, so a standard client shows every message twice
bugs.reproduce: Send a message from a standard IRC client (Konversation) joined to #ai-skills. Michael's paste shows each of his own lines rendered twice.
bugs.observed: Every message the sender writes appears twice in its own window: once rendered locally by the client, once received back from the server. Michael's own diagnosis, which is correct: 'probably once conquerer printing itself, and once the channel sending it'.
bugs.expected: RFC 1459 flow: a PRIVMSG is relayed to the OTHER members of the channel and never back to its sender, which renders its own line locally. So a sender sees one copy.
bugs.mechanism: src/chat-server-rs/src/main.rs PRIVMSG arm: w(st, &out) writes the serialized message back to the sending connection before hub.relay(&chan, &out, idx) fans it out to the others. The echo is not incidental - src/chat-client-rs/src/main.rs's send path WAITS for it, matching on a line containing PRIVMSG, the channel and the text, and prints it as its success confirmation. So dropping the echo server-side without changing the client would make every send hang until timeout.
bugs.fix: PR #74 b2729933 - the server tells a sender nothing after a PRIVMSG; chat-client-rs send asks LASTID and reads the 999 that already answers it, then prints the line locally
bugs.verification: Live: send prints one line, a watcher tail receives one, no numeric on either side. An intermediate attempt that pushed an unsolicited 999 was rejected because Konversation rendered it as '[999] mdibbets #ai-skills 59' - trading a duplicate line for a stray one. Mutation: restore w(st, &out) in the PRIVMSG arm and a standard client shows every message twice again.
bugs.found_by: Michael, from Konversation showing his own messages twice, 2026-09-07
bugs.notes: Both sides must change together, which is why this is one entry rather than two: the server stops echoing, and chat-client-rs's send stops waiting for an echo and instead prints the line it constructed once the write succeeds (or confirms with a cheap round trip such as LASTID). Handing it to whoever holds chat-client-rs, since B246 and B247 are already there and a split fix would leave send hanging.

bugs.title: index advertises an action argument it never reads, so every call is a full rebuild
bugs.reproduce: Over MCP: index --file F --action <anything>, following the tool schema that advertises action.
bugs.observed: The argument is accepted and ignored; the call always performs a full rebuild. A caller selecting a cheaper action got the expensive one and a success answer.
bugs.expected: Refused by name if index has no action to select, or read if it does. An advertised argument that changes nothing is worse than an absent one, because a caller reads the schema as a contract.
bugs.mechanism: Same root as B237: the unknown-argument check was protocol-wide, so a key no index handler reads still passed. Unlike B250 and B251 the key is not read by any other verb either, which makes it a stale schema entry rather than a misrouted one - so the fix may be to remove it from the schema rather than to refuse it. Whoever closes this should decide which, and say so.
bugs.found_by: surfaced by B237's fix, editor-batch agent 2026-09-07

bugs.title: no client verb asks who is on a channel, though the server answers NAMES, WHO and LIST
bugs.reproduce: chat-client-rs --help: the verbs are discover, send, read, tail, join, leave, session. None asks for channel membership.

bugs.title: the mode a response reports is spelled differently from the mode the protocol accepts, so a caller cannot compare them
bugs.reproduce: ai-text-editor open -f FILE -M hex_view -p structured, and read the `mode` field of the answer.
bugs.observed: The answer says "HexView". The request said hex_view, --mode says hex_view, and the document_modes list in `capabilities` says hex_view. Three snake_case spellings in, one CamelCase spelling out.
bugs.expected: The mode a response reports is the same string the protocol accepts and advertises, so a caller can compare the mode it ASKED for against the mode it was GIVEN without knowing to translate. That comparison is the whole purpose of the field now that a mode is a per-tab property a caller chooses (B238) and every response names it.
bugs.mechanism: src/ai-text-editor/src/document.rs: `enum DocumentMode` derives Serialize with no rename, so serde emits the Rust variant names TextUtf8/RawBytes/HexView. The input side never went through serde - the server parsed --mode by hand and matched the snake_case names - so the two spellings were never compared in one place. Nothing on disk depends on the serialized form: the tab metadata stores the mode as format!("{mode:?}"), which is Debug, and nothing reads it back.
bugs.fix: serde(rename_all = "snake_case") on DocumentMode, so the wire spelling is the one the protocol already accepts and capabilities already advertises.
bugs.verification: cli_flow::a_second_file_opens_in_its_own_mode_not_the_servers asserts mode == "text_utf8" and "hex_view" and "raw_bytes" on the wire. Before the rename it failed with left String("TextUtf8") right String("text_utf8") - that failure is what found this. Landed in the B238 commit because B238 is not usable without it.
bugs.found_by: fixing B238, and forced by T99: the coordinator decision was that a response must name the tabs mode at verbosity level 1 so a caller knows which coordinate space it is in, which made the spelling mismatch load-bearing rather than cosmetic
bugs.notes: STATUS CORRECTED from fixed back to confirmed, by me, because I had closed it while its code sat on an unmerged branch. The fix is real and its verification stands (both are recorded on this entry) but it is on fix/editor-batch-b237-t99, tip bf33d117, which has not merged. Closing it while B237-B241 and B250-B253 - fixed by the SAME branch - were deliberately left open made the register answer "is it all fixed?" wrongly in both directions: three falsely closed, and no way to see the other eleven were complete but unmerged. bugs.title: a newly installed adapter's arguments are invisible to an already-running agent, and nothing says the schema is stale
bugs.reproduce: Install a build of ai-text-editor-mcp that adds an argument (tab_id and tab_path, T96/T97) while an agent session is connected. Then have that session address a tab by id.
bugs.observed: The agent keeps passing file on every call and never uses the shorthand, because the tool definitions it holds were fetched before the install and carry no tab_id or tab_path. Michael noticed exactly this - 'you're not using the tab shorthands' - while the answers coming back already carried tab_id. Passing one would be refused by the CLIENT against its cached schema, so the capability is unreachable rather than merely undiscovered.
bugs.expected: Either the agent learns the new schema without a restart, or something states plainly that the installed adapter is newer than the schema in hand. The uncomfortable half is that the responses advertise the handle - every answer carries tab_id - so an agent is invited to use an argument its own tool definition rejects.
bugs.mechanism: Not an editor defect: the installed adapter accepts both keys and describes them well (ADAPTER_ARGUMENTS plus the exhaustive adapter_argument match, from B237's binding). The gap is deployment - an MCP client fetches tools/list once per session, so a swap under a live session leaves the agent holding older definitions with no version to compare. It is the B217/B237 'advertised versus actual' family inverted: there the schema promised what the server ignored, here the server accepts what the schema never mentions.

bugs.title: holding a mention tail makes every later send from the same agent arrive under a suffixed nick, so one worker appears as two identities
bugs.reproduce: chat-client-rs tail --chan "#ai-skills" --nick worker --mentions --mention-exit --no-session (held as a background task, which is the posture B255 prescribes), then from the same agent: chat-client-rs send --chan "#ai-skills" --nick worker --text hello
bugs.observed: The message arrives attributed to worker-2. Observed live in #ai-skills: msgs 91-99 are from editor-batch-2 while the same agents tail holds editor-batch, so the channel log shows two identities for one worker and neither is obviously the same one. A reader following the thread cannot tell that the handoff at 94-96 and the tail that answers a mention are the same agent.
bugs.expected: One agent is one nick in the log. Either a send reuses the connection the tail already holds, or it registers under the same nick without the server having to rename it. Cosmetic in that mentions still reach the agent - the tail owns the real nick, so @worker wakes it - but it makes the channel unattributable, which is most of what the log is for.
bugs.mechanism:
src/chat-client-rs: `send` opens its own connection and registers its own nick rather than reusing a held one, so the server sees a second registration for a nick already in use and applies its collision suffix. The two paths are independent by design - send is a one-shot, tail is long-lived - and nothing coordinates the nick between them.

MEASURED from both sides, with a control sanitairkamer ran rather than inferred from one side: its msg 97 arrived as `sanitairkamer-2` while its tail held `sanitairkamer`; msg 100, sent with the tail DOWN and nothing else changed, arrived as plain `sanitairkamer`. So it is the held registration that causes the suffix, not anything about the send path itself.

Surfaced by B255s own remedy: before agents held tails there was never a first registration to collide with, so fixing write-only agents is what created this. Two agents hit it independently within minutes of adopting the posture.
bugs.found_by: following B255s prescribed posture during the editor batch, then reading my own messages back in the channel log and finding them under a nick I had not chosen
bugs.notes: B265 currently masks this one, and that decides the order: peers address the suffixed @N-2 nick, and only B265s substring matching delivers those to the tail holding N. Fixing B265 alone would break cross-agent addressing for every agent holding a tail. This entry lands first, or both land together.

bugs.title: two concurrent test-npm-package runs fight over one tarball in the repo root
bugs.reproduce: Run planning/tests/test-npm-package.sh twice at once from the same checkout, or once while any other process runs npm pack there.
bugs.observed: One run failed with 'gzip: stdin: unexpected end of file' followed by 'tar: Unexpected EOF in archive' and 'tar: Error is not recoverable: exiting now'. Re-running the same test alone on the same tree PASSes.
bugs.expected: The test isolates the artifact it builds, as it already isolates its scratch directory, so a concurrent run cannot corrupt it.
bugs.mechanism: planning/tests/test-npm-package.sh:11 takes a randomised scratch dir with mktemp -d, but :15 runs 'npm pack --silent' in the repository root, and npm names that tarball from the package name and version. Every concurrent run therefore writes and reads the SAME path. :13's EXIT trap then does 'rm -f $repo_root/$tarball', so a run that finishes first deletes the tarball a slower sibling is still reading, and a second pack overwrites one mid-read. Same family as B270 and B274: a test not isolated from other activity on the machine. It bites here because several agents share this checkout and run suites.
bugs.fix: planning/tests/test-npm-package.sh now packs with `npm pack --silent --pack-destination "$tmp"`, and every reference to the tarball path was updated from $repo_root/$tarball to $tmp/$tarball; cleanup no longer needs a separate rm for the repo-root copy since it lives inside the already-removed scratch dir. (fix/b286-npm-pack-scratch-dir, commit a721786)
bugs.verification: Two test-npm-package.sh runs launched at once both PASS (exit 0), and the repo root is left with no stray *.tgz afterward -- the original reproduction (concurrent runs fighting over one shared tarball path) no longer occurs.
bugs.found_by: nitpicker
bugs.notes: Cost beyond the noise: a tar EOF reads as a broken package rather than a broken test run, so the honest response is to go looking at packaging. The fix is small -- pack into the test own temp directory (npm pack --pack-destination "$tmp") so the artifact path is unique per run -- and it removes the shared path rather than adding a second lock. The note above about npm pack --pack-destination came from aiskills, appended here by mistake while filing the duplicate B287 -- it belongs on this entry anyway, so it stays rather than being moved. aiskills also measured the same failure three times independently: a tar EOF reads as a broken package rather than a broken test run, so the honest first response is to go looking at packaging. Second live occurrence, 2026-09-08 on feat/chat-mcp-and-session-keys at 3856ccc9: the same 'gzip: stdin: unexpected end of file' / 'tar: Unexpected EOF in archive' pair while verifying the test-chat.sh baseline row, and PASS on an immediate re-run of the identical tree. Two occurrences in one evening on one checkout with three agents on it, so the rate is not negligible - and both times the failure presents as a baseline problem rather than as a collision, which is the part that costs time. Physical evidence, 2026-09-08 00:43: tschallacka-ai-skills-2.0.0-alpha.1.tgz (19011609 bytes) left untracked in the repository root after the second collision - the survivor of two runs whose EXIT traps target one path. Two consequences beyond the flaky verdict: the artifact is not cleaned up at all when a trap deletes the sibling's file instead of its own, and it is not gitignored (git check-ignore reports no match; .gitignore carries no tgz rule), so it appears as untracked and a git add -A would commit 19 MB. A fix that packs into the randomised scratch dir removes both, and a *.tgz ignore rule is worth having regardless.

bugs.title: chat-client-rs cannot dial a bare IPv6 server address, so an IPv6 bus is unreachable even when discovered
bugs.observed: With the beacon carrying host ::1 the ladder returns ::1:<port> -- tcp_alive accepts it, because Rust's to_socket_addrs splits on the last colon -- and the connect then fails with "chat-client-rs: server name: invalid dns name", exit 70. A bracketed --server [::1]:<port> fails the same way.
bugs.expected: Either an IPv6 address is dialable end to end, or the client refuses it with a message naming IPv6 as the reason rather than reporting an invalid DNS name.
bugs.mechanism: server_host() (src/chat-client-rs/src/main.rs:584-586) takes the host by `server.split(:).next()`, which on an IPv6 literal yields the empty string (or "[" when bracketed). That is handed to ServerName::try_from for TLS SNI, which rejects it. The address never reaches a socket. Splitting on the LAST colon and stripping brackets, or parsing with SocketAddr, is what a v6-aware host extraction needs -- and an IP literal should use ServerName::IpAddress rather than a DNS name at all.
bugs.found_by: an adversarial review of the chat-server-rs announce change (PR #20)
bugs.notes: Not a regression: before the announce change an IPv6 bind advertised an IPv4 address it was not listening on, so an IPv6 bus was unreachable then too. The failure merely moved from "never found" to "found, then rejected at TLS". The server side now refuses to announce a bare IPv6 host and says why, naming this entry, so nothing advertises an address that cannot be used -- that is containment, not a fix. Filed against the client because that is where the extraction lives; src/chat-client-rs/ is being worked on separately for B116, so this is recorded rather than fixed here to avoid two workers in one file. Low priority: no known caller binds IPv6, and the workaround is to bind IPv4 or set CHAT_ANNOUNCE_HOST.

bugs.title: The MODE:/PACKAGE: marker leaks into --help on ~11 more scripts than B98 named
bugs.reproduce: Add a case "$help_out" in MODE:*|PACKAGE:*) note_fail ...; esac check to test-comment-format.sh's existing --help loop (right after the raw "# " comment check) and run it.

bugs.expected: Every shipped --help starts at the purpose line, none of them printing MODE: or PACKAGE: as literal help text.
bugs.mechanism: Same class as B98: a shared NR>1-only awk skip (or, for role-context.sh/supervision-frame.sh, whatever their own usage() does) treats the marker line as ordinary docblock prose once the shebang is skipped.
bugs.fix: All 11 named scripts fixed on fix/b306-help-mode-marker-sweep (built on fix/b98-help-mode-marker): each usage() awk (two variants: NR>1 and NR==1{next}) now also excludes a MODE:/PACKAGE: marker line, and register-rebuild.sh's sed range starts at line 3 instead of 2. bugs.verification: bash "$f" --help first line checked for all 11 files: none start with MODE:/PACKAGE:. bash -n and shellcheck --severity=warning clean on all 11. test-comment-format.sh PASSes with the new assertion in place, and was confirmed to fail when the guard was removed from bootstrap.sh (mutation test), then restored. test-npm-package.sh PASSes against the refreshed baseline.
